docs.title: Kargo Promotion Design
docs.text: Document Kargo Promotion Design Version 1.0 Status Foundation merged; awaiting Kargo control-plane health and UI-access validation Audience Platform engineers, application teams, and production change approvers Purpose Define a visibility-first Kargo rollout, then automated GitOps promotion of selected applications through dev, stage, prod. Last Updated July 2026

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: First make the release position of each onboarded application visible: which immutable artifact is known, and which of dev, stage, and prod has accepted it. Then progressively automate promotion for a small, explicitly approved set of applications. Kargo is the promotion orchestrator; ArgoCD remains the only reconciler/deployer.

docs.title: Current rollout checkpoint
docs.text: The prod-2 Kargo control plane, configuration repository, initial Project resources, Vault/VSO integration, and OIDC configuration are merged. The immediate work is operational validation: ArgoCD sync/health, Kargo Pod readiness, VSO destination-Secret readiness, ALB target health, and Google login. Until that checkpoint is recorded as successful, this design remains visibility-only and contains no Warehouse, Stage, Git credential, or promotion behavior.

docs.title: Kargo Model
docs.text:
Kargo object Platform use Project An application-domain/team boundary, such as de-v2. Kubernetes namespace RBAC applies per Project. Warehouse Discovers releasable immutable artifacts, normally ECR image digests and/or OCI Helm chart versions. Freight The immutable artifact collection discovered by a Warehouse. This is the promoted release identity. Stage One lifecycle position: dev, stage, or prod. PromotionTemplate The reviewed sequence that changes desired state, waits for ArgoCD, and runs validation.

Use immutable image digests for production. A mutable tag may help discovery but is not a sufficient production release identity.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Visibility Only
docs.text:
Start with two deliberately different candidates: a Temporal Cluster infrastructure Helm release and de-v2's Context Cluster application release. Model the parent Helm chart as the initial Freight signal for each. Context Cluster's shared component-image ECR repository is supporting release evidence in the first phase, not an independently selected Freight source. Create separate Kargo Projects, Warehouses, and dev/stage/prod Stages, then seed each Stage from the revision currently deployed in its Git branch so Kargo starts from a truthful baseline. See the Kargo Implementation Plan for the staged rollout and prerequisites.

Do not give Kargo Git write credentials or enable a PromotionTemplate that changes Git during this phase. Verify:

  1. Warehouse discovery sees the expected immutable artifact.
  2. The known Freight and its dev/stage/prod position agree with the Git/ArgoCD deployed state.
  3. Platform users can see the release train in the Kargo UI/CLI and access is limited by Project RBAC.
  4. Controller health, backup/restore, and Kargo observability work in the prod-hosted topology.

Kargo is not an automatic inventory of every historical ArgoCD deployment. Its view is authoritative for applications that are modeled as Warehouses/Stages and seeded with the current revision. Expand application coverage deliberately; fleet-wide visibility follows full onboarding.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Automated Promotion for an Allow-list
docs.text:
For an approved application, Kargo changes only the application's version reference in the target branch. It must not merge an entire source branch into the next environment.

Promotion Target branch Default completion check Warehouse → dev main Dev ArgoCD Application is healthy dev → stage release/stage Stage ArgoCD health plus progressively added smoke/CI checks stage → prod release/prod Prod ArgoCD health plus required production gates

The existing de-v2 workflows create broad PRs for main → release/stage and release/stage → release/prod. They must be disabled or scoped for an application once Kargo owns its promotion path; otherwise broad branch promotion and Kargo's narrow version promotion will race.

For the initial standard, Kargo creates narrow PRs to protected release branches and never auto-merges them. A Platform/SRE CODEOWNER approves after the configured validation and human-review evidence is attached. Kargo's Git and ArgoCD promotion steps support this GitOps handoff; see Kargo's ArgoCD integration and promotion-step reference.

docs.title: Rollout Gates
docs.text:
Grow checks slowly, but make each enabled gate explicit in the PromotionTemplate:

Rollout stage Required gates Visibility Artifact discovery, seeded baseline match, controller health First dev automation Git change allow-list and dev ArgoCD health First stage automation Dev evidence, stage ArgoCD health, smoke test and GitHub Actions where available First prod automation Stage evidence, prod ArgoCD health, smoke test, GitHub Actions, and required approval/change-control policy

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Rollback is an audited promotion of the last known-good immutable Freight into the affected environment's Git branch, followed by normal ArgoCD reconciliation. Do not force-push or rewrite release-branch history.

docs.title: Application-image discovery implementation follow-up
docs.text:
When the first shared-image-repository application is onboarded, update this document and Application Cluster CI/CD Standard with the implemented Kargo configuration:

  1. One image subscription per component in the application's shared ECR image repository.
  2. An anchored tag allow-regex that can select only that component's <component>-<version>-<short-sha> tags.
  3. The selected strategy and discovery limit, justified against registry load and release ordering.
  4. The relationship between component-image Freight and the parent Helm chart's SemVer release signal.

Do not turn these implementation details into an application-scaffolding open question: they are part of the Kargo rollout work and must be recorded with the first production configuration.

docs.title: Initial Decisions Still Needed
docs.text:
1. Record the exact ArgoCD Application names and GitOps paths for temporal-cluster-2 and Context Cluster in dev-1, stage-1, and prod-2.
  2. Decide whether dedicated Karpenter capacity is needed at initial installation or after measuring Kargo resource use.
  3. Confirm the Platform/SRE CODEOWNER team for manual stage/prod Kargo PR approval. Initial policy is no Kargo auto-merge.
  4. Convert the approved Temporal and Context smoke-gate descriptions into runnable commands/workflows before enabling Git mutation.

docs.title: Kargo Topology Decision
docs.text: Document Kargo Topology Decision Version 1.0 Status Accepted; foundation merged, awaiting prod-2 live validation Audience Platform engineers and application teams using GitOps promotion Purpose Record where Kargo runs and how it promotes across the independent dev, stage, and prod EKS clusters. Last Updated July 2026

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Run one logical Kargo control plane in the existing prod EKS cluster for the initial rollout. It hosts Kargo's API/UI and persistent promotion data. Run a controller agent in each cluster that has an independent ArgoCD control plane: dev, stage, and prod. Each agent is restricted to its own cluster and ArgoCD instance.

This is deliberately not three independent full Kargo installations. Separate control planes would fragment the Freight lineage, promotion history, RBAC, credentials, and release-train view that we need to manage one dev → stage → prod lifecycle.

The long-term preferred topology is a dedicated management EKS cluster if the platform gains that capability. The prod-hosted control plane is the accepted initial design because no management-cluster plan exists today and it avoids making a non-production cluster the authority for production promotion.

The control-plane and configuration AppProjects are intentionally separate. The control-plane project owns the Helm chart and its cluster-level installation resources. The protected configuration repository can manage Kargo CRs across future Project namespaces, but cannot create arbitrary Kubernetes resources or modify the Helm control plane.

docs.title: Why This Fits the Existing GitOps Model
docs.text:
Every standard GitOps repo has three protected desired-state branches:

Branch Cluster it represents main dev release/stage stage release/prod prod

The prod bootstrap already reads GitOps configuration from release/prod. Kargo does not deploy to clusters directly. It promotes an immutable application version by committing a small, application-specific desired-state change to the appropriate branch; ArgoCD then reconciles that branch into its own cluster.

GitHub GitOps branches                    Cluster-local reconciliation
main ──────────────► dev ArgoCD ─────────► dev EKS
release/stage ─────► stage ArgoCD ───────► stage EKS
release/prod ──────► prod ArgoCD ────────► prod EKS

                 ▲            ▲            ▲
                 │            │            │
          dev controller  stage controller  prod controller
                 └────────── Kargo control plane (prod) ──────────┘

Kargo's distributed controller model is designed for this pattern: one control plane with controllers sharded per ArgoCD control plane. See the Kargo architecture documentation.

docs.title: Consequences and Required Controls
docs.text:
Hosting Kargo in prod makes it a platform-critical service. The initial installation must include:

  • A dedicated namespace, resource requests/limits, a PodDisruptionBudget, monitoring, backups, and a tested restore/runbook.
  • NetworkPolicy and mTLS rules following the platform's standard GitOps security model.
  • Node affinity/tolerations prepared for future isolation. Add a dedicated Karpenter-provisioned node pool when capacity or blast-radius measurements justify it.
  • SSO/OIDC, TLS, and non-public access to the Kargo UI/API.
  • Separate least-privilege credentials for each controller's local ArgoCD/Kubernetes access. The central control plane must not have a multi-cluster administrator identity.

Kargo's availability affects release visibility and future promotion, but ArgoCD continues reconciling the already-committed desired state if Kargo is unavailable.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text: Alternative Decision Full Kargo installation in every environment Rejected. It creates three isolated release histories and promotion systems. Shared Kargo control plane in dev Not selected for the initial rollout. It puts a platform service that will control production promotion in a non-production cluster. One controller with administrator access to every EKS cluster Rejected. It creates an unnecessary multi-cluster blast radius. Dedicated management EKS cluster Preferred future topology, deferred because no such cluster is currently planned.

docs.title: Network Policy & mTLS
docs.text:
Document Network Policy & mTLS Conventions Version 1.0 Status Living Document Audience Anyone writing NetworkPolicy/CiliumNetworkPolicy/PeerAuthentication in k8s-security Purpose The exact pattern used cluster-wide, why it's shaped this way, and the gotchas that break silently. Last Updated November 2026

All of this lives in k8s-security, v1/objects/netpol/manifests/<namespace>/, deployed as a single ArgoCD app (apps/foundation/netsec/netpol in argocd-eks-stack) covering the whole tree. llm-gateway-1-ns-1 is the cleanest reference namespace to copy from.

docs.title: The Shape of Every Namespace
docs.text:
<namespace>/
  kustomization.yaml                      # resources: [ingress, egress, <optional PeerAuthentication>]
  <name>.strict-mtls.peerauthentication.yaml   # if mTLS is enforced here (see below)
  ingress/
    kustomization.yaml
    namespace-wide.default-deny.yaml      # always
    <workload>.netpol.yaml                # only if something calls in; k8s-native
    <workload>.ciliumnetpol.yaml          # same rule, Cilium form
  egress/
    kustomization.yaml
    namespace-wide.allow-required.yaml    # DNS + istiod, always
    namespace-wide.deny-missing-netpol-label.yaml   # catch-all
    <workload>.allow-required.yaml        # whatever this workload specifically needs

docs.title: Why Both NetworkPolicy and CiliumNetworkPolicy
docs.text:
The cluster's CNI is Cilium, so CiliumNetworkPolicy is what actually gets enforced with full fidelity (L3/L4 with named Cilium "entities" like kube-apiserver, world, cluster, host). Plain networking.k8s.io/v1 NetworkPolicy is added in addition, for two reasons: it's portable if the CNI ever changes, and some tooling/audits expect to see standard NetworkPolicy objects. Where both exist for the same rule, they should express the same intent — the Cilium one is just able to be more precise.

Not every namespace has both. Namespaces where the only need is kube-apiserver-entity-based ingress (which plain NetworkPolicy literally cannot express — the EKS control plane isn't a cluster pod, so there's no valid podSelector/namespaceSelector/ipBlock for it) go Cilium-only for that specific rule. Positive ingress from another pod in the mesh (e.g. the istio gateway) should still get both forms.

docs.title: Network-policy label convention
docs.text:
All new application policies use the dedicated label budybot.io/netpol: <component>. It is separate from application metadata and is the sole workload identity for NetworkPolicy/Cilium selectors. Render it on every actual Pod template, including WorkerDeployment templates and any Job with its own policy.

metadata:
  labels:
    budybot.io/netpol: file

Use that exact value in both selector forms:

# Kubernetes NetworkPolicy
podSelector:
  matchLabels:
    budybot.io/netpol: file

# CiliumNetworkPolicy
endpointSelector:
  matchLabels:
    "k8s:budybot.io/netpol": file

The plain app / k8s:app convention is legacy and remains only for existing policy pairs until they are migrated. Do not add new app-based selectors. Standard app.kubernetes.io/* labels remain useful metadata but never satisfy this dedicated network-policy identity.

k8s-security now delivers the BudyNetpolIdentity Gatekeeper template to dev, stage, and prod. For every new application namespace, add a namespace-scoped BudyNetpolIdentity constraint with enforcementAction: deny and an explicit allow-list of that namespace's component values. The template validates Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob, and Temporal WorkerDeployment Pod templates; it intentionally does not validate generated Pods after their controller has been admitted.

Add the constraint under k8s-security/v1/objects/opa-policy/manifests/additional-policy-by-ns/<namespace>/, add that folder to its kustomization.yaml, and use this shape:

apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: BudyNetpolIdentity
metadata:
  name: <namespace>-approved-netpol-identities
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  match:
    namespaces: [<namespace>]
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [apps]
        kinds: [Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet]
      - apiGroups: [batch]
        kinds: [Job, CronJob]
      - apiGroups: [temporal.io]
        kinds: [WorkerDeployment]
  parameters:
    allowedValues:
      - api
      - worker
      - migration

This is deliberately namespace-scoped: adding the reusable template does not alter admission for any existing production Pod or controller. The first constraint for a new namespace is the point at which denial begins, and its allow-list is part of the namespace security review.

This convention supports a deny-missing-network-policy-label catch-all: any application pod without budybot.io/netpol gets a blanket egress deny (cluster, world, host, remote-node, kube-apiserver, unmanaged, health, init — everything). Migrate that selector together with application policies and preserve legacy app handling until the namespace is fully migrated.

Gotcha: Helm-hook Jobs (cert-gen jobs run on install/upgrade, migration jobs) frequently do not carry the chart's pod-label override. Render the chart and inspect every Job/Pod-producing resource. Give each Job that needs traffic an approved budybot.io/netpol value and a narrow allow rule, or make a deliberate, reviewed exclusion for a bootstrap-only Job.

docs.title: Tenant Workload Network Profiles
docs.text:
Pods that a platform operator creates inside a tenant namespace (for example the sandbox pods of sandbox-operator-1, or Dynamo workers) do not get a per-namespace policy pair. Each kind of workload has a network profile: one CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, in k8s-security under v1/objects/rbac/cluster/manifests/<profile-dir>/, that selects pods by both:

  • the pod label budybot.io/netpol: <profile> (k8s:budybot.io/netpol in the Cilium selector), and
  • the namespace label platform.budy.ob1.ai/managed-by: user-org, which the user-org composition puts on tenant namespaces (ob1-uo-<org>-ns-2). A pod with the profile label anywhere else is not matched.

A pod in a tenant namespace without a profile label falls under the namespace's egress deny. The profile is the only egress the workload has; the policy lists it and denies the rest.

docs.title: Example: sandbox-coder-1
docs.text:
File: v1/objects/rbac/cluster/manifests/tenant-sandbox-netpol/sandbox-coder-1.allow-required.yaml (policy egress-tenant-sandbox-coder-1-allow-required).

Allowed egress Port Note kube-dns / coredns in kube-system 53 UDP and TCP The rule carries the DNS proxy rule (matchPattern: "*") that toFQDNs needs; it only lets the pod resolve names sts-service (ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-auth-1-ns-1) 15008 (HBONE) Token exchange. The inner port is 8080 npm-proxy-1 (ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-npm-proxy-1-ns-1) 15008 (HBONE) Inner port 4873 api.anthropic.com, platform.claude.com 443 By name (toFQDNs)

Explicitly denied (egressDeny, which wins over any allow added later in the namespace): the entities kube-apiserver, host and remote-node, and the instance metadata address 169.254.169.254/32. Ingress is denied by the namespace default deny; the operator reaches a sandbox through pods/exec, which does not use the pod network. There is no GitLab rule, because no GitLab proxy exists yet.

docs.title: Keeping the label reserved
docs.text:
The profile label grants egress, so Gatekeeper BudyNetpolReserved constraints (v1/objects/opa-policy/manifests/additional-policy-by-ns/reserved-netpol-identities.yaml) keep it out of ordinary workloads:

  • sandbox-coder-1-reserved-outside-tenant-namespaces: denied in every namespace that is not labelled managed-by: user-org.
  • sandbox-coder-1-reserved-to-sandbox-operator-1: inside tenant namespaces, only an object labelled app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: sandbox-operator-1 may use it. The check reads the label of the object under review, not the creator, so it guards against mistakes and copying; who may create pods is limited by RBAC and the operator's admission policy. The label is not inherited by pod templates, so a Deployment or Job needs it on the controller object itself.

A new profile adds its policy, its two reservation constraints, and its value in the allow-list rules of the destinations it calls.

docs.title: Ambient and destination-side port limits
docs.text:
Tenant namespaces and the operator namespace (ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-sandbox-1-ns-1, label istio.io/dataplane-mode: ambient in cloud-management v2/stacks/shared-infra/k8s/v1/namespaces.tf) are Istio ambient. A call from a tenant pod to an in-mesh service leaves the pod as HBONE to the destination pod's port 15008, so Cilium on the source cannot see the real port, and each destination service therefore needs two things:

  1. a Cilium ingress rule that admits the profile's pods on 15008, and
  2. an Istio AuthorizationPolicy with action: DENY that limits tenant callers to the one service port: rules.from.source.namespaces: ["ob1-uo-*"] with to.operation.notPorts: ["<port>"] (examples: sts-service-deny-tenant-other-ports, notPorts: ["8080"]; npm-proxy-1-deny-tenant-other-ports, notPorts: ["4873"]).

Use DENY with notPorts, not ALLOW: an ALLOW policy turns the destination into an allow-list and cuts every caller it does not name (see AGENTS.md, "Istio ambient", in k8s-security). Istio has no egress policy for ambient pods without a waypoint, so the source-side control stays in Cilium: keep each rule to exact destination endpoints and port 15008. The operator's own egress policy (sandbox-operator-1-egress-allow-required) follows the same rule: it names the kube-apiserver and the database, and no in-mesh service port.

docs.title: Using the kube-apiserver Entity
docs.text:
Controllers that watch/patch cluster resources (which is most operators) need egress to kube-apiserver. Admission/conversion/mutating webhooks need the reverse — ingress from kube-apiserver, since the API server calls the webhook synchronously. Cilium's dedicated kube-apiserver entity resolves the control plane's actual (and potentially rotating) address dynamically:

# egress: workload -> kube-apiserver
egress:
  - toEntities: [kube-apiserver]
    toPorts:
      - ports: [{port: "443", protocol: TCP}]

# ingress: kube-apiserver -> workload (e.g. an admission webhook)
ingress:
  - fromEntities: [kube-apiserver]
    toPorts:
      - ports: [{port: "<webhook port>", protocol: TCP}]

Never substitute a static CIDR block for this — the control plane's addressing isn't a stable target to hardcode, and the entity-based rule is both simpler and correct by construction.

docs.title: PeerAuthentication (mTLS)
docs.text:
Istio sidecar injection is on cluster-wide, but that alone doesn't enforce mTLS — it just makes it possible. Whether traffic is required to be mTLS is controlled per-namespace by a security.istio.io/v1 PeerAuthentication object:

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: <name>-1-strict-mtls
  namespace: ob1-tf-eks-<name>-ns-1
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

Every new application namespace must receive this STRICT policy. Istio sidecar injection is enabled by default, but injection alone does not enforce mTLS. Existing namespaces without an explicit policy are legacy state and must not be copied as a new-application baseline.

docs.title: The Webhook Exception
docs.text:
If anything outside the mesh calls the workload directly — the canonical case is kube-apiserver calling an admission/mutating/validating/conversion webhook — that caller has no Istio sidecar and no mTLS certificate. Under STRICT mode, that connection gets flatly rejected. Fix with a port-level exception, leaving the rest of the namespace STRICT:

spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
  portLevelMtls:
    "8000":              # the webhook's container port - MUST be a quoted string key
      mode: PERMISSIVE

The quoted-string key is not optional. Istio's API represents portLevelMtls as map<uint32, MutualTLS>; when this gets converted through YAML → JSON (which kustomize build/kubectl apply do), an unquoted integer key produces map[interface{}]interface{} internally, which fails JSON marshaling with an opaque json: unsupported type error. A quoted string key ("8000":) round-trips correctly. This is easy to get wrong from memory since some documentation examples show it unquoted — always verify with an actual kubectl kustomize/helm template build, not just YAML-lint.

docs.title: Project Whitelisting
docs.text: PeerAuthentication is a namespaced resource, so it needs the owning AppProject's namespaceResourceWhitelist to include {group: security.istio.io, kind: PeerAuthentication}. It rides on the same fnd-network-policy-acd-proj-1 project as NetworkPolicy/CiliumNetworkPolicy (see Repos & the App Model) — check it's actually listed there before assuming any namespace can just add one.

docs.title: PostgreSQL Database Provisioning
docs.text: Application PostgreSQL databases are provisioned through the shared PostgreSQL control plane, not as application Terraform database resources. The same database/role SQL must work against the dev/stage CloudNativePG service and the production RDS service.

docs.title: Environment model
docs.text:
Environment PostgreSQL host Provisioning contract dev CloudNativePG Shared bootstrap and grant jobs connect with the cluster superuser stage CloudNativePG Same job/configuration contract as dev prod RDS The same SQL jobs run using the RDS connection, IRSA, Secrets Manager runtime configuration, and RDS CA verification

Do not create a CNPG Database resource or a database-specific AWS resource for an application. That would couple the application to only one runtime.

docs.title: Standard databases
docs.text:
The standard three-role databases are listed, one per line, in the inventory ConfigMap manifests/postgres-cluster-1/jobs/standard-db-inventory-1.configmap.yaml (argocd-eks-stack, v2/apps/platform/dbsrv/postgres-objs). The apply Job loops over that list: it creates the <database>-admin-role, -user-role and -read-role group roles, grants them to the Vault admin user WITH ADMIN OPTION, and applies the standard schema and default privileges (objects the admin role creates are read-write for the user role and read-only for the read role). An application then needs only its Vault roles (below) and its own migration Job, run as the admin role.

Database Owner ob1-context-file-provider-db-1 context-cluster-1 (file provider) ob1-context-store-2-db-1 context-cluster-1 (context store) ob1-authz-manager-db-1 auth cluster (authz-manager-1) ob1-authz-db-1 auth cluster (OpenFGA) ob1-studio-artifacts-db-1 studio-services-cluster-1 ob1-pitcrew-db-1 pitcrew-cluster-1 ob1-dt-consulting-services-db-1 dt-consulting-services-1 ob1-mission-registry-db-1 dt-consulting-services-1 mission-registry-1 (the Mission registry; its own database so it can move to another cluster) ob1-gitjib-db-1 gitjib-cluster-1 ob1-gitjib-gitlab-db-1 gitjib-cluster-1 (GitLab) ob1-karkhana-db-1 karkhana-cluster-1 and the sandbox operator (one schema per service, see Shared database with per-schema roles) ob1-janus-db-1 janus-cluster-1 ob1-dt-manager-db-1 dt-manager-1 ob1-nainai-db-1 nainai-cluster-1

Hosts: postgres-cluster-1-rw.ob1-tf-eks-postgres-ns-1.svc.cluster.local in dev and stage (CloudNativePG); the RDS endpoint in prod (set per environment in GitOps values).

docs.title: Add one application database
docs.text:
Work in abb-gitops-repos/argocd-eks-stack/v2/apps/platform/dbsrv/postgres-objs. A new application database is a standard three-role database:

  1. Add the database name, on its own line, to databases.list in manifests/postgres-cluster-1/jobs/standard-db-inventory-1.configmap.yaml. This is the only required change: the bootstrap CronJob creates every missing inventory database, and the apply Job creates the three NOLOGIN group roles, grants them to ob1_pgo_postgres_vault_admin_user WITH ADMIN OPTION and applies standard-db-grants-1 (admin owns and creates, user reads and writes, read selects).
  2. Only if the database needs extensions or other one-time setup: add a <database>.sql entry to postgres-db-bootstrap-db-run-1.configmap.yaml; the bootstrap CronJob runs it after creating the database. Only if it needs privileges beyond the standard ones: add them to standard-db-custom-grants-1.configmap.yaml. Example: ob1-pitcrew-db-1.sql creates the meta and content schemas owned by the admin role (the migration role has no CREATE on the database, so it cannot create them), gives the user role DML on both, gives the read role SELECT on meta only, and sets default privileges FOR ROLE the admin so later migrations stay covered. That is how a console reads non-confidential data from the database while customer content stays unreadable to it.
  3. Run the bootstrap once through the approved operational workflow (the CronJob is intentionally suspended; create a one-off Job from it). The apply Job reruns on its own when the watched ConfigMaps change.
  4. Add the application's Vault roles (next section) and give the application a migration Job that runs as the admin role.

Databases created before the inventory existed (for example ob1-temporal-db, ob1-billingServices-db) are still wired by hand in postgres-db-bootstrap-db-run-1, postgres-db-grants-1, per-application <application>-db-grants-1 ConfigMaps and vault-postgres-db-grants-2. Do not add new databases that way.

docs.title: Shared database with per-schema roles
docs.text:
Use this when several services share one database but must not reach each other's data. The standard three roles are database-wide, so this pattern gives each service its own schema and its own roles instead. Worked example: ob1-karkhana-db-1, schema sandbox (karkhana-cluster-1 sandbox-manager-1 and the sandbox operator sandbox-operator-1).

The database is a standard inventory database (above), so it also gets the three standard roles; the standard user and read roles are deliberately given nothing in the service schema.

Role (<db> = ob1-karkhana-db-1) Used by Rights in schema sandbox <db>-admin-role the migration Job (Vault static credentials) owns the schema and what the migration creates <db>-sandbox-rw-role the manager, sandbox-manager-1 (Vault dynamic credentials) USAGE; default privileges for DML and sequences, which the migration then narrows to exact tables and columns <db>-sandbox-operator-rw-role the operator, sandbox-operator-1 (Vault dynamic credentials) USAGE only; no default table privileges; the migration grants exact tables and columns <db>-sandbox-ro-role reporting and the SQL exporter USAGE and SELECT (default privilege for new tables); no Vault role is defined for it in services.catalog.tf

Who does what:

  1. Platform job (argocd-eks-stack, standard-db-custom-grants-1.configmap.yaml, key ob1-karkhana-db-1.sql, run by the apply Job after the standard grants). It creates the three service roles as NOLOGIN group roles if missing, grants each CONNECT on the database and grants it to the Vault admin user WITH ADMIN OPTION. As the admin role it creates schema sandbox (IF NOT EXISTS, owned by the admin role), revokes PUBLIC, grants USAGE to the three roles, and sets the manager and read grants and the admin role's default privileges. Role names are built from current_database(). Re-running is safe.
  2. Owning service migration (karkhana-cluster-1, components/sandbox-manager-1/internal/store/migrations/00001_init.sql). It runs as the admin role. It first fails with an explicit error if <db>-sandbox-rw-role or <db>-sandbox-operator-rw-role does not exist ("apply the platform database grants ... before this migration"). It then creates the tables, revokes everything from the manager and operator roles and grants exactly the tables, columns and sequences each needs (for example the operator can update only named columns of the command and file tables, and nobody gets DELETE). The migration does not check the read role.
  3. Vault (vault-gitops, v2/stacks/vault-cluster-2/de-v2-services/v1/services.catalog.tf). pg.precreated_roles names the one role per service: readwrite = ["ob1-karkhana-db-1-sandbox-rw-role"] for karkhana_cluster_1_sandbox_manager_1, readwrite = ["ob1-karkhana-db-1-sandbox-operator-rw-role"] for sandbox_operator_1. The migration Job uses static_pg with ob1-karkhana-db-1-admin-role. A service never gets the database's standard user role, so it cannot reach another schema.

A new service in the same database adds its own schema and roles to the same <database>.sql block, never a grant on another service's schema, and its own precreated_roles entry. The platform job must have run before the service's migration, which fails otherwise.

docs.title: Vault database credentials
docs.text:
Work in abb-gitops-repos/vault-management-1/v2/stacks/vault-cluster-2/<group>/v1.

The shared pg_db module creates a vault_database_secret_backend_role and the matching read policy under db-eng-1/creds/<role>. Add the application's service entry to services.catalog.tf with a pg.precreated_roles map:

pg = {
  ttl_seconds = local.defaults.db_default_ttl_seconds
  precreated_roles = {
    readonly  = ["<database>-read-role"]
    readwrite = ["<database>-user-role"]
    admin     = ["<database>-admin-role"]
  }
}

The existing pg.module.tf fan-out instantiates one pg_db module for every requested suffix and attaches its policy to the exact Kubernetes-auth role. Use that route rather than hand-writing a duplicate Vault database role or policy. Application database users, including any explicitly static or dynamic consumer, are administered through the Vault database engine; never place a database password in application values or a ConfigMap.

The application chart renders generic VaultDynamicSecret resources. GitOps values provide the non-secret mount: db-eng-1, credential path, VaultAuth reference, destination Secret name, and renewal behavior. Give a migration Job its own admin credential only when it genuinely needs schema ownership; runtime workers should receive read, read/write, or admin membership according to their actual need.

docs.title: Security and validation
docs.text:
• Add database egress only for the approved PostgreSQL endpoint/port in k8s-security; do not make database egress a namespace baseline.
  • Keep application-facing database host, TLS, and destination-Secret values in GitOps profile values, not in application code or secret payloads.
  • Validate the full PostgreSQL Kustomize aggregate and the production profile overlays after editing the shared job.
  • Validate the affected Vault stack and confirm the generated dynamic role grants only the intended pre-created group role.
  • In dev, verify bootstrap, grant reconciliation, VaultDynamicSecret readiness, connection as each privilege level, denied access outside the intended role, and credential rotation. Verify the equivalent flow in stage and the RDS/TLS path in prod before declaring the application ready.

docs.title: Terraform module rule
docs.text: Prefer the existing catalog/module fan-out or direct resources in a purpose-named .tf file. Introduce a new custom module only when there are at least three present or planned uses. When three existing direct implementations are about to gain a fourth, introduce the shared module with Terraform moved blocks so resources are not recreated.

docs.title: Repos & the App Model
docs.text: Document Repos & the App Model Version 1.1 Status Living Document Audience Anyone writing or reviewing an app.yaml, an AppProject, or Terraform namespace changes Purpose Explain what each repo owns, the app.yaml schema, the AppProject access-control model, and naming conventions. Last Updated July 2026

docs.title: 1. The two ArgoCD application models
docs.text:
Product application clusters and shared infrastructure applications are intentionally separated.

Model GitOps repository Manifest shape Product applications de-v2, design-services, or execution-services A real ArgoCD Application with an OCI Helm source from ecr-1 plus the GitOps repo as the values source Shared infrastructure argocd-eks-stack A repository-specific app.yaml abstraction rendered by platform tooling

Product source repositories publish immutable images and OCI charts to ecr-1; promotion updates the pinned chart targetRevision in the appropriate group GitOps repo. Application security resources remain in k8s-security.

docs.title: argocd-eks-stack — shared infrastructure workloads
docs.text:
Repo: Budybot/ob1_mn_github_argocd_eks_stack, root v2/.

This is where shared cluster infrastructure is defined, one app.yaml per application, organized by tier:

v2/
  critical/sys/<app>/app.yaml          # cluster-critical addons (ArgoCD itself, ALB controller, Reloader)
  apps/foundation/<category>/<app>/    # Karpenter, KEDA, VPA, Goldilocks, netpol, RBAC, gateway/ingress...
  apps/platform/<category>/<app>/      # cert-manager, Vault, Kafka, Postgres, Redis, Temporal, service mesh...
  apps/observability/monit/<app>/      # Prometheus, Grafana, Loki...
  apps/goverance/policy/<app>/         # OPA/Gatekeeper
  env/<environment>/apps/...           # environment-specific overlays, mirrored path-for-path against apps/

An app.yaml is a custom, repo-specific abstraction — not a raw ArgoCD Application spec. Some external tooling (not in this repo) reads these files and generates the real ArgoCD Application/ApplicationSet objects. There are two types:

docs.title: type: helm
docs.text:
project: fnd-autoscaling-acd-proj-1

type: helm

destination:
  namespace: ob1-tf-eks-vpa-system-ns-1

helm:
  repoURL: 'https://kubernetes.github.io/autoscaler'
  chart: vertical-pod-autoscaler
  version: "~0.10.0"
  deployedReleaseName: vpa-1

values:
  - $values/v2/apps/foundation/auto-scale/vpa/values/base.values.yaml
  - $values/v2/apps/foundation/auto-scale/vpa/values/{{profile}}.values.yaml

syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: true
  syncOptions:
    - ServerSideApply=true
  • version is pinned with a ~ (patch-range) constraint — matches the chart version at the time the app was added, not floating on latest.
  • values is an ordered list of files that get layered (later files override earlier ones): always base.values.yaml first, then a profile-specific file. Each app also typically keeps an untouched default.values.yaml — a straight copy of the upstream chart's own values.yaml (via helm pull <chart> --version <x> --untar), kept purely for reference and never referenced by app.yaml.
  • deployedReleaseName fixes the Helm release name (and by extension resource name prefixes) so it doesn't depend on the ArgoCD Application name.

docs.title: type: git
docs.text:
project: pfm-cfg-sources-acd-proj-1

type: git

destination:
  namespace: ob1-tf-eks-reflector-ns-1

sources:
  - repoURL: https://github.com/Budybot/ob1_mn_github_argocd_eks_stack.git
    path: v2/apps/platform/cfg/reflector-sources/profiles/{{profile}}/manifests

Used for raw Kustomize/manifest-based apps (RBAC objects, ConfigMaps, ingress definitions, CRs). sources can list multiple repo/path pairs — ArgoCD merges their rendered output. This is how env/{{environment}}/apps/... overlays get combined with the base apps/... manifests without one Kustomize tree reaching across into the other (see §3).

docs.title: {{profile}} vs {{environment}}
docs.text:
These are two different template variables, resolved by the external tooling per deployed cluster:

  • {{profile}} — one of dev / stage / prod. A tier of configuration (resource sizing, replica counts, feature toggles).
  • {{environment}} — the specific cluster instance: dev-1, stage-1, prod-2 (see budy-cloud-management/v2/env/). Today each environment maps 1:1 to a profile, but the split exists so a future second dev-2 environment could reuse the dev profile while still getting its own environment-specific overrides (e.g. via env/dev-2/apps/.../manifests).

Most type: helm apps only layer base + {{profile}}. Apps that need genuine per-environment (not just per-profile) patching — e.g. the ingress hostnames, which differ per environment even within the same profile — use a full chain: common → profile → environment, each layer a real Kustomize overlay that can add/patch on top of the one below (see the reflector-sources app for a worked example: manifests/ → profiles/{dev,stage,prod}/manifests → env/{dev-1,stage-1,prod-2}/apps/.../manifests). Don't reach for the full three-layer chain unless you actually need per-environment (not just per-profile) divergence — it's more scaffolding than most apps need.

docs.title: Product application GitOps repositories
docs.text:
The group repositories contain real ArgoCD Application resources, normally under charts/apps/<application>/. A current de-v2 application uses:

spec:
  project: apps-de-v2-services-acd-proj-1
  sources:
    - repoURL: <ecr-1-account>.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/ob1-helm-chart-repo-v1
      chart: context-cluster-1-repo-1
      targetRevision: 0.2.40
      helm:
        valueFiles:
          - $values/charts/apps/context-cluster-1/base.values.yaml
    - repoURL: https://github.com/Budybot/ob1_mn_gh_de-v2_gitops_repo_1.git
      targetRevision: main
      ref: values

Profile Kustomizations append dev/stage/prod values. Environment overlays are used only where a specific environment differs from its profile.

docs.title: 2. argocd-critical-stack — the AppProjects
docs.text:
Repo: Budybot/ob1_mn_gh_argocd-critical-stack_repo_1, projects live under v2/env/_base/bootstrap/projects/<tier>/<name>.project.yaml.

Every app.yaml's project: field must name an AppProject defined here. A project is the access-control boundary — it decides, independent of what any individual app claims:

  • sourceRepos — which git/Helm repos this project's apps are even allowed to pull from.
  • destinations — which namespace an app under this project may deploy into (supports globs and negation, e.g. !kube-*).
  • clusterResourceWhitelist / namespaceResourceWhitelist — which resource kinds (by API group) are allowed. Cluster-scoped kinds (ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, CRDs...) are usually locked down separately from namespaced kinds.

Projects are organized by tier, matching argocd-eks-stack's own tiering (critical/, foundation/, platform/, observability/, governance/, applications/), and named {tier-prefix}-{logical-name}-acd-proj-1:

Prefix Tier fnd- Foundation (cluster addons, autoscaling, networking, RBAC, gateway) pfm- Platform (databases, messaging, service mesh, secrets, workflow orchestration) obs- Observability gov- Governance apps- Application-tier services

Before writing a new app.yaml, check whether an existing project already fits — reusing one is strongly preferred over minting a new project per app. When a new operator genuinely doesn't fit anywhere (e.g. it needs a namespace/resource-kind combination no existing project grants), extend an existing project's destinations/sourceRepos/namespaceResourceWhitelist rather than create a new one, unless the access pattern is genuinely orthogonal to every existing project's purpose.

Some projects have destinations for namespaces that don't exist yet, deliberately pre-staged (commented out) for a known future addition — check for these before assuming you need a brand-new project.

docs.title: 3. budy-cloud-management — namespaces (and everything else Terraform)
docs.text:
Repo: Budybot/ob1-budy-cloud-management. The relevant file for GitOps purposes is v2/stacks/shared-infra/k8s/v1/namespaces.tf, which defines every Kubernetes namespace in the cluster as a Terraform map entry:

goldilocks = {
  name = "ob1-tf-eks-goldilocks-ns-1"
  labels = {}
  annotations = {}
}

A namespace must exist here before any app.yaml can target it. This is also where namespace-level opt-in labels live — e.g. Goldilocks only watches namespaces carrying goldilocks.fairwinds.com/enabled: "true", and that label is set here, per-namespace, not in any Helm chart.

Namespace naming convention: ob1-tf-eks-<name>-ns-1.

docs.title: 4. k8s-security — everything that governs the namespace, not what's deployed in it
docs.text:
Repo: Budybot/ob1_mn_github_k8s-security_gitops_repo_1, root v1/objects/, split by concern:

Path Contains rbac/cluster/manifests/<ns>/ Cluster-scoped ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding objects — used when a workload's own Helm chart RBAC is either too broad (grants more than it should) or you disable it entirely (rbac.enabled: false) in favor of a hand-scoped role here. netpol/manifests/<ns>/{ingress,egress}/ NetworkPolicy and CiliumNetworkPolicy objects, plus namespace-scoped PeerAuthentication (mTLS). See Network Policy & mTLS. opa-policy/ Gatekeeper/OPA constraint templates and constraints. scrt/ Vault-related security objects.

Both rbac/cluster and netpol are deployed via a single app.yaml each in argocd-eks-stack (apps/foundation/rbac/cluster and apps/foundation/netsec/netpol) that points at this whole tree — adding a new namespace here means adding a new subdirectory and wiring it into the relevant top-level kustomization.yaml's resources: list, not creating a new ArgoCD app.

docs.title: Naming Conventions Quick Reference
docs.text: Thing Pattern Example Namespace ob1-tf-eks-<name>-ns-1 ob1-tf-eks-vpa-system-ns-1 AppProject {tier}-{name}-acd-proj-1 fnd-autoscaling-acd-proj-1 Helm release name <name>-1 vpa-1, goldilocks-1, reflector-1 ClusterRole / ClusterRoleBinding ob1-acd-eks-<name>-cr-1 / -crb-1 ob1-acd-eks-reflector-1-cr-1 Plain app pod label (for netpol selectors) <release>-1 or <release>-1-<component> for multi-component charts vpa-1-recommender, vpa-1-admission-controller

docs.title: Scaffolding an Application Repository
docs.text:
Document Application Repository Scaffolding Version 0.3 Status Draft — confirmed platform recipe; remaining owner decisions are linked Audience Engineers creating a new product/application repository and the platform reviewers who provision its dependencies Purpose Define the intended repository, Temporal, GitOps, Vault/VSO, and Kubernetes-security work for a self-contained app. Last Updated July 2026

This guide complements Adding a New Operator. That guide is for installing shared infrastructure. This guide is for a product application cluster: source code and application deployment resources owned together, usually a Go multi-module monorepo containing several Temporal workers.

It is a proposed platform recipe, grounded in the local Context Cluster and LLM Router implementations. Those references use an umbrella chart, separately deployable workers, Temporal worker versioning, and a stable Nexus contract.

docs.title: 1. Default architecture
docs.text:
Use one self-contained repository and one Kubernetes namespace for a bounded application domain. The normal shape is:

flowchart LR
    callers["Other Temporal callers"] --> nexus["Nexus endpoint"]
    nexus --> gateway["Entrypoint worker / gateway"]
    gateway --> componentA["Component worker A"]
    gateway --> componentB["Component worker B"]
    componentA --> deps["Vault-backed dependencies"]
    componentB --> deps
    git["Application repo"] --> image["Image and chart release"]
    image --> gitops["argocd-eks-stack"]
    gitops --> cluster["Application namespace"]
  • The entrypoint worker owns the only externally visible Nexus service, request validation, authorization boundary, and routing. It should stay thin: no component-specific business logic or persistent state. Other workers and sub-applications are internal to the cluster and are not independently accessible from outside it.
  • Each worker component owns a task queue, workflow/activity registrations, its own image, and its own dependency permissions. Internal routing is normally child workflows on the component task queues; use another Nexus endpoint only where the boundary crosses an independently owned service or Temporal namespace.
  • Keep a stable, typed/versioned external contract. Additive operations are preferred; breaking input/output changes require a new operation or version.
  • A simpler app with one worker does not need a gateway split. It still needs a named task queue, a service account, a deployment contract, secret access, and the GitOps/security work below.

This is a design convention, not a requirement to create microservices. Split a worker only for an independently deployed capability, different scaling/failure characteristics, materially different secret/RBAC needs, or a clear contract boundary.

docs.title: 2. Choose the ownership and names before creating files
docs.text:
Record these values in the app README and deployment values. Do not use one generic name for every component.

Concern Recommended value Example Application slug lowercase, hyphenated domain name context-cluster-1 Kubernetes namespace ob1-tf-eks-<app>-ns-1 ob1-tf-eks-context-cluster-1-ns-1 Helm release <app>-1 context-cluster-1 Temporal namespace one per application domain by default context-cluster-1 Entrypoint task queue <app>-gateway-tq or a deliberate equivalent context-gateway-tq Component task queue one queue per component context-file-tq Service account distinct per workload and privilege set <app>-gateway-sa-1 Vault role/policy bound to the VSO service account and namespace confirm exact naming

At design time, list each worker's inbound contract, task queue, dependencies, data stores, Vault paths, Kubernetes API access, and expected network peers. This becomes the source for the Vault policy, VSO resources, RBAC, and network policy.

docs.title: 3. Create the application repository
docs.text:
Create the GitHub repository in github-infra/v1/stacks/repos/repos-applications/<group>/v1. Select thinking-mode, muscle-memory-mode, or shared-apps. Add a standard repository to standard-repos-declare.tf; use a repo-specific <name>-repo.tf only when its settings differ. Import a legacy UI-created repository before apply. Reuse existing modules/direct resources; introduce a custom module only once there are at least three present or planned uses, migrating existing direct resources with moved blocks before the fourth use.

There is no canonical application source template yet. Start a new repository from scratch and select the GitHub Go .gitignore template for new application repositories. Do not copy Context Cluster history or application-specific configuration; use its layout and the common modules as a reference instead.

For the usual multi-worker app, start with this repository shape:

<app>/
  README.md                         # owners, architecture, local run, operational links
  docs/
    design/                         # HLD, ADRs, contracts, data/security decisions
    runbooks/                       # deploy, rollback, incident and secret-rotation notes
  shared/                           # contract/bootstrapping module only; no component business logic
  gateway/                          # Nexus entrypoint worker
  components/
    <component-a>/                   # independent Temporal worker
    <component-b>/                   # independent Temporal worker
  charts/
    <app>/                          # umbrella chart: shared Temporal/config resources
    gateway/
    <component-a>/
  configs/                          # non-secret ConfigMaps/capability manifests
  .github/workflows/                # CI, image/chart release, GitOps update
  Makefile

The Context Cluster reference is a Go multi-module monorepo (go.work, shared, gateway, and components/*) with an umbrella chart and independent subcharts. New applications should normally follow this Go shape and consume github.com/Budybot/ob1_tf_gh_budy-common-modules-1_repo_1/go/runtimeconfig and /go/worker at explicit versions. The local reference clone is under aa-budy-OB1-micro-services/shared-ref-packages/ob1_tf_gh_budy-common-modules-1_repo_1.

Minimum repository deliverables:

  1. An architecture README identifying the entrypoint, each worker, contracts, task queues, Temporal namespace, and data dependencies.
  2. Versioned contract definitions and compatibility tests for every Nexus-facing interface.
  3. Dockerfiles and Helm templates/values for every deployed component; no plaintext credentials or build tokens in the repo, image layers, cache, or chart values. Retrieve private modules using the organization GitHub App token passed as a BuildKit secret.
  4. CI that runs unit/workflow tests, static analysis, image build, and helm lint/helm template.
  5. Release automation that follows the Application Cluster CI/CD Standard: immutable image/module/chart versions, required approvals, and the controlled GitOps version update.

Follow Application Cluster CI/CD Standard for the required PR validation, component matrix, Changesets, approvals, image/module/chart tags, chart publication, and GitOps handoff.

docs.title: Current application CI variable contract
docs.text:
Use the Context Cluster workflows as the current reference:

Name Type Purpose GLOBAL_REFPACKAGE_APP_1_ID GitHub variable GitHub App client ID used to create a short-lived private-module token GLOBAL_REFPACKAGE_APP_1_PEM GitHub secret Private key for the reference-package GitHub App GLOBAL_GITOPS_APP_1_ID GitHub variable GitHub App client ID used for the application GitOps version-bump PR GLOBAL_GITOPS_APP_1_PEM GitHub secret Private key for the GitOps GitHub App AWS_ECR_1 GitHub variable Central ECR account ID AWS_REGION_MAIN GitHub variable ECR/AWS region GLOBAL_VAR_AWS_ECR_IMAGE_BUILDER_2_ROLE_1_ARN GitHub variable OIDC role used to publish images/charts GLOBAL_ECR_HELM_REPO_V1 GitHub variable Helm OCI root/prefix; the workflow appends the parent chart name to address the cluster's Helm ECR repository

Generate the private-module token with actions/create-github-app-token, map it to BuildKit secret github_token, and consume it only in RUN --mount=type=secret,id=github_token. Do not persist the token in an ARG, ENV, .netrc, .gitconfig, image layer, or exported build cache.

docs.title: Artifact layout
docs.text:
• Provision one container image ECR repository per application cluster.
  • Publish all component images into that repository with tags <component>-<version>-<short-sha>.
  • Provision exactly one Helm ECR repository per application cluster.
  • Publish only the parent/umbrella chart to that repository. Bundle subcharts as local dependencies; do not publish a Helm repository per subcomponent.
  • The release workflow uses GLOBAL_ECR_HELM_REPO_V1 as the root/prefix and appends the parent Chart.yaml name to reach the application's Helm repository path.

docs.title: 4. Design the Temporal deployment first
docs.text:
Before creating the cluster resources, decide and document:

  • Which worker is the Nexus entrypoint and the exact service/operation names it owns.
  • Whether components are reached by child workflow (default inside the application Temporal namespace) or by Nexus (cross-service/cross-namespace contract).
  • One task queue and one deployment/versioning unit per independently released worker.
  • Workflow IDs/idempotency keys, retry/timeout policy, and activity idempotency. All network/database/Kubernetes I/O belongs in activities, not workflow code.
  • A rollout and rollback policy. The reference applications use Temporal Worker Deployment Versioning with pinned executions so in-flight workflows finish on their starting build.

docs.title: Worker Deployment Versioning contract
docs.text:
For a Kubernetes-deployed Temporal worker, render a temporal.io/v1alpha1 WorkerDeployment with its connection reference, Temporal namespace, task queue/workload template, and rollout policy. The application supplies the deployment spec and its image/build input; the WorkerDeployment controller injects the authoritative runtime values.

Worker code must enable versioning only when TEMPORAL_WORKER_BUILD_ID is present, and use these controller-injected values directly:

  • TEMPORAL_WORKER_BUILD_ID as the Temporal Build ID;
  • TEMPORAL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME as the Temporal deployment name.

Do not substitute a chart-local BUILD_ID, derive a deployment name from the component name, or invent a second identity. A chart may use its image tag or appVersion as the WorkerDeployment build input, but the process must consume the controller-injected values at runtime. This keeps local development versioning-off when no controller injects TEMPORAL_WORKER_BUILD_ID, while ensuring deployed workers register with the exact controller/Temporal identity.

The application chart should own application-level Temporal CRs (for example, Temporal namespace, connection, Nexus endpoint, and WorkerDeployment) only after confirming that the target cluster has the relevant CRDs and that the app's AppProject permits them. Do not create a second endpoint for each internal component without a consumer-driven contract need.

docs.title: 5. Provision the platform dependencies in dependency order
docs.text:
The following is the confirmed end-to-end ownership flow. Exact file names should still be located from the current repository before editing because stacks evolve.

Order Owner/repository Change 1 github-infra Declare the application repository in the correct application-group stack; configure teams/protection/Actions settings and import any legacy UI resource before apply. 2 budy-cloud-management ECR stack Add exactly one container image ECR repository and one Helm ECR repository for the application cluster. All component images share the image repo with prefixed immutable tags; only the parent/umbrella chart is published to the Helm repo. 3 budy-cloud-management Kubernetes stack Create the application's dedicated Kubernetes namespace in v2/stacks/shared-infra/k8s/v1/namespaces.tf; add only required namespace labels. 4 Shared PostgreSQL control plane When the application needs PostgreSQL, add idempotent database/bootstrap, role/grant, and Vault-admin role-grant ConfigMaps to the shared job; do not create an application CNPG/AWS database resource. 5 vault-management-1 Add services to the correct catalog and create narrow policies/Kubernetes-auth roles bound to exact service accounts and the application namespace. Add pg.precreated_roles so Vault database-engine users receive only the required DB group role. 6 k8s-security Create RBAC, default-deny and positive network policy, Cilium policy, Istio PeerAuthentication, and other externally governed security policy. 7 Application repo Define workloads, ConfigMaps, Services, umbrella/subcharts, application Temporal resources, and generic VaultAuth/VSO templates. Vault roles, mounts, paths, and destination configuration must be values-driven. 8 argocd-critical-stack Reuse/extend the matching application AppProject under projects/applications/ so its GitOps repo, ECR chart source, namespace, and application resource kinds are allowed while security kinds remain separated. 9 Group application GitOps repo Add the ArgoCD Application, base/profile values, and pinned OCI chart revision to de-v2, design-services, execution-services, or shared-services as appropriate. 10 CI/CD and ArgoCD Render/lint every profile, reconcile in dev, run Nexus/security/dependency smoke tests, then promote by PR through stage and prod.

The namespace must exist before ArgoCD deploys anything into it. The AppProject must allow every application resource kind before ArgoCD can reconcile it. See Repos & the App Model for the current layering and AppProject rules.

docs.title: Numbered PR handoff
docs.text:
A new application/installation normally spans multiple repositories. Open and review those changes as a numbered change set in dependency order rather than presenting reviewers with unrelated PRs. Prefix each PR title with [app-onboard N/M], where N is its merge order and M is the number of required PRs (omit conditional entries such as PostgreSQL when they do not apply).

Use the table above as the default order: 1 GitHub repository, 2 ECR, 3 Kubernetes namespace, 4 PostgreSQL when needed, 5 Vault, 6 Kubernetes security, 7 application source, 8 AppProject when needed, and 9 application GitOps. The application-source PR may be prepared once its repository exists, but do not merge a dependent deployment PR ahead of the namespace, Vault/security, and published-chart prerequisites. The GitOps deployment PR is last because it pins an artifact that must already exist.

Every PR description must state:

  • Change set: N/M — <application> and the intended environment(s).
  • Prerequisites: #<PR links> and whether their Terraform, render, or release checks have passed.
  • Next approval: N+1/M — <repository> — <PR link or “not opened; create after <condition>”>.
  • Reviewer action: approve now or wait for <named check/PR/artifact>.
  • Rollback/hold point: the last merged PR that can safely remain without deploying a workload.

Update the prior PR’s Next approval line with the real link once the next PR is opened. This creates a reviewer-visible queue: approve one PR, wait for its checks and reconciliation, then approve exactly the named next PR. Keep release automation PRs (version-packages, chart-release, and GitOps chart bump) in the same format; their next step is the protected environment approval or GitOps PR specified by the CI/CD standard.

docs.title: 6. Vault and VSO: model access per workload
docs.text:
Use VSO to materialize the minimum secret data a workload needs into a Kubernetes Secret. VSO authenticates to Vault through a VaultAuth resource; for Kubernetes auth the service account used by VaultAuth must be in the consuming namespace. HashiCorp's VSO authentication documentation describes that namespace constraint, and its VSO overview describes the source-to-destination Secret reconciliation model.

Recommended access model:

  1. Define a dedicated VSO/VaultAuth identity in the application chart for each approved privilege boundary. Do not let every application pod authenticate to Vault directly unless that is an explicit platform decision.
  2. In Vault management, create a policy constrained to the exact KV paths or dynamic-credential roles required, and a Kubernetes auth role bound to that ServiceAccount and namespace. Never use a wildcard application namespace or broad KV mount policy as a shortcut.
  3. Template VaultAuth and the required VaultStaticSecret/VaultDynamicSecret in the application chart. Keep templates generic. Supply role, auth mount, secret-engine mount/path, destination Secret, refresh/rotation, and environment-specific values from the group application GitOps repository.
  4. Mount/reference only the destination Secret in the workload that needs it. Add exact destination Secret names to the Pod-template annotation secret.reloader.stakater.com/reload; add consumed ConfigMap names to configmap.reloader.stakater.com/reload. Reloader rolls the workload after VSO or configuration updates, preventing stale database credentials, environment values, and mounted content.
  5. Give migration/one-shot Jobs a separate service account and Vault role when their credentials or permissions differ from the long-running worker. The Context Cluster file reference uses this separation for its database migration Job and worker.

Do not put secret values in Git, ConfigMaps, Helm values, workflow inputs, logs, or Temporal search attributes. Keep Vault paths, destination Secret names, consuming workloads, and rotation/reload behavior in the app's operations documentation.

For PostgreSQL specifically, use the Vault database engine and VaultDynamicSecret, not static application passwords. Dev/stage use the CNPG-hosted shared PostgreSQL service and prod uses RDS, so create the database and its three group roles through the shared PostgreSQL bootstrap/grant jobs rather than through an application CNPG or AWS database resource. See PostgreSQL Database Provisioning for the exact cross-repository contract.

docs.title: VSO review checklist
docs.text:
• VaultAuth service account, Vault role, policy paths, and Kubernetes namespace exactly agree.
  • Every VaultStaticSecret/VaultDynamicSecret has an explicit destination Secret and an owning workload.
  • Every Deployment, StatefulSet, WorkerDeployment, and long-running Job that consumes a VSO Secret or non-hot-reloaded ConfigMap has the exact resource name in the appropriate Reloader Pod-template annotation.
  • PostgreSQL credentials are issued through the Vault database engine and VaultDynamicSecret; do not replace them with a static KV application password.
  • Pre-install/pre-upgrade Jobs that require generated credentials account for asynchronous VSO reconciliation (or are sequenced with an approved hook/readiness pattern).
  • The AppProject permits secrets.hashicorp.com resources.

docs.title: 7. Kubernetes roles and security
docs.text:
Most Temporal workers do not need Kubernetes API access. Give them no Kubernetes RBAC by default. When a component genuinely needs it (for example, a Kubernetes-resource component), declare the exact resource, verb, namespace/cluster scope, and reason in its design doc.

  • Prefer a namespaced Role/RoleBinding for one namespace. Use ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding only when the workload must access cluster-scoped resources or multiple namespaces.
  • Put hand-scoped cluster RBAC in k8s-security/v1/objects/rbac/cluster/manifests/<ns>/ and add it to the parent kustomization.yaml, as documented in Repos & the App Model.
  • Use a distinct ServiceAccount for each materially different privilege set. Do not reuse the VSO ServiceAccount as an application worker identity unless the platform explicitly approves it.
  • Start with default-deny ingress, DNS, Istio control-plane/mTLS, and approved Temporal egress. Add database, OTEL, Kubernetes API, external, and cross-namespace paths only for a documented need. Add STRICT PeerAuthentication for every new application namespace according to Network Policy & mTLS. Every deployed pod needs the dedicated budybot.io/netpol label used by those policies.
  • Set a distinct, stable budybot.io/netpol: <component> label on every component Pod template, including worker deployments and Jobs with their own traffic policy. Standard app.kubernetes.io/* labels and the legacy plain app label do not replace this selector. Use the exact same value in the matching NetworkPolicy and Cilium k8s:budybot.io/netpol selector. Add the namespace's deny-mode BudyNetpolIdentity allow-list constraint in k8s-security before onboarding the namespace; it is the admission control for this standard.
  • If a Kubernetes API caller or other non-mesh client must reach an app webhook, add only the required port-level mTLS exception and test it.

docs.title: 8. Deploy through ArgoCD
docs.text:
Add the ArgoCD Application to the correct group GitOps repository: de-v2, design-services, execution-services, or shared-services for an application used by multiple groups. shared-services has the same application/profile Kustomize and human-approved promotion shape as the group release repositories. Application charts are published as OCI artifacts in the shared ecr-1 account. argocd-eks-stack remains the workload/configuration repo for shared infrastructure applications, not the canonical home for product application releases.

The app.yaml should:

  • use the application-tier AppProject (extend/reuse it rather than creating a broad new project);
  • target the Terraform-created namespace;
  • pin the application chart/image release—never latest;
  • layer base.values.yaml then {{profile}}.values.yaml, using environment overlays only for real per-environment differences;
  • enable automated reconcile only under the existing policy; and
  • include all non-secret configuration references required for the app to start.

The application AppProject must whitelist the application GitOps/chart source, destination namespace, and application-owned namespaced resource kinds such as Temporal and VSO CRDs. Allow cluster-scoped kinds only by explicit name; deny all other cluster-scoped resources. RBAC, network, Cilium, Istio, OPA, and other externally governed security policy reconcile through the security GitOps path and are denied from the application project. Render the final chart before opening the GitOps PR, then test ArgoCD health plus a Nexus call and each dependency path after reconcile.

docs.title: 9. Definition of done
docs.text:
An application is scaffolded when all of the following are true:

  • Repository, ownership, protections, CI, release automation, and runbooks exist.
  • The entrypoint/worker boundaries, task queues, Temporal namespace, and Nexus contract are documented and tested.
  • Namespace, AppProject, ArgoCD app, and profile values reconcile cleanly from Git.
  • Vault policy/role, VSO resources, and destination Secret consumers are least-privilege and tested without plaintext secrets in Git.
  • Kubernetes RBAC is absent unless justified, then least-privilege; netpol/mTLS rules permit only required paths.
  • Image/chart versions and Temporal worker build/version rollout are observable and have a tested rollback path.
  • Dev smoke tests include one external Nexus request (where applicable), worker/task-queue readiness, Secret/VSO readiness, and each protected dependency.
  • Apps listed in the GitOps repo's .github/kargo-managed-apps are promoted dev → stage → prod by their own Kargo release train with bake checks; any app not yet listed still uses bulk human approval. Enabling an app's train also needs its Project in the kargo.akuity.io/github-token-scopes annotation of kargo-github-app.vss.yaml (v1/objects/scrt/vso-secrets/infra-1/manifests/kargo-shared-resources-ns-1/ in ob1_mn_github_k8s-security_gitops_repo_1).

docs.title: GitOps Repository Guide
docs.text:
The platform is a chain of repositories rather than a single deployment repo. Use this section to find the source of truth for each concern before making a change.

Repository Owns New application change? New infrastructure app change? github-infra GitHub organizations, repositories, teams, and repository controls Yes Yes, if a repo is needed platform-actions Shared reusable GitHub Actions workflows and composite actions Consume for CI/CD No budy-cloud-management AWS resources, one image ECR repository per application cluster, EKS namespaces, and cloud infrastructure Yes Usually vault-management-1 Vault policies, auth roles, and secret-engine roles When secrets/credentials are needed When secrets/credentials are needed k8s-security RBAC, network policy, Cilium, Istio, OPA, and infrastructure VSO resources Yes Yes argocd-critical-stack ArgoCD AppProjects and bootstrap access boundaries Yes Yes argocd-eks-stack Shared infrastructure application definitions and configuration No product app release Yes de-v2 de-v2/thinking-mode application releases When classified here No design-services design/thinking-mode application releases When classified here No execution-services execution/muscle-memory application releases When classified here No shared-services shared application releases used by multiple groups When classified here No Application source repositories Go workers, charts, contracts, CI, images, and chart releases Yes Only for internally built infra apps

docs.title: Terraform module rule
docs.text: Use an existing module or direct resources in a purpose-named .tf file. Create a custom module only when the same abstraction is used at least three times. Do not add a one-use wrapper module merely for visual consistency.

docs.title: Application flow
docs.text:
github-infra
  → budy-cloud-management (ECR + namespace/AWS dependencies)
  → vault-management-1
  → k8s-security
  → argocd-critical-stack
  → application source release to ecr-1
  → de-v2 | design-services | execution-services | shared-services
  → ArgoCD reconcile and promotion

docs.title: Infrastructure application flow
docs.text:
upstream research
  → budy-cloud-management (namespace/AWS dependencies when needed)
  → vault-management-1 (when needed)
  → k8s-security
  → argocd-critical-stack
  → argocd-eks-stack
  → ArgoCD reconcile

docs.text:
Primary local references:

  • /Users/samaykohli/GitHub/aa-budy-OB1-micro-services/thinking-mode-services/aaa-de-v2/llm-router-1

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: An application source repository owns business code, Go modules, contracts, Docker builds, application Helm charts, CI, versioning, and publishing images/charts into the ecr-1 account. It owns application Temporal resources in its chart. It does not own AWS resources, Vault policy, Kubernetes security policy, or the ArgoCD application release.

docs.title: Standard cluster shape
docs.text:
go.work
shared/
components/gateway/ or entrypoint/
components/
charts/<application>/
charts/<component>/
configs/
docs/
.github/workflows/
Dockerfile

Only one entrypoint exposes the application Nexus contract. Internal Temporal workers/pods use private task queues and are not externally addressable. Keep I/O in activities, contracts versioned, and workflows deterministic/idempotent.

docs.title: Private Go modules
docs.text: Set GOPRIVATE/GONOSUMDB for the Budybot organization. Consume the versioned common modules go/runtimeconfig and go/worker. Generate a short-lived token with GLOBAL_REFPACKAGE_APP_1_ID and GLOBAL_REFPACKAGE_APP_1_PEM. Pass it to BuildKit as --mount=type=secret,id=github_token; use it only during dependency download/build and ensure it is absent from committed config, final layers, cache exports, and logs.

docs.title: Release responsibilities
docs.text:
Follow Application Cluster CI/CD Standard.

  1. Test/lint each Go module and render/lint the umbrella chart.
  2. Version components and build immutable component image tags.
  3. Push every component image to the cluster's single ECR image repository using <component>-<version>-<short-sha> tags. Publish only the parent/umbrella chart to the cluster's single Helm ECR repository; local subcharts are bundled dependencies.
  4. Open/trigger a PR that updates the pinned chart revision in the correct group GitOps repository.
  5. Keep rollback possible by retaining immutable prior chart/image versions.

Use the shared workflow library at Budybot/ob1_mn_github_platform-actions_repo_1 pinned to @v1 for Go validation, image builds, Go module tags, chart publication, and the GitOps chart-version PR. Keep the caller workflow responsible for event triggers, component catalog, Changesets, release classification, and protected-environment approvals. GitHub fetches reusable workflow YAML through the organization Actions access setting; use the REF PACKAGE App only for private Go dependencies and the GitOps App only for the GitOps PR.

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text:
The chart owns workloads, Services, ConfigMaps, application Temporal resources, and generic VaultAuth/VSO templates. Group GitOps values supply Vault roles, mounts, paths, destinations, and environment settings. RBAC, NetworkPolicy/Cilium, Istio, and OPA belong in k8s-security. Rendered names, labels, ports, ServiceAccounts, and Secret references form the cross-repository contract.

Put a distinct budybot.io/netpol: <component> label on every Pod template; new security policies select it as budybot.io/netpol/k8s:budybot.io/netpol, not through standard app.kubernetes.io/* labels or the legacy plain app label. The application onboarding PR must add every component/Job value to its namespace-scoped deny-mode BudyNetpolIdentity allow-list in k8s-security. Put Reloader annotations on the Pod template for every VSO destination Secret and every ConfigMap that the process cannot hot-reload:

metadata:
  labels:
    budybot.io/netpol: file
  annotations:
    secret.reloader.stakater.com/reload: file-db-credentials
    configmap.reloader.stakater.com/reload: file-config

Use comma-separated resource names for multiple dependencies. Do not annotate only parent workload metadata: Reloader must see the Pod-template annotation.

docs.title: Repository: argocd-critical-stack
docs.text: Local path: /Users/samaykohli/GitHub/abb-gitops-repos/argocd-critical-stack

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
This repository bootstraps ArgoCD and owns AppProjects—the source, destination, and resource-kind access boundary for every ArgoCD application.

Application projects live at:

v2/env/_base/bootstrap/projects/applications/

Current groups include de-v2 services/operators, design services, execution services, DT apps/success, operator services, and user-org apps.

docs.title: New application work
docs.text:
1. Select the existing project matching the application group.
  2. Add the group GitOps source repo and central ECR Helm registry only if absent.
  3. Add the dedicated application namespace to destinations.
  4. Permit the regular application-owned namespaced resource groups/kinds required by the rendered chart, including Temporal and VSO resources where applicable.
  5. Keep security resources out of the application project/chart; use the security deployment projects.
  6. Add a new AppProject only when the trust/source/destination boundary is genuinely different.
  7. Build the bootstrap Kustomization and verify the ArgoCD Application namespace is in sourceNamespaces.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• An AppProject is a security boundary, not organizational decoration.
  • Allow cluster-scoped resources only as individually named kinds; deny all other cluster-scoped resources.
  • For namespaced resources, allow regular application-owned kinds and explicitly deny resources governed by k8s-security, including RBAC, NetworkPolicy/Cilium policy, Istio policy, and OPA/Gatekeeper policy.
  • Existing broad whitelists are legacy evidence, not the template for new projects. Start from the application AppProject template when it is introduced; until then, enumerate the rendered chart's required kinds and review every expansion.

docs.title: Repository: argocd-eks-stack
docs.text: Local path: /Users/samaykohli/GitHub/abb-gitops-repos/argocd-eks-stack

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
This is the deployment/configuration repository for shared cluster infrastructure applications: foundation, platform, observability, governance, and related operators/tools. It is not the canonical release repository for product application clusters; those use the group application GitOps repositories.

The repo uses its custom app.yaml abstraction for Helm and Git sources, with base/profile/environment layering described in Repos & the App Model.

docs.title: New infrastructure app work
docs.text:
1. Research the upstream chart/repository, supported versions, CRDs, RBAC, hooks, ports, dependencies, and chart defaults.
  2. Add the infrastructure app under the correct v2/apps/<tier>/<category>/<app> path.
  3. Pin the chart version; keep unmodified upstream defaults for reference where that convention applies.
  4. Add base/profile values and environment overlays only when a true environment-specific difference exists.
  5. Coordinate namespace/AWS, Vault, security, and AppProject work in their owning repositories.
  6. Render all profiles and build every touched Kustomization before PR.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• Do not use this repo to bypass budy-cloud-management, vault-management-1, k8s-security, or AppProject ownership.
  • Do not embed security policy in an operator chart when it belongs in the security repo.
  • Do not apply manifests manually to compensate for a missing GitOps dependency.
  • The shared PostgreSQL bootstrap/role/grant jobs live here because they must work for CNPG in dev/stage and RDS in prod. Product applications add database SQL to that control plane; they do not create their own CNPG or AWS database resource. See PostgreSQL Database Provisioning.

docs.title: ECR and OCI Helm repositories
docs.text:
Path: v2/stacks/shared-infra/ecr/v1.

Each application cluster gets one container image repository in ecr-1. All subcomponents publish to that repository using component-prefixed immutable tags, for example gateway-0.2.3-a1b2c3d and file-provider-0.4.1-a1b2c3d.

Each application cluster also gets exactly one Helm ECR repository. It contains only the parent/umbrella application chart. Subcharts are bundled into the parent chart and do not receive their own ECR Helm repositories. GLOBAL_ECR_HELM_REPO_V1 supplies the common OCI root/prefix to CI; the workflow appends the parent chart name, which addresses the application cluster's Helm repository.

Reference application: Context Cluster uses:

  • image repo under ob1-ecr-repo-v2/...context-cluster-1...;
  • one Helm ECR repository addressed by the OCI root plus parent chart name context-cluster-1-repo-1;
  • GitHub source mapping to the application repository.
