  3. Add the dedicated Kubernetes namespace in the shared Kubernetes namespace stack.
  4. Add direct AWS resources or instantiate existing modules for any queues, databases, buckets, or roles.
  5. Create a custom module only when the abstraction has at least three uses.
  6. Validate from the touched Terraform stack and review cross-account policies.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• Do not create AWS resources from application source repositories.
  • Do not put workload credentials in Terraform values/state when a Vault integration exists.
  • Do not assume a scaffolded account is a promotion target.
  • Every application cluster uses one image repository with component tag prefixes.
  • Every application cluster has one Helm ECR repository containing only its parent chart; subcomponents do not get separate Helm repositories.

docs.title: New application work

docs.title: Application initialization
docs.text: There is no canonical application source template today. Create new Go application repositories from scratch with the GitHub Go .gitignore, and use Context Cluster/LLM Router as layout references without copying their history or application configuration. The current mandatory CI/CD variable and secret contract is documented in Application Cluster CI/CD Standard.

docs.title: Repository: k8s-security
docs.text: Local path: /Users/samaykohli/GitHub/abb-gitops-repos/k8s-security

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
This repository owns Kubernetes security resources separately from application and infrastructure charts:

  • cluster RBAC under v1/objects/rbac/cluster;
  • namespaced RBAC and security-owned ServiceAccounts under v1/objects/rbac/non-cluster;
  • NetworkPolicy, CiliumNetworkPolicy, and PeerAuthentication under v1/objects/netpol;
  • infrastructure/shared VSO secret resources under v1/objects/scrt/vso-secrets;
  • Gatekeeper/OPA policy under v1/objects/opa-policy.

Shared VaultAuthGlobal resources live in the Vault Secret Operator security area and are application-group scoped where appropriate.

docs.title: New application work
docs.text:
1. Create the namespace security folder in each required tree.
  2. Confirm the application chart's VSO identities and destination Secrets agree with externally governed RBAC and network policy; infrastructure VSO resources may still live here.
  3. Add no Kubernetes RBAC by default; introduce Role/RoleBinding or ClusterRole/Binding only for a documented API requirement.
  4. Add namespace default-deny ingress, baseline DNS/mesh/Temporal egress, app-specific ingress/egress, Cilium entities/FQDNs where needed, and STRICT PeerAuthentication.
  5. Ensure every selected pod has the expected budybot.io/netpol label and account for hook/migration Jobs. New NetworkPolicy/Cilium selectors use budybot.io/netpol/k8s:budybot.io/netpol; plain app is legacy only.
  6. Add a deny-mode BudyNetpolIdentity constraint under v1/objects/opa-policy/manifests/additional-policy-by-ns/<namespace>/. Match only that namespace and allow-list every component label, including Job/migration identities. The reusable template is delivered to all environment profiles; a namespace constraint is what activates enforcement.
  7. Wire every new folder into its parent Kustomization and build the full object tree.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• RBAC, NetworkPolicy/Cilium, Istio, and OPA do not belong in application charts. Application VaultAuth/VSO templates are the approved exception and must remain values-driven.
  • Match references against rendered application resources: ServiceAccounts, labels, Services, ports, and Secret names.
  • Start every namespace at least privilege: standard DNS, Istio control-plane/mTLS, and approved Temporal access are the baseline. Database, OTEL, Kubernetes API, external FQDN, cross-namespace, and other paths require an explicit need-based allow.
  • Require STRICT mTLS for every new application namespace because Istio sidecar injection is enabled by default. Use a narrowly scoped port-level exception only for a verified non-mesh caller, and test it.
  • Reject application charts that hard-code Vault roles, mounts, KV/database paths, or environment-specific VSO destinations instead of accepting them through GitOps values.

docs.title: Repository: platform-actions
docs.text: Local clone: /Users/samaykohli/GitHub/aa-budy-OB1-micro-services/shared-ref-packages/platform-actions_repo_1

docs.title: Status and ownership
docs.text:
Scaffolded. github-infra declares the private repository as ob1_mn_github_platform-actions_repo_1 in v1/stacks/repos/infra-repos/v1/standard-repos-declare.tf. Its companion Terraform resource sets the repository's GitHub Actions reusable-workflow access level to organization.

The remote was created through GitHub infrastructure and has a first reusable-workflow library. Continue managing repository settings through GitHub infrastructure rather than the GitHub UI.

docs.title: What belongs here
docs.text:
• Proven reusable workflows under .github/workflows/ with on: workflow_call.
  • Tested composite actions with action.yml when a reusable unit is step-level rather than job-level.
  • Versioned workflow release notes, contract tests, and minimal examples.

Keep application-specific event triggers, component catalogs, release metadata, deployment values, and application secrets in each caller repository. Keep the workflow library free of secrets: callers supply narrowly scoped permissions and secrets through workflow_call inputs/secrets.

docs.title: Access and authentication
docs.text:
Call a reusable workflow by immutable reference, for example:

jobs:
  validate:
    uses: Budybot/ob1_mn_github_platform-actions_repo_1/.github/workflows/validate-go-module.yml@v1
    permissions:
      contents: read

GitHub Actions supplies a scoped, short-lived token for the private reusable-workflow download when the repository is accessible to the organization. Do not use GLOBAL_REFPACKAGE_APP_1_ID or GLOBAL_REFPACKAGE_APP_1_PEM for this purpose; those remain for private Go dependency/source access. Add a separate GitHub App only when a workflow needs an explicit GitHub API capability beyond the caller's GITHUB_TOKEN, and scope its installation and permissions to that operation.

docs.title: Current workflow library
docs.text:
.github/workflows/
  validate-go-module.yml
  build-image.yml
  publish-go-module.yml
  publish-chart.yml
  gitops-update.yml
actions/
  detect-components/action.yml
  generate-chart-changelog/action.yml
  setup-private-go/action.yml
  validate-chart/action.yml
  verify-immutable-artifact/action.yml
docs/
  workflow-contracts.md

validate-go-module.yml accepts the REF PACKAGE App credentials only for private Go dependency resolution. build-image.yml uses caller-supplied AWS OIDC configuration and pushes only when push: true. publish-go-module.yml creates/verifies Go module tags, publish-chart.yml checks version == appVersion before OCI publication, and gitops-update.yml uses the separate GitOps App to create or update the chart-version PR.

The supporting composite actions are intentionally limited to stable step-level work: private Go setup, component detection, chart validation, immutable Git/ECR artifact verification, and chart-only diff changelog generation. The reusable Go validation workflow enables monorepo-safe caching by hashing all **/go.sum and **/go.work.sum files by default. Dependabot proposes weekly action dependency updates; review those PRs before merging.

Start by moving only behavior proven in two or three application repositories. Release the library with semver tags plus a moving major tag (v1). Callers pin to @v1 and receive compatible fixes automatically; a breaking contract change ships as a new major (v2) that callers adopt deliberately, and @v1.x.y is available when a caller must freeze. See Application Cluster CI/CD Standard for caller state-machine boundaries and workflow contracts for the library API.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: This Terraform repository owns Vault-side configuration: policies, Kubernetes authentication roles, KV access, database credential roles, JWT/PKI integrations, and related secret-engine permissions. Application charts may template Kubernetes VaultAuth/VSO resources, while the corresponding role/mount/path values are supplied by group GitOps values and must agree with this Terraform configuration.

docs.title: Application stacks
docs.text:
The current Vault cluster has group-oriented stacks such as:

v2/stacks/vault-cluster-2/
  de-v2-services/v1/
  design-services/v1/
  execution-services/v1/
  infra-services/v1/

The de-v2 stack uses services.catalog.tf as the service inventory. Modules derive Kubernetes auth and optional KV, PostgreSQL, Redis, or JWT policies. The Kubernetes auth role binds exact service_account_name and namespace values and aggregates only the selected policies.

docs.title: New application work
docs.text:
1. Identify each distinct workload/job identity and credential requirement.
  2. Add catalog entries to the correct application-group stack.
  3. Bind every Kubernetes auth role to the exact ServiceAccount and application namespace.
  4. Enable only required engines/roles and minimum capabilities.
  5. Separate migration/admin credentials from long-running worker credentials.
  6. Export/reference stable role and secret-engine names for the matching k8s-security resources.
  7. Run Terraform validation and inspect the plan for unintended policy expansion.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• Never bind * service accounts or application namespaces.
  • Do not combine unrelated applications into one policy.
  • PostgreSQL application credentials use the Vault database engine and VaultDynamicSecret; do not substitute a static KV application password. Map each consumer only to its pre-created read, user, or admin database role.
  • Changes in Vault and Kubernetes security must agree on role, audience, namespace, ServiceAccount, mount, and path.

docs.title: Micro-Services Index
docs.text:
This folder is the platform index for micro-services and service groups.

Each service or subsystem should keep a short info.md file in its folder. The file starts with YAML front matter for basic metadata, then ends with a compact index of child services, related docs, features, builds, and release candidates.

Use template/info.md when adding a new service or subsystem.

docs.title: Standard
docs.text:
• Use info.md as the canonical index file for every service and subsystem folder.
  • Treat a subsystem as a service node that can contain child service nodes.
  • Keep metadata short enough to scan in one screen.
  • Link every child service, related feature, build, release candidate, and GitHub repository directly from the relevant info.md.
  • Use status values consistently: active, deprecated, not-being-developed.
  • Use kind values consistently: platform, subsystem, service, library, operator, worker, contract, unknown.
  • Prefer unknown or tbd over leaving ownership, repo, or lifecycle fields ambiguous.
  • Keep detailed design, runbooks, API contracts, and CRDs in separate docs and link them from info.md.

docs.title: Root Subsystems
docs.text: Subsystem Description Status Index Thinking Mode Services Services for deliberate reasoning, planning, context synthesis, and higher-latency workflows. tbd thinking-mode-services.info.md Muscle Memory Mode Services Services for fast, repeated, operational, or learned execution workflows. tbd muscle-memory-mode-services.info.md Shared Services Cross-cutting platform services used by multiple subsystems. tbd shared-services Execution Mode Services Application clusters for DT worker deployments, tenant workflow code hosting, the Agent Success UI, the coding service and event ingestion. active execution-mode-services

docs.title: Info File Shape
docs.text:
Every info.md should follow this order:

  1. YAML front matter with stable metadata.
  2. A one-paragraph summary.
  3. A compact index table for child services or subsystem contents.
  4. Links to related features, builds, release candidates, and detailed docs.

For example:

---
name: Context Cluster
kind: service
description: Context orchestration service for Mark 2 workflows.
part_of_subsystem: thinking-mode-services
primary_owner: tbd
github_repo: tbd
status: not-being-developed
---

docs.title: Execution Mode Services
docs.text:
Five application clusters provisioned together in October 2026. Their source repositories are declared in the github-infra stack repos-applications/execution-mode/v1; their ECR/Helm repositories and Kubernetes namespaces are declared in budy-cloud-management; their namespaces are allowed in the ArgoCD apps-de-v2-services-acd-proj-1 project.

All five follow the repository standard in the wiki skill scaffold-nexus-cluster-repo (skills/scaffold-nexus-cluster-repo/SKILL.md at the wiki repository root): Go monorepos, the shared platform-actions@v1 entry workflows, a component catalog, umbrella plus sub-charts on the platform-app-cluster library (plus platform-capability in the gateway), shared Go modules from budy-common-modules, and an AGENTS.md carrying the platform context.

All five are the same Nexus type (owner decision, October 2026): each has at least one Nexus gateway and one worker component, every gateway authenticates callers the same way (STS bearer token verified over HTTP against the auth cluster's JWKS endpoint), and every repo has the capability registry with dynamic routing and discovery. They may also contain non-Nexus components; those are catalog entries like any other. What differs is the contract, the components and the extra components:

Cluster Components (proposed) Non-Nexus components (proposed) nainai-cluster-1 deployer (read-only stub verb built) none dt-consulting-services-1 engagement-manager-1 (built), delivery-lead-1, release-qa-1 (planned) console-1 (tenant console) karkhana-cluster-1 sandbox-manager-1 (built, not yet promoted to dev at the time of writing: sandbox requests and desired state; the sandboxes are run by sandbox-operator-1, released as its own chart) console-1 (tenant console, built as a shell) events-cluster-1 one per watcher type webhook-ingress (HTTP) janus-cluster-1 connection registry, Vault manager, publish (tuple writer), outbound policy, proposed November 2026 intake-1 (HTTP, from connections-1), outbound-gateway-1 (Envoy egress gateway), and its own Vault janus-vault-cluster-1 as a de-v2 Application studio-services-cluster-1 artifact-store-1 (implemented: docs and dashboards, versioning, sharing) artifact-web-1 (HTTP renderer for owners and shares) pitcrew-cluster-1 ticket-engine-1 (built, in review: tickets and their SOP-driven workflow) console-1 (operator console, system scope, in review), sql-exporter-1 (queue and time-limit metrics) gitjib-cluster-1 provisioning (groups, repos, registry scopes) wrapper charts for GitLab and the npm registry

janus-cluster-1 and studio-services-cluster-1 were provisioned afterwards, the same way and gateway-only first, from the same standard; janus-cluster-1's owner decisions of November 2026 are on its page and its component list is still a proposal, and studio-services-cluster-1 has since gained its components (see its own page).

karkhana-cluster-1 was added in November 2026, the same way and gateway-only first, from the same standard; it is not one of the original five, and its first component, sandbox-manager-1, is built and its operator is released (see its own page and Karkhana sandboxes).

nainai-cluster-1 is the reference instance of the standard and is built end to end; the other four are copied from it. Component lists for the other four are proposals drafted from their one-paragraph briefs, to be confirmed by the owner.

docs.title: Cross-cluster questions (open)
docs.text:
1. Who calls whom. The five briefs imply flows (gitjib → nainai packages; events → published workflows, now defined by the Mission registry; dt-consulting → Karkhana sandboxes and PR hosts) that are not written down anywhere in the wiki. Each service doc lists its assumed callers and callees as open questions; resolve them together so contracts line up.
  2. Overlap with the platform operator. budy-platform-operator-1 already reconciles BudyWorkerPool/BudyWorker per userOrg. Decide whether nainai-cluster-1 drives those CRDs, replaces part of that behaviour, or manages a different class of worker.
  3. Overlap with comms-gateway. The comms gateway already ingests channel webhooks (Slack, Gmail). Decide the boundary with events-cluster-1.
  4. Language for UI. Resolved for Pit Crew: the operator console is a React single-page app and a Node backend-for-frontend on @budybot/console-kit, as the platform console standard prescribes; the services behind it are Go.
  5. Glossary. "DT Dynamo Worker" does not appear in the wiki; add a glossary entry when defined.

docs.title: DT Consulting console
docs.text:
The tenant console of dt-consulting-services-1: one tenant's engagements, started and followed from the platform portal. It is built on the Platform Console Standard and is the first tenant-scope console that writes. The service-side design is docs/design/console.md in Budybot/dt-consulting-services-1_repo-1.

Status (November 2026): built, not yet deployed. Bring-up order and checks: docs/design/phase-0-test-plan.md in the service repository.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Lets a person, assuming a digital teammate of a tenant, start an engagement and watch it move through its stages, and lets a DT manager see the tenant's engagements, before any DT calls the cluster itself.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text: Component console-1 in dt-consulting-services-1_repo-1 (non-Nexus, Node component on @budybot/console-kit), chart off by default Scope Tenant scope only. Reads for any tenant session; writes need an editor session and, in engagement-manager-1, the active_digital_teammate tier Hosts dtcs.dev-1.orangebox.ai, dtcs.stage-1.orangebox.ai, dtcs.prod-2.orangebox.ai (wildcard DNS and certificate), OIDC-protected ALB ingress Sign-in Platform UI route dt-consulting-services-console-1, a nexusTarget route (endpoint ob1-nexus-dt-consulting-services-1-endpoint-1, service DTConsultingServiceV1), so the session's audience is the gateway's and one token serves the console and the gateway (the standard's nexusTarget audience case). The person picks the tenant, a target (the DT to act as) and a role Reads The engagement store, ob1-dt-consulting-services-db-1, as a Vault-issued member of its read role, every query filtered by the token's tenant: the standard's own-store exception to the pod-credential rule Writes startEngagement and closeEngagement through the gateway as the user, over Temporal's Nexus HTTP endpoint (no callback; outcomes read back from the store) Session key Vault KV v1/de-v2/ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-dt-consulting-services-1-ns-1/dt-consulting-services-1-console-1/session, key sessionSecret, synced by VSO Network Ingress from istio-gateway-1 on 3000; egress to sts-service 8080, the Temporal frontend 7243, Postgres 5432. docs.title: Differences from the nainai console
docs.text:
• Tenant scope, and it writes. console-kit serves reads only, so the two write routes are local to the component (same authentication, same-origin JSON only). A Nexus transport and write routes belong in console-kit once a second console needs them.
  • No Kubernetes access (no ClusterRole, no Argo cluster-resource whitelist entry).
  • Its data is in Postgres, so it holds database read credentials as well as the session key.

docs.title: DT Consulting Services: engagement flow (platform context)
docs.text:
Platform-level context for how dt-consulting-services-1 fits with the clusters around it. Service-internal design (workflows, workers, schemas, phases) lives in the service repository under docs/design/ (Budybot/dt-consulting-services-1_repo-1: engagements.md, console.md, phase-0-test-plan.md); this page holds what other clusters and readers need.

Status: draft (November 2026). Owner decisions are marked Decided. Phase 0.1 (engagement intake from the tenant console) is built and being brought up in dev-1; everything after it is designed, not built.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Dynamo worker A Temporal worker, one per DT workbench, that runs the DT's deterministic workflows. Workflows may contain prompts and call external and internal systems. Its source is one repository per digital teammate (DT) in GitLab (gitjib-cluster-1), created from a template; once an image built to the required spec (task queue, common modules) is pushed, the worker is deployed automatically by nainai-cluster-1. Engagement A PRD-style request from a DT to this cluster to add or change a Dynamo-worker workflow: outcome, context, audience, do's and don'ts, success criteria, references to existing resources. Nothing technical or implementation-specific. Live engagement An engagement that is not closed. Decided: a DT has at most one. Coding sandbox A Claude Code pod of sandbox type claude-coder-1, requested from Karkhana (KarkhanaServiceV1); there is no sandbox custom resource per sandbox, only the platform's SandboxType catalog entry. It writes the code; it has no general internet and installs packages only from the approved npm proxy. See Karkhana sandboxes.

docs.title: Actors and clusters
docs.text: Cluster Role in the flow DT workbench (one worker per DT) The caller, in the context of a conversation thread between the DT manager and the DT (the communication cluster attaches each conversation to a workbench thread). Later phases: the DT calls through skills and tools this cluster publishes as CRs. dt-consulting-services-1 Owns engagements: intake, state in its database ob1-dt-consulting-services-db-1, orchestration, the tenant console, and the outcome (a published, running workflow). gitjib-cluster-1 GitLab, the approved npm proxy and the platform's npm modules. Hosts each DT's worker repository; its CI builds and pushes the image on merge. Provisioning (groups, repositories, users) is gitjib's own provider. nainai-cluster-1 Deploys the Dynamo worker version; asked whether the new version is healthy. studio-services-cluster-1 Artifacts (documents, dashboards) an engagement can reference or render to. Its gateway is the authentication pattern this cluster follows. janus-cluster-1 Connections (for example Google Calendar, OAuth done) a workflow may use. context cluster People profiles and other context at known keys. dt-manager-1 (DT reviewer) Decided: the review gate for package approvals and code review. It decides or escalates to pitcrew. Until integrated, review steps auto-approve (dev only). pitcrew-cluster-1 Where DT reviewer escalates; not called by this cluster directly. karkhana-cluster-1 Runs the coding sandbox. delivery-lead-1 requests it through KarkhanaServiceV1 as the coder service role (svcrole-dtcs-coder-1, service user dtcs-coder-1), in the engagement's tenant. Capabilities used: requestSandbox, getSandbox, putFiles, runCommand, getCommand, pauseSandbox, resumeSandbox, deleteSandbox (see Karkhana sandboxes).

docs.title: Workers
docs.text:
Decided (November 2026): split by identity and permission boundary.

Worker Owns engagement-manager-1 Engagement record and lifecycle, one-live rule, the DT thread (questions, feedback), PRD to HLD research and feasibility, package requests. Built (phase 0.1: intake and lifecycle). delivery-lead-1 Planning, requesting the sandbox from Karkhana and putting the PRD and HLD into it with putFiles, supervising the coding agent (runCommand, getCommand), the compile and CI error loop, pause and resume with context in S3, opening the PR. release-qa-1 Review and merge, CI watch (image pushed), publishing the workflow's trigger, verifying the new worker version is healthy. console-1 The tenant console at dtcs.<env>.orangebox.ai (see Console). Built.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
DT (or the console) ─startEngagement─▶ gateway-1 ─▶ engagement-manager-1: record, start EngagementWorkflowV1
   discovery   PRD → HLD: research, approved packages, referenced resources; questions to the DT thread (awaitingFeedback)
   planning ── delivery-lead-1: requestSandbox + putFiles (PRD + HLD), Claude Code writes the code, PR in the DT's worker repo (gitjib)
   reviewing ─ release-qa-1: DT reviewer review, merge
   publishing  gitjib CI builds and pushes the image; nainai deploys; the workflow's trigger is registered
   verifying   the new worker version is healthy ─▶ done
DT ─closeEngagement─▶ closed at any stage; the lifecycle workflow cleans up (sandbox, branches, unpublished triggers)

Decided: done is the workflow published and the new worker version healthy, not the PR merged and not the image pushed.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text: Nexus service DTConsultingServiceV1 on ob1-nexus-dt-consulting-services-1-endpoint-1, the generic Execute and DescribeCapabilities. Component engagement-manager-1 capabilities: startEngagement, getEngagement, listEngagements, closeEngagement (built); provideFeedback (planned). The payload schemas are in the gateway's capability manifest; the typed payloads in the contract module. Callers need a tenant-scope STS session whose subject is a digital teammate of the tenant in an editor session (active_digital_teammate).

docs.title: Worked example (first target)
docs.text: A DT asks for a workflow that produces an office display board for a team of five or six: a shared calendar plus a light daily activity shown each morning. The engagement references an existing Studio artifact type to render to, people profiles in the context cluster at given keys, and an existing Janus connection to Google Calendar.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Decided: phases 1 to 3 build npm (TypeScript) workers only; Go later.
  • Decided: the coding sandbox installs only from the approved npm proxy and the platform's npm modules in gitjib; it has no general internet. Workers outside it may research on the internet.
  • Decided: phase 0 depends only on this cluster and gitjib: no DT reviewer, pitcrew or DT caller. The console drives it.
  • Decided: no user has cross-tenant access. The cluster's system roles assume a small set of bootstrapped GitLab user types (viewer, PR author, reviewer) per repository, each worker only the type it needs.
  • Authentication follows the platform gateway pattern (STS bearer token verified over HTTP); see the Studio services gateway.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phase Outcome 0 Console through the portal (ingress, STS handoff), database migrated, chart deployed to dev-1 0.1 From the console, as a DT: start an engagement, see it registered and started by its workflow, close it 1 Discovery (PRD to HLD, feasibility), auto-approved review steps 2 Delivery (sandbox from Karkhana, coding, pause and resume, PR) 3 Release (review and merge, CI, publish, verify: done) later DT skills and tools (CRs), DT reviewer and pitcrew integration, feedback over the DT thread, Go workers

docs.title: Open cross-cluster questions
docs.text:
1. Which gitjib operations this cluster needs (branch, merge request, repository read, CI status) and whether they are Nexus operations on GitjibHostingServiceV1.
  2. The sandbox contract is settled in Karkhana sandboxes: type claude-coder-1, network profile sandbox-coder-1 (npm through the approved proxy), pause and resume. Still open: GitLab access from a sandbox is not wired yet (no GitLab proxy in front of gitjib's token broker, no GitLab egress for the profile), so the git branch source (git {projectPath, branch} on requestSandbox) does not work yet; putFiles does. No end-to-end run on a cluster yet.
  3. How a workflow is given Studio artifacts, context keys and Janus connections, and who checks the DT may use them.
  4. The DT reviewer request and response contract for package approvals and code review.
  5. The thread reference a DT passes (workbench session or workflow id) and how the engagement manager posts to that thread.
  6. Which cluster registers a published workflow's trigger: proposed events-cluster-1 for all kinds (webhook, internal, email, schedule); see events-cluster-1 trigger model.

docs.title: dt-consulting-services-1
docs.text:
dt-consulting-services-1 separates coding from DT Workbench. A digital teammate submits an engagement, a PRD-like request to add or change a workflow of its Dynamo worker; the cluster researches and designs it, has the code written by a sandboxed coding agent, gets the PR reviewed and merged in the DT's worker repository, and sees the workflow through to published and running, with its own permissions and context.

Status: phase 0.1 built (November 2026), being brought up in dev-1. DTs submit engagements (PRD-style requests to add or change a Dynamo-worker workflow); see Engagement flow for the cross-cluster picture and Console for the tenant console. Service design: docs/design/ in the repository.

docs.title: Mission registry (mission-registry-1)
docs.text:
The platform's answer to "what is a published workflow?"

  • A publication is an act of publishing, recorded as pub_<ULID>: it publishes one workflow of a digital teammate's (DT's) Dynamo worker, at a commit, as its automation (the workflow the publication's triggers start), together with that workflow's tree (the workflows it calls and the activities they call) and its triggers. "Automation" is the role the workflow has in this publication, not a kind of workflow: any published workflow can be the automation of a publication. Publishing the same workflow again, at a new commit or with other triggers (a schedule and on demand), is a new publication that replaces the earlier one.
  • A mission is a grouping of a DT's publications, with metadata: today a name and a description, which say its theme (managing people, month-end close). It belongs to one DT of one tenant. The engagements that produced its publications are filed under it too.

The Mission registry holds the missions and is the publish-time ledger and orchestrator of publications. It records each publication and fans it out to the runtimes that keep a slice of it: Janus (connections and request rules), events-cluster (triggers) and nainai (the worker version). It is not a runtime dependency: nothing reads the registry while a workflow executes.

Status (November 2026): built, released together with release-qa-1 (switched off until it is tested). That covers missions, createPublication with the events and Janus steps of the saga, and the console's Mission registry area. Observing the worker version on nainai and retirement are not built yet. The design, decisions R1 to R18, and "how to move it" are in docs/design/mission-registry.md in Budybot/dt-consulting-services-1_repo-1. Bring-up and checks are in docs/design/mission-registry-test-plan.md.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
Component mission-registry-1 in dt-consulting-services-1_repo-1 Service A component of DTConsultingServiceV1 on ob1-nexus-dt-consulting-services-1-endpoint-1, with no separate Nexus service. Call Execute with {"component":"mission-registry-1","capability":...} Capabilities createMission and getMission: a DT names and describes a mission, and the registry mints its id (msn_<ULID>). Names are unique per DT. createPublication and getPublication: a Publication manifest and its source (repository, commit, path). It returns a publication (pub_<ULID>) and starts the publish saga Workflows MissionRegistryWorkflowV1 (entry) and PublishWorkflowV1, whose workflow id is the publication id. Every saga step passes that id to the runtimes as its idempotency key Database ob1-mission-registry-db-1, its own standard three-role database. Tables: mission, mission_request, publication (with mission_id), published_id (claimed ids) and step. Row-level security is on every table: the worker's role sees every row, and the read role sees only the rows of app.tenant_id Callers A DT in an editor session (for itself), and release-qa-1 (for a DT of its tenant). The dt-consulting-services console reads missions and publications directly through the read role, under row-level security for the session's tenant

Separability: the registry shares no code, table, role or identity with the rest of dt-consulting-services-1. To move it to another cluster, copy the component, its chart, its manifest and its contract file, then repoint the callers. The database stays as it is.

docs.title: Missions and engagements
docs.text:
1. A DT creates its missions in the console, or with createMission.
  2. Every engagement is opened under one of them: brief.missionId is required.
  3. When the engagement releases, release-qa-1 files each publication under the engagement's mission (metadata.mission). The builder never names one.
  4. The registry refuses a mission that is not an active mission of the publishing DT.

docs.title: The Publication manifest
docs.text: publication.yaml sits at the root of the DT worker repository. It holds one YAML document per publication, separated by --- as kubectl reads them. Each document is apiVersion: publication.budy/v1alpha1, kind: Publication, with exactly one automation. The coding agent writes it.

docs.title: Published ids
docs.text:
Temporal type names are the published ids (D18):

Prefix Is pwf_ a workflow type pact_ an activity type

Each is followed by a ULID (a 26-character Crockford base32 id that sorts by creation time). Whether a workflow is a publication's automation or a workflow it calls is decided by the publication, not by its id.

  • The builder mints them at build time. The registry validates them and claims each one for its tenant, DT and kind on first publication.
  • An id is claimed forever by its tenant, DT and kind: another DT, another tenant or another kind never uses it (D19). Reuse across DTs goes through npm and Go packages.
  • The same DT reuses its ids. A workflow or activity keeps its id when its code changes (the code is versioned in git and the worker is versioned in Temporal), and a later publication may use ids an earlier one used.
  • One live publication per id (v1). An id may sit in the tree of only one live publication of a DT at a time; the registry refuses a publication whose tree overlaps another live publication's, except the one it replaces. So a change to a workflow or activity changes exactly one publication's behaviour.
  • Open: shared trees. Letting two publications share a workflow or activity needs a check that a change to the shared piece is right for every publication using it (the research of the engagement making the change would have to find and review them). Until that exists, sharing is refused.

docs.title: The publish saga
docs.text:
record publication (pending → publishing)
  → Janus registerPublication, per automation   ⟲ retirePublication   (skipped when no connection is declared)
  → events-cluster registerTriggers (paused)    ⟲ removeTriggers
  → nainai: observe the worker version          (not built: recorded skipped; nainai is push-driven and never commanded)
  → events-cluster unpauseTriggers; record active

Failure: a step refused after its retries undoes the accepted steps in reverse order. The publication is then recorded failed with the refusing runtime's reason, which goes back to the DT as feedback.

docs.title: What each runtime receives
docs.text: Runtime Receives janus-cluster-1 registerPublication / retirePublication on publish-1: tenant, DT, the automation, its workflows, each activity's connection ids, and the worker's namespace and service account (D72) events-cluster-1 registerTriggers (paused), unpauseTriggers, removeTriggers: the automation's workflow type (its pwf_ id), its typed triggers (schedule, internal, webhook with its response mode, email) and the worker name. Events keeps the handles it issues; the registry records each trigger's id, kind and state and an email trigger's address, never a webhook URL or secret (a person reads those with Reveal in the events console) nainai-cluster-1 Nothing yet: a worker deploys when its image is pushed. Observing the worker version is a to-do

docs.title: Not built
docs.text:
• Retirement, and retiring the previous publication when a republish becomes active.
  • Reading the manifest from GitLab at the commit.
  • The pre-merge checks in the worker repository's CI (schema, ids that match the registered types, rules with tests).

docs.title: events-cluster-1
docs.text:
events-cluster-1 routes incoming webhooks to published workflows and watches supported external events through polling. New watcher types require an approved PR. Unsupported cases fall back to scheduled workflows.

Status: built, not deployed (November 2026). The repository's draft pull request carries the contract, admin-1, webhook-ingress-1 and console-1; see Trigger model for the open decisions. The design below and in the linked documents is a draft written from the owner's trigger model (see Trigger model); items marked Decided are owner decisions, the rest is proposal.

docs.title: Boundary (proposed)
docs.text: Owns Does not own Triggers of published workflows: registering them at publish time and starting the workflow when one fires (webhook, internal call, email, schedule) Authoring and publishing workflows (dt-consulting-services-1 and its mission registry; gitjib-cluster-1 hosts workflow code) Polling-based watchers for supported external event sources (later) Channel message ingestion owned by the comms gateway (Slack, Gmail); SMTP and the per-tenant mail subdomain (a teammate's address is <name>@<tenant subdomain>) The set of supported watcher types and the rule that a new type needs an approved PR Running the target workflows (the workers that execute them) The scheduled-workflow fallback for unsupported event sources

docs.title: Proposed shape
docs.text:
Repository type Nexus-first (gateway + components) plus a non-Nexus HTTP ingress component Components gateway-1 (Nexus), admin-1 (Temporal worker: registry, dispatch, schedules, email admission), webhook-ingress-1 (public HTTP), console-1 (tenant view); watchers later. See the HLD Where the capability registry fits Each watcher type is a capability: a manifest declares its config schema and task queue, so adding a watcher type is a component plus a manifest, and the approved-PR rule applies to exactly those files Fallback Unsupported sources are expressed as scheduled workflows rather than new code paths

The Nexus-gateway rules apply to the gateway and components; the HTTP ingress is a separate externally reachable, non-Nexus component and needs its own security review (see questions).

First pass (October 2026): the gateway only (gateway-1), like nainai-cluster-1; the components above are added one at a time afterwards, each as a catalog entry.

docs.title: Names (derived from the standard)
docs.text: Kubernetes namespace ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-events-1-ns-1 Nexus endpoint (control surface) ob1-nexus-events-cluster-1-endpoint-1 Nexus service (decided) EventsServiceV1 Gateway component, task queue gateway-1, events-cluster-1-gateway-1-tq Netpol label, Vault Transit role budybot.io/netpol: events-gateway-1, ob1_crossplane_vault_transit_events_gateway_1 Umbrella chart events-cluster-1-repo-1 Image repository ob1-ecr-repo-v2/ob1_tf_aws_ecr_events-cluster-1_repo-1 Helm repository ob1-helm-chart-repo-v1/events-cluster-1-repo-1

docs.title: Callers and callees (assumed, unconfirmed)
docs.text:
• Inbound: external systems calling webhooks; pollers calling external APIs.
  • Outbound: starts "published workflows" through the Dynamo worker's Nexus endpoint (or, for schedules, directly in the tenant Temporal namespace). It keeps its own slice of each publication, registered by the Mission registry of DT Consulting Services (the only registration caller); the registry is not read at trigger time.
  • Kubernetes: reads DynamoWorker resources (dynamoworkers.platform.budy.ob1.ai, read only, cluster-wide) when triggers are registered, to take the worker's status.nexusEndpoint and status.taskQueue. Nothing is read from Kubernetes when a trigger fires.

docs.title: Dynamo worker Nexus contract
docs.text:
events-cluster-1 is the only caller of a Dynamo worker's Nexus endpoint, and both worker bases (dynamo-worker-go_repo-1, dynamo-worker-ts_repo-1) serve the same contract. Its source is shared/contract in events-cluster-1_repo-1 (dynamo.go and dynamo-worker-nexus.schema.json); the bases vendor the schema with a $comment naming the source commit and test against it, so the two sides cannot drift.

Endpoint The worker's own, DynamoWorker.status.nexusEndpoint, read at registration and stored on the trigger Service DynamoWorkerV1 Operations One per workflow type the worker registers; the operation name is the workflow type (its pwf_ id). Every workflow is exposed: only a trigger registered here can reach one Input { "workflowId": "...", "input": <any JSON> }. The worker starts the workflow type named by the operation, on its own task queue, with that workflow id, and passes input as its single argument (none when absent or null) Workflow id Set by events: <workflowType>/<triggerId>/<deliveryId>, the same on every attempt of one delivery Duplicates A running workflow with the same id is attached to; a closed one fails the start with a Nexus Conflict error, which events counts as already started. A delivery never runs a workflow twice Output The workflow's result, delivered by Temporal's Nexus completion callback

docs.title: Responses to callers
docs.text:
Results come back through a callback, never through polling, and no workflow stays open while a long run goes on (design; events-cluster-1 HLD, "Responses").

  1. Dispatch starts the worker's operation over Temporal's Nexus HTTP API, with the URL of admin-1's callback service (events-admin-1-callback, port 3001) and a signed callback header naming the trigger and delivery. The endpoint's server-assigned id is read from its TemporalNexusEndpoint at registration and stored with the trigger, re-read only when a start reports it unknown.
  2. When the run closes, Temporal's History service posts the completion to that service. Events records it on the delivery (completed or workflow_failed) and keeps the result, encrypted, up to 256 KiB (getDelivery); a larger result keeps its size and hash.
  3. A webhook caller's answer is chosen per trigger at publish (webhook.response):
Mode The caller gets accepted 202 with the delivery id as soon as the call is admitted started (default) 200 with the delivery id and run id once the workflow has started; 503 if it could not start in time sync 200 with the workflow's result when it ends within syncTimeoutSeconds (default 20, at most 25); otherwise 202 with the delivery id async Future mode, not built: 202 with a job id and a status URL to poll

Posting a result to a caller-declared callback URL is a later round, with its own security review.

docs.title: Trigger handles
docs.text: Events issues a webhook's URL and secret and an email trigger's address, and keeps them: the URL token and the shared secret encrypted with a Transit key only admin-1 uses (ob1_tf_vault_events-cluster-1_handle_key_1), beside the hashes the ingress matches. A person (a tenant editor) reads them with Reveal and replaces them with Rotate in the events console (revealTriggerHandle, rotateTriggerSecret), after which the old ones keep working for 24 hours; every call is audited. Neither is a teammate tool, so a secret never enters a model's context. The mission registry never holds a URL or a secret: getPublication lists each trigger's id, kind and state, and an email trigger's address.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. ~~What is a published workflow?~~ Answered (November 2026): a workflow (pwf_<ULID>, its Temporal workflow type) that a publication in the Mission registry publishes as its automation, with its typed triggers. Its publish saga registers the triggers here through registerTriggers (paused), then unpauseTriggers; retirement calls removeTriggers. ~~The DT Nexus endpoint contract~~ Answered: the Dynamo worker Nexus contract below.
  2. Webhook identity and tenancy. How is each webhook source authenticated (signatures, per-tenant secrets) and mapped to a tenant? Which paths are public and how are they exposed (ingress, gateway, mesh policy)?
  3. Boundary with the comms gateway. The comms gateway already handles Slack and Gmail ingestion. Which sources belong here, and is there any overlap to retire?
  4. Watcher framework. The first watcher types, polling intervals and rate limits, checkpointing (cursor storage), de-duplication, and at-least-once versus exactly-once expectations.
  5. Approved-PR rule. How is "new watcher types need an approved PR" enforced (CODEOWNERS on the manifest and component directories, a required review)?
  6. Scheduled fallback. Where do scheduled workflows live and who owns the schedule definitions?
  7. Delivery guarantees. Retries, dead-letter handling, and replay for failed webhook deliveries.

docs.title: events-cluster-1: trigger model (platform context)
docs.text:
Cross-cluster context for how a published workflow gets started. Service-internal design (components, schemas, contracts) is in the repository under docs/ (Budybot/events-cluster-1_repo-1: prd.md, hld.md, trd.md, nexus-contracts.md). Keep the two in step: service design there, cross-cluster facts here.

Status (November 2026): built. The contract, admin-1, webhook-ingress-1 and console-1 are in events-cluster-1_repo-1. The Mission registry's publish saga calls registerTriggers (paused), unpauseTriggers and removeTriggers; it registers schedule triggers only so far, and the other kinds follow.

docs.title: Where it fits
docs.text:
A digital teammate (DT) asks dt-consulting-services-1 for a workflow. That cluster writes the code, adds it to the DT's Dynamo worker, and publishes it. Publishing means the workflow is live and can be started from outside its own worker. Triggers are how it gets started:

DT ─engagement─▶ dt-consulting-services-1 ─publish─▶ mission-registry-1 (saga, one publication = one workflow published with its triggers)
                                                      ├─ janus: register publication
                                                      ├─ events-cluster-1: register triggers (paused)
                                                      ├─ nainai: observe the worker version (push-driven; not built)
                                                      └─ events-cluster-1: unpause triggers
trigger fires ─▶ events-cluster-1 ─Nexus─▶ DT's Nexus endpoint ─▶ workflow in the DT's Temporal namespace

A digital teammate can have several Dynamo workers; each is reached through its own Nexus endpoint, which the DynamoWorker XRD creates and publishes in status.nexusEndpoint (with the worker's task queue in status.taskQueue). The Temporal namespace is per user org and shared by that org's workers. Starting a workflow needs three things: the endpoint, the workflow type (its published id, pwf_<ULID>, used as the Nexus operation name) and the input. When triggers are registered, events reads the worker's DynamoWorker (by user org, digital teammate and worker name; read-only cluster RBAC on dynamoworkers.platform.budy.ob1.ai) and stores its endpoint and task queue on each trigger; when a trigger fires it uses only the stored values. A worker whose DynamoWorker publishes no endpoint cannot be registered.

The worker side is the Dynamo worker Nexus contract (service DynamoWorkerV1, one operation per workflow type, input {workflowId, input}, workflow id <workflowType>/<triggerId>/<deliveryId> set by events), owned by events-cluster-1 shared/contract and vendored by both worker bases; see the service page. The result comes back through Temporal's Nexus completion callback to admin-1's callback service and is kept on the delivery. A webhook's caller gets accepted (202 at once), started (the default: once the workflow has started) or sync (the result within 25 seconds at most), chosen per trigger at publish; an async mode with polling is a future mode. The webhook's URL and secret stay with events, and a person reads them with Reveal in the events console (see the service page).

docs.title: Trigger kinds
docs.text:
Family Kind Exposure and protection On demand webhook Public URL with an unguessable token; protection none, shared secret or signature On demand internal Another platform workflow calls events-cluster-1 over Nexus; same-tenant only On demand email A unique address per trigger (two safe words and four digits, on the tenant's mail subdomain), with a required allowed-senders list. The comms router forwards mail it cannot resolve to a teammate to events, which decides silently Scheduled schedule A Temporal Schedule owned by events-cluster-1 and reconciled against the registered trigger to repair drift. Recommended home is the tenant's Temporal namespace, so it fires without Nexus and without events being up (pending a spike on Temporal rights) Later watcher Polling of supported external sources, each type an approved PR

Every webhook, internal and email delivery is checked against the workflow's declared input schema; rejections happen at the edge from a Redis copy of each trigger's admission data, so turned-away traffic never creates a workflow. Public webhooks are served at /v1/triggers/<token> on events.<env>.orangebox.ai (dev, stage) and events.budybot.ai (prod), through the Istio api-gateway. Schedules are different on purpose. A schedule that lives in the tenant namespace starts the workflow directly, so no per-delivery admission runs when it fires: its fixed input is validated against the schema at registration, and whether it may fire is enforced by pausing or deleting the schedule itself, which the registry does on pause, remove and publication retirement and which a reconcile loop (every minute) repairs, so a stale state can persist for up to about a minute. If per-fire checks and delivery history are needed, schedules can instead live in the events namespace and start the dispatch workflow (SCHEDULE_HOME). Every trigger belongs to one publication, tenant and DT, is registered paused and unpaused only once the worker version is healthy, and is removed when its publication is retired. Before starting a workflow, the cluster checks that the trigger is active and the publication live.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text: Boundary Rule communication cluster Owns Mailgun, the per-tenant subdomain and conversation email. The router forwards unresolved recipients to events (deliverEmail); events owns trigger addresses and allowed senders. Attachments are not kept by the inbound gateway today. dt-consulting-services-1 The only caller of registration. Owns publication state. DynamoWorker XRD (crossplane) Creates the per-worker Nexus endpoint (composed by the UserOrg) and publishes its name and the worker's task queue in status; events reads both at registration. nainai deploys the worker but does not create the endpoint. Dynamo worker bases Serve the Dynamo worker Nexus contract (DynamoWorkerV1) that events-cluster-1 shared/contract owns. Temporal (platform) Allows events' callback endpoint as a Nexus completion callback address, so History can post a workflow's result to events (as it already does for events' console). janus-cluster-1 Not involved at trigger time.

docs.title: Open cross-cluster questions
docs.text:
1. ~~The Nexus endpoint name format agreed with the XRD owner.~~ Built: the XRD creates ob1-nexus-dw-<userOrgId>-<digitalTeammateId>-<n>-endpoint-1 and publishes it in DynamoWorker.status.nexusEndpoint, which events reads at registration. Remaining: the existing events database.
  2. ~~The trigger schema inside the publish manifest (mission-registry M2).~~ Decided: typed triggers in the Publication manifest (ref, kind, schedule {cron, timezone, overlap, input, catchupWindow}), with the automation's inputSchema.
  3. The deliverEmail forwarding scope with the communication cluster owner.
  4. Live check: Nexus failure alone, or registry publication state as well.
  5. ALB OIDC exemption for /v1/* on the shared dev and stage host; WAF and mesh policy (separate security review).
  6. Posting a result to a caller-declared callback URL: its authentication and the security review of events' outbound POST (not in this round). The async response mode (job id and polling) is a future mode.

docs.title: gitjib-cluster-1
docs.text:
gitjib-cluster-1 hosts self-managed GitLab and a private npm registry. It supports tenant-private workflow repositories and platform-visible shared repositories, approved dependencies, versioned packages, forks, and PR-based contributions.

Status: active in dev. The repository holds gateway-1, admin-1, console-1, token-broker-1 and package-gate-1. This page describes the public package allow-list and token-broker-1; admin-1 and console-1 are described in the repository (docs/admin-1.md, docs/console-1.md). Sections marked proposed are drafted from the original brief and the cluster standard and are not decisions.

docs.title: Public package allow-list
docs.text:
Which public npm packages and Go modules the platform's CI package proxies serve. Internal packages (npm scope @budybot/, Go host git.budy.internal and each environment's GitLab) are always served and are never on the list. There are no tenant packages.

Source of truth The GitJib admin database (ob1-gitjib-db-1): one row per entry, an append-only audit trail (who requested it, when, why, the list version that carried it; UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE are refused) and hourly pull counters per package. Changes System-scope capabilities of admin-1 over Nexus (GitjibHostingServiceV1): addPublicPackage, addPublicPackages (up to 500 names), removePublicPackage, listPublicPackages, listPublicPackageEvents, getPublicPackagePulls. Writes need may_administer_gitjib_1 and reads may_view_gitjib_1 on platform:budy-sl-platform-1, with the token's live platform session. No pull request, no restart. Entries npm: exact names (lodash, @types/node). Go: module path prefixes matched by whole segments (github.com/google/uuid covers /v2); a bare host or account (github.com/google) is refused. Delivery admin-1 renders the active entries into the ConfigMap public-package-allowlist-1 in each proxy namespace (both replicas serialise on a database lock). The package-gate-1 container in each proxy pod re-reads it every 2 s. An entry becomes published (or removed) only when every gate reports exactly the list version that carries it (or no longer carries it). Enforcement package-gate-1 sits in front of Verdaccio (npm-proxy-1) and Athens (go-proxy-1) and answers 403 for anything public that is not listed, whether or not the proxy has it cached. It fails closed: with no readable list after GATE_MAX_STALE (15 min), public traffic is refused. The proxies' own rules cannot do this: Verdaccio keeps serving a cached package after its rule is removed, and Athens never reloads its filter. Starting list Seeded once per environment by admin-1 migrations: 0004 (what an ARM64 build of the TypeScript worker installs, and the Go worker's go.sum) and 0005 (the shared libraries repository's build tooling). A seed never re-adds a package an administrator removed. Pull metrics Each gate counts lookups, pulls and refusals per name on its stats port (9100, admin-1 only); admin-1 stores the deltas per hour, so getPublicPackagePulls shows use and refused requests per day.

Where things live:

What Where Capabilities, tables, sync loop, seed Budybot/gitjib-cluster-1_repo-1: components/admin-1, docs/admin-1.md ("The public package allow-list") The gate Budybot/gitjib-cluster-1_repo-1: components/package-gate-1 Design history (spikes) Budybot/gitjib-cluster-1_repo-1: docs/spikes/ Proxy deployment (gate image tag, ports, scope @budybot) Budybot/ob1_mn_gh_de-v2_gitops_repo_1: charts/apps/npm-proxy-1, charts/apps/go-proxy-1, docs/package-proxies.md Network policy, RBAC for the ConfigMap write Budybot/ob1_mn_github_k8s-security_gitops_repo_1

Shared platform packages are published from GitLab only: the GitHub repository dynamo-worker-libs_repo-1 is mirrored into the GitLab group budybot, whose pipeline publishes @budybot/* npm packages to that project's registry and tags Go modules modules/<name>/v<version> (module path git.budy.internal/budybot/dynamo-worker-libs_repo-1.git/modules/<name>).

docs.title: token-broker-1
docs.text:
token-broker-1 is an HTTP component of gitjib-cluster-1 (not a Temporal worker, no capabilities, not reached through gateway-1). Code and README: components/token-broker-1 in Budybot/gitjib-cluster-1_repo-1; chart charts/token-broker-1. It has two jobs: an Envoy ext_authz endpoint that lets pods and agents use their STS token as a GitLab token, and an exchange of a GitLab CI ID token for short-lived AWS builder credentials.

GitLab role of a session Resolved from OpenFGA, not from the user id: the role whose tenant relation the session's user holds on the session's tenant. config.authz.roleRelations (chart default): coder is active_svcrole_dtcs_coder_1, reviewer is active_svcrole_dtcs_reviewer_1. A user with none, or with the relations of more than one role, is refused; so is any OpenFGA error. Session fact Each check carries the token's session as a contextual tuple (user:<sub> session_<sessionBoundary> tenant:<tenant>); a token without a viewer, editor or admin sessionBoundary is refused. current_time Every OpenFGA check carries current_time (UTC, RFC 3339), because the coder relation can be held through a time-bound grant (non_expired_grant); without it OpenFGA answers with an error. A positive result is cached for authz.cacheTtl (default 30s, at most 1m), never past the token's expiry. See Component Authorization Module Standard. Teammate The token's optional glassboxId is the billing entity. When it equals the spec.name of one of the tenant's DigitalTeammates, that teammate is the session's teammate and the request is confined to that teammate's GitLab group; a glassboxId that names no teammate of the org is refused. Without it (or equal to the tenant id) the teammate is picked per request from the project path, the DynamoWorker project id or the X-Budy-Teammate header. Accounts One coder and one reviewer GitLab service account per org (UserOrg.spec.gitlab.identities); the caller never sees a GitLab credential.

State at the time of writing (de-v2 main, verified in charts/apps/gitjib-cluster-1/values):

  • The component is disabled in every environment: token-broker-1.enabled: false in the chart default values, with no override in the base, environment or profile values. Dev has its OpenFGA store id and AWS role ARNs set. Enabling it in dev is de-v2 PR 2415, open on 13 November 2026.
  • The GitLab proxy in front of it is not built: no Envoy route or filter that sends GitLab requests to the broker's /authz endpoint was found in the gitjib chart or the de-v2 gitjib values (the tested Envoy configuration is only a spike file, per the component README); the fact sheet says the proxy is not yet built. Sandboxes therefore have no GitLab access (the sandbox-coder-1 network profile has no GitLab rule either).

docs.text: Owns Does not own Running GitLab and the npm registry in the cluster, their configuration and upgrades The workers that execute workflow code (nainai-cluster-1) The visibility model: tenant-private versus platform-shared repositories Tenant lifecycle and identity (platform operator, auth cluster) The approved-dependency policy and versioned package publication Which events trigger workflows (events-cluster-1) Forking and PR (GitLab merge request) contribution flow between shared and tenant repositories

docs.title: Proposed shape
docs.text:
Repository type Nexus-first (gateway + provisioning component) plus hosted software behind thin wrapper charts Components Wrapper charts for GitLab and the registry; a provisioning component (Go/Temporal) that creates tenant groups, repositories and registry scopes Nexus surface A control gateway (GitjibHostingServiceV1) exposing the provisioning operations to platform callers, built on the shared kit like every other gateway

The standard's gateway rules (STS authentication, capability registry, tenancy twice) apply to the control gateway and the provisioning component. The hosted software itself is configured, not rewritten; it is a non-Nexus component with a catalog entry, wrapper charts and the same CI, charts, README and changesets as everything else.

First pass (October 2026): the gateway only (gateway-1), like nainai-cluster-1; the components above are added one at a time afterwards, each as a catalog entry.

docs.text:
• Consumers of packages and workflow repositories: nainai-cluster-1 (loads updates), events-cluster-1 ("published workflows"), dt-consulting-services-1 (code changes and PRs), build pipelines (assumed).
  • Identity: platform SSO / auth cluster for GitLab login and token exchange (assumed).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. ~~Registry choice.~~ Decided: platform packages are published to GitLab's package registry (group budybot, scope @budybot); CI resolves everything through the Verdaccio and Athens proxies (see Public package allow-list).
  2. Packaging unit. What is published as an npm package in a Go-first platform: workflow definitions, SDKs, DT code? Who consumes it and how is a version pinned?
  3. ~~Approved dependencies.~~ Decided: an allow-list in the GitJib admin database, changed through admin-1 system capabilities by platform administrators and enforced by package-gate-1 (see Public package allow-list).
  4. Tenancy mapping. One GitLab group per tenant? How does the platform tenant map to GitLab identity, and how is platform-visible content shared read-only to tenants?
  5. Forks and PRs. Fork from shared repositories into tenant space and contribute back by merge request; what is the review authority for shared repositories?
  6. Hosting model. GitLab's Helm chart with managed PostgreSQL, Redis and object storage, or an omnibus-style install? Sizing, backup and restore, and upgrade policy. This is infrastructure work that crosses budy-cloud-management, Vault and k8s-security.
  7. GitHub versus GitLab. The rest of the platform is on GitHub. Who uses GitLab (tenants, DTs, platform), and is there any GitHub synchronization?
  8. Control surface. Is a Nexus provisioning gateway needed, or is the cluster operated through GitLab's own API from other services?

docs.title: Janus Cluster — High Level Design
docs.text: As built, 2026-11-17. This describes what is deployed in dev from Budybot/janus-cluster-1_repo-1 (chart 0.1.24 and later) and the platform repositories around it. Outbound enforcement is not described here as a design: outbound-policy-1 and outbound-gateway-1 exist but do not enforce anything yet, and the owner is taking that work. Facts that could only be checked in the repositories, not on the live cluster, are marked (repo-verified); facts that could not be checked at all are marked (unverified) and listed again at the end. Repository-level detail (every capability, every environment variable) lives in the repository's docs/content/; this document keeps the architecture and the reasons.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Janus is the platform's connection manager. A connection is a tenant's authorised link to an external system (Google Calendar through Nango, or any service reached with an API key, basic auth or a bearer token). Janus stores the secret in a Vault of its own, records who made the connection and why, decides who may use it, and shows what exists. It is the only place in the platform that holds connection secrets, and it replaces the retired connections-1 credential intake in the auth cluster (D47).

It is a Go, Temporal-first Nexus cluster, built the way the other application clusters are: one Temporal namespace (ob1-temporal-janus-cluster-1-ns-1), a Nexus endpoint (ob1-nexus-janus-cluster-1-endpoint-1) that exposes one service, ConnectionServiceV1, and a set of components that each own a task queue (janus-cluster-1-<component>-tq). Callers never talk to a component directly. They call Execute on the endpoint with a component name, a capability name and a payload; gateway-1 verifies the caller's STS token, validates the payload against the capability's schema, fixes the tenant and user from the token, and starts a child workflow on the component's queue. Two components are HTTP services instead of workers (intake-1, oauth-provider-1) because a browser or a third party calls them.

The shape follows one idea: separate the secret from everything that describes it. Metadata (types, providers, connections, who, why, when) is in Postgres and is visible to people and DTs. The secret value is in the Janus Vault and is written by exactly one component (intake-1, or oauth-provider-1 for refresh tokens) and destroyed by exactly one (vault-manager-1). No capability, log line or audit row carries a secret.
