docs.title: Deployment Model
docs.text:
All components deploy from one umbrella chart, janus-cluster-1-repo-1, as one Argo CD Application (janus-cluster-1-app, project apps-janus-cluster-1-acd-proj-1) into ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-janus-1-ns-1, promoted by Kargo through the de-v2 GitOps repository (repo-verified). Images are built per component and tagged <component>-<version>-<sha>; versions come from changesets.

Component Kind Replicas Ports Notes gateway-1 Temporal worker (Nexus handler + workflow) 2 (1 in dev) health 3000 Stateless. Capability manifests are rendered from charts/gateway-1/files/capabilities/*.yaml. connection-registry-1 Temporal worker 1 health 3000 The system of record for types, providers, connections, revisions, metadata and audit. Runs a pre-upgrade migration Job (Argo PreSync hook). publish-1 Temporal worker 1 health 3000 Janus's slice of a Mission publish; writes OpenFGA tuples. vault-manager-1 Temporal worker 1 health 3000 Only writer of Janus Vault configuration; carries out the destroy queue. outbound-policy-1 Temporal worker + gRPC ext_authz 1 health 3000, callback 3001 Built; listener off. intake-1 HTTP 1 8080 (Service 80), health, callback 3001 Behind api-gateway-1; own callback Service janus-intake-1-callback. oauth-provider-1 HTTP + worker 1 8080 (Service 80) Internal OAuth providers; none enabled, answers provider_disabled. console-1 Node web app (console-kit) 1 (Recreate) 3000, callback 3001 Host janus.<env>.orangebox.ai; own callback Service console-1-callback. openfga-bootstrap-1 Job (Sync hook) + hourly CronJob n/a n/a Creates the store and writes the model; the CronJob never creates a store. janus-openfga-1, janus-vault-cluster-1 third-party charts via de-v2 (D7) per chart per chart Own namespaces for the Vault (...-janus-vault-1-ns-1) and OpenFGA. outbound-gateway-1 Envoy (de-v2 app) 1 per config Deny-all placeholder (D49).

Every worker and service runs with request 50m CPU / 64Mi (console 128Mi) and limits 1 CPU / 256Mi (console 500m / 512Mi) by chart default. The three components that wait for Nexus results are single replica by design (see "The Nexus async pattern"). Postgres is ob1-janus-db-1 for the registry, publish-1 and vault-manager-1; OpenFGA has its own ob1-openfga-janus-db-1 (D45).

docs.title: The Nexus call every capability uses
docs.text:
// Request to ConnectionServiceV1.Execute (Temporal Nexus HTTP API: POST .../endpoints/<id>/services/ConnectionServiceV1/Execute?callback=<url>)
interface ExecuteRequest {
  component: "connection-registry-1" | "publish-1" | "vault-manager-1" | "outbound-policy-1";
  capability: string;                // a name from that component's manifest
  payload: object;                   // validated by gateway-1 against the capability's JSON schema (additionalProperties: false)
  idempotencyKey?: string;           // becomes the gateway's workflow id; without one the id is derived from the request
  auth: { token: string };           // the caller's STS token; tenant and user are taken from it, never from the payload
}

// What a component receives (set by gateway-1, not by the caller)
interface ComponentRequest {
  scopeType: "tenant" | "platform";
  tenantId: string;                  // empty for platform scope
  user: string;                      // the token's sub
  sessionBoundary: "viewer" | "editor" | "admin";   // STS session boundary
}

// Answer, delivered to the callback (HTTP 201 first: {"token": ...})
type ExecuteAnswer = { ok: true; data: unknown } | { ok: false; error: { code: "UNAUTHORIZED" | "PERMISSION_DENIED" | "NOT_FOUND" | "INVALID_ARGUMENT" | "FAILED_PRECONDITION" | "UNAVAILABLE"; message: string } };

Authorization decisions that belong to a capability (platform scope only, editor boundary, internal callers only) are made in the component, which sees the ComponentRequest; the gateway only authenticates and validates.

docs.title: The provider split
docs.text:
// A connection type is what callers think in; a provider is what holds and refreshes the credential.
interface ConnectionType {   // e.g. "google-calendar", "generic-api-key"
  code: string; name: string; description: string; category: string;
  credentialKind: "oauth2" | "api_key" | "basic" | "bearer";
  placement: { in: "header" | "query" | "context"; name?: string; format?: string };  // where the credential goes on a call
  host?: string; pathPrefix?: string;   // fixed for a service type; empty for the generic types (the connection carries them)
  defaultScopes: string[]; state: "active" | "retired";
}
// type x provider: which provider serves the type; exactly one is active (new connections use it).
interface TypeProviderLink { state: "active" | "available" | "deprecated" | "retired"; settings: { integrationKey?: string } }

docs.title: Connection (metadata only)
docs.text:
interface Connection {
  id: string;                  // conn_<26 chars>. Immutable.
  tenant: string;              // asserted from the token at the gateway, never a request field.
  name: string;                // Made by the registry: the type's name, then "<name> 2", "<name> 3" (never reused).
                               //   Generic types: "<Type> – <host><path>", e.g. "API key – welcomehome.com". Unique per tenant+type (index).
  typeCode: string; providerCode: string;
  host?: string; pathPrefix?: string;     // set for generic types at request time
  state: "pending" | "active" | "needs-reauth" | "revoked";
  currentRevision: number;     // 0 until a secret is stored; each stored secret is a new immutable revision.
  createdBy: string;           // the user (or later a DT) who made it: the "creator" right (D42).
  reason: string;              // why it was requested, 1..500 chars, required. Also in the audit row.
  metadata?: Record<string,string>;  // display-only (D63). Keys ^[a-z][a-z0-9_.-]{0,63}$, values 1..500 chars, max 20. Never a secret and
                                     //   never an input to an allow/deny decision. First intended use: account_label.
  createdAt: string; updatedAt: string;
}

docs.title: requestConnection
docs.text:
interface RequestConnectionRequest { typeCode: string; reason: string; idempotencyKey?: string; host?: string; pathPrefix?: string; forceNew?: boolean | "true" | "false" }
interface RequestConnectionResponse {
  connection: Connection;
  link: { url: string; message: string; expiresAt: string };  // url has the one-time session in its #fragment; lives 60 minutes
  reused: boolean;             // an earlier pending request of the same user, type, host and path was still inside the window
  reusedFromRequestedAt?: string;  // when reused, message starts by telling the reader this is the same pending connection
}

docs.title: gateway-1
docs.text: The front door of ConnectionServiceV1. It resolves the capability from the manifests, authenticates the STS token (issuer https://auth.budy.internal/sts, audience urn:budy:nexus:ob1-nexus-janus-cluster-1-endpoint-1:ConnectionServiceV1, Nexus access to Execute and DescribeCapabilities), validates the payload, sets ComponentRequest, and runs GatewayExecuteWorkflow, which runs a ValidateSchema activity and then a child workflow of the component (for the registry, ConnectionRegistryWorkflowV1). The workflow id is derived from tenant, user, capability, boundary and the idempotency key or a hash of the payload, so two identical calls in flight at once collide ("Workflow execution is already running"). Callers that can send the same call twice (reads, retries) must send a fresh idempotencyKey per try; console-1 and intake-1 do. (repo-verified; gateway-1 itself is built from the platform's shared go/capability library.)

docs.title: connection-registry-1
docs.text:
Owns the metadata in Postgres and every rule about it. Capability groups:

Group Capabilities Who may call Tenant reads listConnectionTypes, getConnectionType, listConnections, getConnection, listConnectionRevisions, listConnectionAudit, listPublications tenant scope (tenant fixed from the token) Tenant writes requestConnection, revokeConnection, createConnection tenant scope (requestConnection checks only the tenant; the console asks for an editor boundary before it shows a working Connect, D59). createConnection takes an explicit name and returns the raw intake session, so it is not published as a DT tool; requestConnection is the path callers use. Internal completeConnection, inspectConnection, setConnectionMetadata, recordCredentialUse platform scope and the caller's user in INTERNAL_CALLERS (janus-intake-1, janus-outbound-policy-1) System (catalog editor) systemListConnectionTypes, systemListProviders, systemConnectionTypeUsage, systemListCatalogAudit (any boundary); systemUpsertConnectionType, systemSetConnectionTypeState, systemDeleteConnectionType, systemSetTypeProvider, systemRemoveTypeProvider, systemCheckTypeProvider (the writes need editor or admin) platform scope

Invariants it enforces: one active provider per type; a retired type takes no new connections; a type with connections cannot be deleted; a connection can only move pending to active through completeConnection, and that call is idempotent; a link in use cannot be removed; every editor write is audited with before and after and is idempotent by its idempotency key (or workflow run id). Providers are code, not data: there is no capability to create or edit one (D60); a provider is added by a registry migration so that where it reads its keys and how it refreshes tokens is reviewed code.

docs.title: intake-1
docs.text: The browser-facing component. Five routes under /v1/connections/: session/inspect, session/connect, session/status, credentials, webhooks/nango. The capability is a signed intake session (HMAC, key shared with the registry and oauth-provider-1, single use, 60 minutes) that requestConnection put in the link's fragment, so no server log ever sees it. It calls the registry as its own workload identity (janus-intake-1) and writes secrets to the Janus Vault under a Kubernetes-auth role that can only write janus-connections/tenants/*. For the form kinds it stores the secret and calls completeConnection; for Nango it creates a connect session lazily when the user clicks, and later completes the connection from Nango's webhook. Per-address and per-connection rate limits, an allowed origin, and a fixed-word error for every refusal.

docs.title: console-1
docs.text: The platform console (console-kit). Two scopes from one deployment. Tenant scope: the tenant's connections and types, with Connect (calls requestConnection with the signed-in user's own token, the same path the DT tool uses). System scope: types, providers (read-only), usage, audit, and the catalog editor. It holds no secret and no database or Vault credential; every call goes to gateway-1 through Nexus with the user's token, so the gateway fixes tenant and user. Sign in is by STS handoff from the platform portal; sign out and expiry send the browser back to the portal.

docs.title: publish-1
docs.text: Janus's slice of a Mission publish (D38, D39). registerPublication (from the publishing service only) validates that every connection named belongs to the tenant and is active, records the publication and its grants, and writes tuples to janus-openfga-1; retirePublication removes them. A request that names a missing or inactive connection is recorded as refused and writes nothing.

docs.title: vault-manager-1
docs.text: The only writer of Janus Vault configuration (D6, D57): auth methods, mounts, policies and component roles, from desired state in Postgres, with drift detection. It also carries out the registry's vault_destroy_request queue: after a revoke it destroys the KV versions of that connection.

docs.title: oauth-provider-1, outbound-policy-1, outbound-gateway-1
docs.text: oauth-provider-1 is the internal OAuth provider surface (authorize, callback, code exchange, refresh tokens in the Janus Vault); it runs with no provider enabled. outbound-policy-1 (ext_authz service) and outbound-gateway-1 (Envoy) are the outbound path of D22; they are built but not enforcing: the ext_authz listener is off and the Envoy configuration is a deny-all placeholder. The owner is taking this work; it is outside this document.

docs.title: Catalog tools and skills (janus-catalog-1)
docs.text: Tools and skills for the DT context catalog, synced by the context operator: list tools (types, connections), request_connection (typeCode, reason, forceNew; the idempotency key is the runtime's tool-call key) and revoke_connection, plus skills that tell a DT when to ask, to give a concrete reason, to share the link unchanged, and to force a second connection only when the user explicitly asks. Tenant scope only: no system* capability and none of the internal ones can be published as a tool (the chart lint refuses them).

docs.title: 1. Request a connection (DT tool or console Connect)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as DT or tenant user
    participant GW as gateway-1
    participant R as connection-registry-1
    participant DB as Postgres
    U->>GW: Execute requestConnection {typeCode, reason, forceNew?} (callback)
    GW->>GW: verify STS token, validate schema, fix tenant + user
    GW->>R: child workflow
    R->>DB: type + provider binding; retired type refused
    alt pending request of same user, type, host, path inside 60 min and not forceNew
        R->>DB: reuse that connection (reused=true)
    else
        R->>DB: insert pending connection, generated name, reason (unique index on name)
    end
    R->>DB: audit link_minted (reason, reused, forced)
    R-->>U: {connection, link #s=<signed session>, expiresAt, reused}
    Note over U: the link is handed to the person; the DT never sees the secret

docs.title: 2. Collect the secret (form kinds) and complete
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Person (browser)
    participant I as intake-1
    participant R as registry
    participant JV as Janus Vault
    P->>I: session/inspect {session}
    I->>R: inspectConnection (workload token)
    R-->>I: connection + type + provider + mode form
    P->>I: credentials {session, fields}
    I->>JV: write new KV revision (CAS), tenants/<t>/connections/<id>
    I->>R: completeConnection {vaultPath, vaultVersion}
    R->>R: pending -> active, revision n recorded, session now spent
    I-->>P: 201 completed

docs.title: 3. Google Calendar through Nango, and the webhook
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Person
    participant I as intake-1
    participant N as Nango
    participant R as registry
    P->>I: session/connect
    I->>N: POST /connect/sessions (API key; tag connection_id)
    I-->>P: Nango connect link (new tab)
    P->>N: authorise at Google through Nango
    N->>I: webhook auth/creation (X-Nango-Hmac-Sha256, signing key)
    I->>I: verify HMAC of the raw body; connection id from the end-user tag
    I->>R: completeConnection {providerRef = Nango connection id}
    P->>I: session/status (poll) -> active

The secret stays in Nango; Janus keeps the reference (providerRef) and the integration key from the type's link settings.

docs.title: 4. Edit the catalog (console, system scope)
docs.text: A staff user with an editor or admin boundary creates or edits a type in console-1; the console validates once (the same rules as the registry), sends systemUpsertConnectionType with the browser's idempotency key and expectedUpdatedAt; the gateway passes sessionBoundary; the registry refuses a viewer, writes the row and a catalog_audit row in one transaction, and answers the row as stored. A stale version is FAILED_PRECONDITION (HTTP 409 to the browser). Making a link active demotes the previous one in the same transaction and affects new connections only (D43). The console shows a warning and requires an acknowledgement first.

docs.title: 5. Publish (Mission to Janus)
docs.text: mission-registry-1 calls publish-1.registerPublication through Nexus with the publication id, tenant, DT, automation, workflows, activities and the connection ids each activity uses. publish-1 checks each connection (tenant, active), records the publication and grants, and writes tuples in the Janus OpenFGA store (found by name, janus-cluster-1). Idempotent per publication id.

docs.title: 6. Revoke
docs.text: revokeConnection sets the connection revoked, writes an audit row and queues a vault_destroy_request (path and versions); vault-manager-1 destroys those KV versions. Not built: deleting the Nango-side connection.

docs.title: The Nexus async pattern (architecture decision)
docs.text:
ConnectionServiceV1.Execute is a workflow-run operation. Temporal answers HTTP 201 with an operation token at once and later POSTs the result to the callback URL the caller put in ?callback=. Consequences designed in (D58):

  • Every caller listens. console-1, intake-1 and outbound-policy-1 each run a callback listener on its own port (3001) and its own Service, with a per-call URL /internal/nexus/callback/<id>.<signature> signed by a key that lives only in that process.
  • One replica per listener, because the key is in memory: a callback delivered to another replica would fail its signature. The console chart refuses replicaCount > 1. A restart between a call and its callback loses that answer; the caller times out and the person retries.
  • Allowlist. Temporal only delivers to addresses in component.callbacks.allowedAddresses (the three callback Services are listed in the eks-stack Temporal values).
  • Network. Cilium lets only Temporal's history service reach port 3001 of each listener; the callers have egress to the Temporal frontend (7243).
  • Mesh. The namespace enforces STRICT mTLS. intake-1 also has an Istio ALLOW policy for the API gateway on 8080; because an allow policy denies everything it does not list, a second policy admits Temporal's service account on 3001. (Missing until 2026-11-17: Temporal showed handler error (UNAUTHORIZED) and intake never received an answer.)
  • Timeouts. The caller's wait and the Operation-Timeout header are the same whole seconds; a timeout is "may still be running", not "failed".

docs.title: Identity and Authorization
docs.text: Concern As built Who is calling STS tokens. A user session carries scopeType (tenant or platform) and sessionBoundary; a workload (intake-1, outbound-policy-1) exchanges its projected service-account token at the STS for a token of platform scope janus-platform-1 (D55). Admission to the endpoint The STS admits tenant:* and platform:* to Execute and DescribeCapabilities (D56). Tenant isolation The gateway sets the tenant from the token; no capability takes a tenant argument. A platform-scope read may span tenants (system scope, D51). Staff rights sessionBoundary from the platform portal's groups: viewer reads; editor and admin write the catalog (D59). Internal capabilities The registry accepts them only from platform scope and a user listed in INTERNAL_CALLERS. (Configuration lives in registry.internalCallers; a misplaced key once left the list empty and every internal call was refused.) Rights on a connection janus_connection_1 in the Janus OpenFGA model (components/publish-1/authz/janus.fga): creator, dt_user, dt_manager, user_activity, can_use, can_revoke (D42). OpenFGA A dedicated instance with its own database (D40, D45). openfga-bootstrap-1 creates the store by name and writes the model; clients find the store by name; one preshared key per consumer (one shared value for now).

docs.title: Postgres ob1-janus-db-1 (metadata only)
docs.text:
Table Purpose credential_kind, provider_credential_kind the four kinds (oauth2, api_key, basic, bearer) and which providers hold which (D50) connection_type, connection_provider, type_provider the catalog; one active provider per type (partial unique index) connection id, tenant, creator, type and provider, state, current revision, host and path, generated name (unique per tenant+type, case-insensitive), request_reason, request key for idempotency connection_revision immutable (a trigger refuses update and delete): connection, revision, Vault path and version, who, when connection_metadata key, value, source per connection; cascades with the connection publication, publication_grant Janus's slice of each publish and its activity-to-connection grants audit, catalog_audit connection events (including the reason) and editor writes with before and after vault_destroy_request work for vault-manager-1

Migrations run as an Argo PreSync Job with a Vault-issued migrator role. Migration 00008 deliberately deleted every connection while nothing was in use; it queued the stored Vault secrets for destruction first and runs once per database in each environment (D64).

docs.title: Janus Vault janus-vault-cluster-1
docs.text: KV v2 mount janus-connections, path tenants/<tenant>/connections/<connection_id>, one key per credential field, immutable revisions. HA with Raft, auto-unsealed by vault-cluster-2's Transit (D14); no human access (D5). Only intake-1 and oauth-provider-1 write; only vault-manager-1 destroys; the registry never sees a value.

docs.title: vault-cluster-2 (platform Vault, read by VSO)
docs.text: Holds the keys Janus components need at startup, in app-kv-secrets-1 under v1/de-v2/ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-janus-1-ns-1/: the intake session HMAC key, each component's Nango key, intake's Nango webhook signing key, the console session secret, and the OpenFGA keys.

docs.title: Secrets and keys
docs.text:
Secret Where Used by Connection secret values Janus Vault KV written by intake-1 and oauth-provider-1 Intake session HMAC key vault-cluster-2, shared signed by the registry, verified by intake-1 and oauth-provider-1 Nango API key vault-cluster-2 (secretKey), one per component scopes by component, recommended: intake environment:connect_sessions:write; registry environment:integrations:read_credentials; outbound-policy environment:connections:read_credentials (D66) Nango webhook signing key vault-cluster-2 (webhookSigningKey) intake-1 only, to verify X-Nango-Hmac-Sha256 OpenFGA preshared keys vault-cluster-2 one per consumer

The Nango API key and the signing key are different secrets in Nango. Janus used one value for both until 2026-11-17, which made every webhook fail verification. The scope names above are from Nango's public documentation as found by search and must be confirmed in the dashboard (unverified).

docs.title: Network and Mesh
docs.text:
• Cilium default-denies ingress and egress in the namespace; each component has a named allow policy. Intake accepts the API gateway on 8080 and Temporal history on 3001; it may reach the STS, the Temporal frontend, the Janus Vault, DNS and Nango (443). The console accepts the Istio ingress gateway on 3000 and Temporal history on 3001, and reaches only the STS and the Temporal frontend.
  • Istio. STRICT PeerAuthentication for the namespace; intake-1 has two AuthorizationPolicy allows (gateway on 8080, Temporal's service account on 3001). Console and outbound-policy-1 have none. Policies use ports and principals only, because L7 attributes (methods, paths) are not enforced without a waypoint. Whether the namespace is enrolled in ambient or uses sidecars was not found in the repositories (unverified).
  • Public routes. The connect page and the intake routes share app-1.<env>.orangebox.ai; api-gateway-1 (generated from the backend-services contracts) routes /v1/connections/* to intake-1 and leaves the connect page routes and the Nango webhook open without a bearer token, because intake authenticates them itself (session capability, webhook signature). The console is at janus.<env>.orangebox.ai behind the portal.
  • Argo CD. An application may only create resources in namespaces its AppProject lists. The backend-services app creates the gateway's ReferenceGrant in the Janus namespace, so ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-janus-1-ns-1 had to be added to the apps-de-v2-services-acd-proj-1 destinations; until it was, the sync failed and the intake route never existed.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Dependency How used Temporal (frontend 7233 gRPC, 7243 Nexus HTTP) workflows, Nexus endpoint and callbacks STS (auth-cluster-1) token issuer and keys; workload token exchange; console handoff redeem Nango Cloud (api.nango.dev) connect sessions, integration reads, webhooks; Google OAuth for Google Calendar vault-cluster-2 + VSO keys and secrets for components janus-vault-cluster-1 connection secrets Postgres ob1-janus-db-1, ob1-openfga-janus-db-1 metadata; OpenFGA state api-gateway-1 (Istio) public routes to intake-1 Context operator and catalog publishes the DT tools and skills frontend-cluster-1 the connect page /connections/connect and the portal route to the console

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Every component honours a log level: console-1 logLevel (default warn), intake-1 and the registry LOG_LEVEL (chart logLevel, default info; the dev profile sets debug). debug is routine per-request events (session inspected, status polls, Nango webhook received, catalog write); info is startup and a connection's lifecycle (requested, completed, revoked, Vault destruction queued); warn is a refusal an operator may want to see (invalid or spent session, rate limit, bad webhook signature); error is a failed dependency, with a fixed-word cause (gateway_timeout, no_callback, operation_failed, gateway_status_<code> and so on). Lines carry ids, outcomes and fixed words, never a session, link, credential, Vault path or answer text. intake-1 takes the edge's X-Request-Id (or makes one), returns it, logs it as request and sends it to the gateway on each try, so a connect attempt can be followed across services; the registry logs the gateway's idempotency key or workflow run id as request (the capability request carries no caller request id). The durable trail is the audit and catalog_audit tables.

docs.title: Failure Modes
docs.text: Failure Effect Notes Registry or its database down Every capability answers UNAVAILABLE; the connect page shows "could not reach the service"; no connection can be requested or completed Pending links stay valid for 60 minutes Nexus callback lost (listener restart, mesh or network denial) The caller times out; the work may still have run Retrying is safe: reads are idempotent and completeConnection is idempotent; requests reuse a pending connection Janus Vault down A secret cannot be stored; the connection stays pending Intake answers unavailable and logs vault_write_failed with a cause Nango down or webhook refused OAuth connection stays pending The webhook is retried by Nango; a wrong signing key refuses every one INTERNAL_CALLERS empty or wrong Internal capabilities refused (this capability is internal) Seen once in dev (misplaced Helm key) Two identical gateway calls at once Second fails "already running" Callers send a fresh idempotency key per try Type retired New requests refused with type_retired; existing connections keep working Hard delete only when no connection exists Provider switched active New connections use it; existing stay on theirs No migration (D43) Migration 00008 re-run not possible: it runs once per database Stored Vault secrets are queued for destruction when it runs

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. The secret never travels with its description. Metadata is in Postgres, secrets are in the Janus Vault, and the code paths that write each are separate components.
  2. The caller never chooses the tenant. The gateway sets it from the token; a capability that needs a platform view says so by scope, and the component decides.
  3. Capabilities are the contract, schemas are strict. additionalProperties: false everywhere, so an unknown field is refused instead of ignored.
  4. A bearer link is a one-time capability in a fragment. The session that lets someone store a secret is signed, single use, 60 minutes, and never in a URL a server logs.
  5. Providers are reviewed code, types are data. What a provider reads and where it keeps secrets is not editable in a UI; what a type is called and which provider serves it is.
  6. Display data is not decision data. metadata, names and reasons help people; enforcement reads types, links and tuples.
  7. Every refusal and failure has a fixed word. Operators can tell a bad key from a lost callback without a secret in the log.
  8. Idempotency is explicit. Reads and retries carry their own key; writes dedupe by key; connection requests reuse a pending one unless forced.
  9. Quiet by default, loud on demand. Info is lifecycle only; dev runs at debug.

docs.title: Design Decisions Log
docs.text:
Decisions D1 to D49 are in the repository's handover.md; D50 to D67 are in build-spec.md. The ones that shape this design:

Question Resolution Where do connection secrets live? In janus-vault-cluster-1, owned by Janus, no human access (D4, D5, D6); revisions are immutable (D50). One type or one provider? Separate. A type is the common name; several providers may serve it; exactly one is active (D35, D50). What happens to existing connections when the active provider changes? Nothing. New connections use the new one (D43). How does a DT get a connection made? The catalog tool request_connection returns a one-time link the person opens (D54). Who names a connection? The registry, from the type (and host for generic types); a reason is required (D62). Can a connection carry extra details? Yes, display-only metadata, set by internal callers, never an input to a decision (D63). Who may change the catalog? Platform staff with editor or admin; providers are code-only (D59, D60). How do callers get results from Nexus workflow operations? Callback listeners, one replica each, allowlisted and netpol-limited (D58). How is OpenFGA run? Dedicated instance and database, bootstrapped by a Job and drift CronJob (D40, D45, D61). What are the Nango credentials? Two secrets: a scoped API key per component and the webhook signing key (D66). How loud are logs? Quiet by default, debug in dev, ids and fixed words only (D65). What did the reset migration do? Deleted all connection data while nothing was in use (D64). When is a request reused? Same user, type, host and path pending within 60 minutes, unless forceNew; the answer says so. Where does the Connect button check the boundary? In the console (editor); the registry's requestConnection checks only the tenant, so a DT is not limited by it (D59).

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• One shared Vault with the platform. Rejected: connection secrets are the most sensitive data in the platform and a trust boundary of their own (D4).
  • Direct HTTP from callers to components. Rejected: the gateway gives one authentication, validation and tenant-fixing point, as in every Nexus cluster.
  • A single value for Nango's API key and webhook signing key. Tried first; it broke webhooks and over-privileges the component that only verifies them.
  • Provider records editable in the console. Rejected: a provider decides where a secret is read from and how it is refreshed, which belongs in reviewed code (D60).
  • Letting a caller name a connection. Rejected: names collided, said nothing for the generic types, and gave a DT a free-text field to maintain.
  • Reusing a pending request by name. Replaced by reuse by user, type, host and path, with an explicit forceNew.

docs.title: Open Questions / TRD Scope
docs.text:
• Outbound enforcement (owner-led): how outbound-policy-1 and outbound-gateway-1 are fed (which per-type and per-connection facts they need, what happens when a new type is created, certificates per host) is deliberately not designed here.
  • Rename and metadata writers: there is no rename capability, and nothing writes metadata yet; the account label from a provider is the first intended use.
  • Nango-side cleanup: deleting the Nango connection on revoke is not built; the scope it needs is environment:connections:delete.
  • Stage and prod: the chart reaches them through Kargo like dev; before prod, the RDS security group, ECR access and the migration 00008 effect (it deletes connections there too) need an explicit decision.
  • Publications after the reset: active publications lost their grants and their OpenFGA tuples name connections that no longer exist; publish-1 or Mission should rewrite them.
  • Mesh mode: confirm whether the Janus namespace is ambient or sidecar and re-check the Istio policies against it.
  • Registry Check scope: environment:integrations:read_credentials lets the registry read integrations' OAuth client secrets though it keeps only scopes; decide whether to keep the scope check.
  • OpenFGA keys: one shared value today; splitting per consumer is documented and not done.

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• Live cluster state (this document was written from repositories; the dev cluster was observed only through logs the owner pasted).
  • Nango scope names and which endpoint needs which (from public documentation found by search; the documentation site could not be opened).
  • Ambient versus sidecar mesh mode for the Janus namespace.
  • Resource sizes beyond chart defaults and replica counts beyond de-v2 base values.

docs.title: janus-cluster-1
docs.text:
janus-cluster-1 is the platform's connection manager. It manages connections to external systems, keeps the secrets behind them in its own Vault, decides which tenant workflows and activities may use each connection, brokers connections to the Temporal workers that run tenant work, and applies policy checks and rate limits to the outbound calls those workers make.

Its main callers are DT Dynamo workers: the per-tenant Temporal workers that run Digital Teammate workflows, deployed and versioned by nainai-cluster-1.

Status: connections work end to end in dev (2026-11-17); outbound enforcement is designed and not enforced. Built and running in dev: the connection registry with its type, provider and connection catalog and an admin editor, the connect page (intake-1) for API key, basic and bearer connections and for Nango-backed OAuth connections, the Nexus gateway, the console (tenant and platform scope, with sign out), the DT tools and skills (catalog), the Janus Vault, Janus's own OpenFGA with its bootstrap, publish and Vault-manager components. Stage and prod run the service at earlier chart versions (0.1.18 and 0.1.17, as reported by the owner on 2026-11-17). Not enforced: outbound calls from DT Dynamo workers do not yet pass through the policy check (the ext_authz listener is off), and run attestation, the worker hook, rotation and Nango-side deletion on revoke are not built. The owner is taking over outbound enforcement; its design is docs/content/outbound-egress-control.md in the repository. The owner decisions below were taken from 2026-11-05 on; what was built and how it behaves is in the PRD, HLD, TRD and Nexus contracts linked under Detailed Docs.

docs.title: Decisions (owner, 2026-11-05)
docs.text: # Decision D1 Janus is the platform's connection manager: connection management, permissions on connections, brokering to DT Dynamo workers, outbound rate limiting, and policy checks and routing on outbound calls. D2 Janus manages every kind of connection: secrets it stores itself (Janus-managed) and connections held by third-party connection providers (provider-managed; Nango today). D3 The existing connections-1 (credential intake in the auth cluster, auth-service-1) and the connections UI (frontend-cluster-1, apps/connections) move into Janus. D4 Janus gets a dedicated HA Vault, janus-vault-cluster-1 (Raft, same structure as vault-cluster-2, nothing shared with it). Connections are stored in KV v2. The connection storage in vault-cluster-2 (user-connections-1) is deprecated after migration. D5 No human access to the Janus Vault; only Janus uses and manages it. A break-glass admin path may exist. D6 Janus manages its Vault's configuration itself, operator-style, with desired state in its own Postgres (ob1-janus-db-1). Not Crossplane CRs, not vault-gitops Terraform. D7 The Vault chart and any other third-party chart Janus needs deploy through the de-v2 GitOps repository as their own Applications, like gitjib's gitlab-1, so Kargo promotes them. D8 No Vault JWT plugin (the outfoxx plugin is deprecated upstream and being removed platform-wide). JWT signing for workers becomes a capability in the auth cluster or in Janus (open). D9 Janus owns its own OpenFGA model (now in its own OpenFGA, D40). The existing connections and credentials modules are V0 and are not the base for Janus. D10 Authorization is per published workflow and per activity within a tenant. Tuples are written at publish time (into Janus's own OpenFGA, D40). D11 Inbound rate limiting stays on api-gateway-1. Janus owns outbound control for DT Dynamo workers; the mechanism (Envoy preferred, in-image inspection before TLS as a candidate) is open. D12 DT Dynamo workers hold no credentials. Authority is per workflow run: a token is issued for the Temporal run id when the run is triggered and flows down through the run's context. D13 Published workflows and their activities have globally unique ids (prefixed UUIDs). Publishing registers worker → workflow within the tenant and workflow → activity. D14 The Janus Vault is auto-unsealed by the environment's main Vault (vault-cluster-2) through Transit. The deployed Vault also takes its TLS certificates from vault-cluster-2's PKI (open question 3), so the main Vault is a dependency for both the seal and TLS. D15 A proxy injects credentials only where that is a standard pattern across many APIs; otherwise the credential is passed in the run's context at execution time. D16 Single seal: Transit auto-unseal from the parent Vault only, no multi-seal. D17 STS signs run tokens. Janus attests a run on its first outbound call (with Temporal and the publish records) and has STS mint the token; the trigger does not mint. D18 Temporal type names are the published ids: workflow types are published workflow ids (pwf_), activity types published activity ids (pact_). A publication names one of its workflows as its automation, the root of the runs its triggers start. D19 Published ids belong to one tenant and one DT and are never used by another DT, tenant or kind. The same DT keeps an id when the code changes and may reuse it in later publications; an id is in the tree of only one live publication of a DT at a time (v1). D20 DT Consulting Services runs the publish step. A publish declares per activity the concrete connection id and type it needs, and may carry request rules (hosts, paths, methods; Rego candidate). D21 Internal services are treated as external: a Nexus call to another cluster (LLM router, context cluster) is a connection; the run token is never forwarded and a target-specific STS token is issued under the same grants and limits. D22 One Janus outbound service does rate limiting, allowed hosts and paths, credential handling and inspection. DT Dynamo workers move to Istio ambient (no sidecars). D23 DT Dynamo workers run TypeScript and Go; hooks are built for both in parallel, TypeScript tested first. D24 Ambient is a prerequisite for DT Dynamo, DT Workbench and the namespaces sandboxes run in (tenant namespaces; the operator namespace ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-sandbox-1-ns-1 is ambient too) (Karpenter spot pools get the ztunnel and istio-cni DaemonSets); sidecars are disabled there. D25 DT Consulting Services' agents write the request rules with the publish, accepted under guidelines at first. D26 Request bodies are inspectable with IAM-style conditional rules (example: a workflow may delete only Salesforce records it is entitled to). D27 One outbound gateway per environment, shared by tenants. D28 The publication registry is not a runtime dependency; runtimes (Janus, nainai, events-cluster) keep their own slice of each publication. D29 The publication registry is its own service and database, built in DT Consulting Services and kept separable; publishing is a Temporal saga workflow (idempotent steps, compensation on failure) that fans out to each runtime. D30 Phase 1 rules are stateless (request, response, caller only); ownership checks come later for supported providers. D31 Rules are written in Rego (OPA), written and audited by LLMs, shipped with their own tests and checked at publish. D32 The first provider is Google Calendar. D33 TypeScript workers first, Go next phase; Go workers build HTTP requests from the activity's context. D34 A credential reaches a call either injected by the outbound gateway (header or query) or in the activity's context for that call; only Janus reads its Vault, through just-in-time tokens scoped to the activity's connections. D35 Connection types and connection providers are separate: each type (for example Google Calendar) can have several providers (Janus internal OAuth, Nango, other third parties), exactly one active for new connections, others available or deprecated. D36 Janus's internal providers hold refresh tokens in the Janus Vault and refresh access tokens themselves. D37 Two UIs: a system-scope admin UI (types, providers, active provider, health, audit) and a tenant UI (the tenant's connections). No UI ever reveals a secret; secrets are write-only. D38 The publication registry is the Mission registry (mission-registry-1, database ob1-mission-registry-db-1); "mission" is the umbrella term for what is published. D39 Publish grants name connection ids, not types; a different connection means a republish. D40 Janus runs its own OpenFGA for publish-time and run-scoped checks; the platform STS and shared OpenFGA stay for tenant-level questions. Replaces the shared-store and authz-manager-1 parts of D9 and D10. D41 Connections exist before an engagement: their ids are a prerequisite of the engagement request, and anything missing goes back to the DT as a feedback request. D42 Two rights on a connection, in Janus's OpenFGA: creator (the user who connected it, or later a DT) and use, shared at most between a DT and its DT manager, who may use but never see it. No tenant-wide sharing. D43 No automatic migration between providers; new connections use the new active provider. D44 Google Calendar launches on Nango with our own, Google-verified OAuth client; Janus's internal Google provider follows. D45 Janus's OpenFGA uses its own database, ob1-openfga-janus-db-1, separate from ob1-janus-db-1. D46 Delivery in four large phases: 0 baseline (Vault and OpenFGA charts, ambient, stub components, admin console, databases), 1 connections, 2 missions and outbound, 3 migration and expansion. D47 The old connection service (connections-1) is deprecated now; nobody uses it. intake-1 takes the connection routes directly, with no coexistence period. D48 Console at janus.<env>.orangebox.ai, system scope, visible to the platform-dev user group. The owner writes the session key (v1/de-v2/ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-janus-1-ns-1/janus-cluster-1-console-1/session, key sessionSecret) before the console PR merges. D49 The outbound gateway starts as a small plain-Envoy de-v2 app (ConfigMap, deny-all). Envoy Gateway is a different product from Istio's gateway; moving to a chart later is open. D50 Four layers: credential kind (oauth2, api_key, basic, bearer), connection type (for example google-calendar), connection provider (vault-static-1 internal, nango-1 third-party), and one active type–provider binding per type. A connection is a tenant's instance of a type. D51 Every read has two scopes: tenant (taken from the gateway-fixed identity) and system (platform admin only). The console is read-only in both and never sees a secret. D52 Secrets enter by two paths: form kinds post to intake-1, which writes the Janus Vault; redirect kinds go through a Nango connect session and webhook. The registry never sees a secret value. D53 Janus uses the platform's existing Nango instance. Without its configuration, calls fail closed with provider_not_configured. D54 A connection is requested with a reason and no name; the user finishes it through a one-time link in another tab; a repeat request within 60 minutes returns the same pending connection (details: docs/content/build-spec.md D54 and the PRD).

docs.title: As-built decisions (2026-11-17)
docs.text:
Decisions taken while building and testing in dev. The numbered decisions above stand; these refine them.

# Decision B1 Providers are code, types are data. A connection provider (where a credential is read from and how it is refreshed) is added in code through a registry migration and is read-only in the console. Platform staff with an editor session manage connection types, their links to providers, and which provider is active; every change is audited. A type is retired while connections use it and can be deleted only when nothing uses it. B2 A type has a common name and a description. Digital Teammates see one name (for example google-calendar) and a plain-text description. The provider behind it is not shown to tenants; a type can have several providers with exactly one active for new connections (D35). Changing the active provider affects new connections only and moves none (D43); the editor says so and asks for an acknowledgement. B3 A connection says why it exists. A request needs a reason (one concrete sentence, kept on the connection and in the audit) and never a name. The registry names connections itself: the type name, then numbered ("Google Calendar", "Google Calendar 2"); a generic type is named after its host ("API key – welcomehome.com"). Names are unique per tenant and type and a number is never reused. B4 Requests are repeat-safe. The same user asking again within 60 minutes for the same type (and host) gets the same pending connection with a fresh link and a message saying so; forceNew starts another and leaves the pending one. A user and a Digital Teammate go through the same capability, so the console's Connect button and the DT tool behave alike (the console needs an editor session). B5 Connections carry display metadata. A key/value set per connection (for example an account label that a provider supplies later), visible in reads, never a secret. Writers and renaming are later work. B6 Two Nango secrets. Nango's API key (scoped per component) and its webhook signing key are different and are stored separately; neither stands in for the other (docs/content/nango-keys.md). B7 Calls to the gateway are asynchronous. ConnectionServiceV1.Execute starts a workflow: callers receive the answer on their own callback listener (console-1, intake-1 and outbound-policy-1 each have one), reachable by Temporal's history service only. B8 Log levels are set per environment. intake-1 and the registry read LOG_LEVEL (default info; dev runs debug). Routine per-request events are debug; logs hold ids, outcomes and fixed-word causes, never a secret, session or link. B9 One OpenFGA bootstrap. A Job at each sync and an hourly check create Janus's OpenFGA store by name and keep its model; clients find the store by name.

docs.title: Boundary
docs.text: Owns Does not own Connection types, providers, tenant connections and their revisions The external systems themselves Secret custody in janus-vault-cluster-1, and that Vault's configuration Platform secret infrastructure for other services (vault-cluster-2, vault-gitops) The Janus authorization model and its own OpenFGA: which workflow and activity may use which connection Caller authentication and tenant roles (the auth cluster's STS and shared OpenFGA) Brokering connections to DT Dynamo workers Building and deploying DT Dynamo workers (gitjib, nainai) Outbound policy, credential injection, rate limiting and audit of connection use Inbound rate limiting (api-gateway-1) Credential intake from people and providers (from connections-1) Tenant-facing UI framework (frontend-cluster-1)

docs.title: Shape (as built)
docs.text: Repository type Nexus-first: gateway + components, one umbrella chart Components gateway-1 (the Nexus front: validates a call, routes it to a component's task queue); connection-registry-1 (types, providers, connections, the editor, the request flow, audit); intake-1 (HTTP: the connect page's session routes, credential form, Nango connect session and webhook); oauth-provider-1 (Janus's internal OAuth providers; present, no provider enabled yet); publish-1 (writes Janus's slice of each publication and its OpenFGA tuples); vault-manager-1 (keeps the Janus Vault's desired state and destroys revoked secret versions); outbound-policy-1 (the Envoy ext_authz engine: grants, rules, credentials; built, listener off); outbound-gateway-1 (placeholder deny-all Envoy, in de-v2); openfga-bootstrap-1 (Job and drift check for Janus's OpenFGA); console-1 (admin and tenant console); janus-catalog-1 (the DT tools and skills) Stores Postgres ob1-janus-db-1 (metadata, grants, audit, Vault desired state); janus-vault-cluster-1 (secret values); Janus's OpenFGA (its own database); Nango (provider-managed connections) Third-party charts HashiCorp Vault and OpenFGA as de-v2 Applications (the gitlab-1 pattern) Not built Outbound enforcement (listener off, real Envoy configuration unvalidated, rules and connections ConfigMaps without a producer, STS run tokens, workers not forced through the gateway), run attestation and the worker hook, rotation and needs-reauth, Nango-side deletion on revoke, connection rename and metadata writers

docs.title: Interfaces, callers and callees
docs.text:
• Nexus (control surface): endpoint ob1-nexus-janus-cluster-1-endpoint-1, service ConnectionServiceV1, operations Execute and DescribeCapabilities. The caller sends {component, capability, payload, auth}; the gateway checks the caller's STS token, the registry checks scope and session boundary. Callers: Digital Teammates (through the catalog tools, tenant scope), the console (as the signed-in user), intake-1 and outbound-policy-1 (workload identities). See Nexus contracts.
  • HTTP behind api-gateway-1: POST /v1/connections/session/inspect, /session/connect, /session/status, /credentials (capability authentication: a signed one-time session in the body, no app bearer token) and POST /v1/connections/webhooks/nango (signature authentication), all to intake-1. The connect page itself is served by frontend-cluster-1 at /connections/connect.
  • Console: janus.<env>.orangebox.ai, tenant and system scope, entered from the platform UI.
  • Dependencies: Temporal cluster and the Janus namespace (Nexus, workflows); STS and authz-config (identities, scope janus-platform-1, session boundary); janus-vault-cluster-1 (secrets) and vault-cluster-2 (seal, TLS, the Vault Secrets Operator's keys); Postgres; janus-openfga-1; Nango (hosted); api-gateway-1 (routes and open paths); k8s-security and ArgoCD projects (network policy, destinations).
  • Callees on behalf of workers (not yet enforced): the external systems behind connections.

docs.title: Open questions (summary)
docs.text:
The full list, with notes, is section 7 of docs/content/handover.md in the repository. The main ones now:

  1. Outbound enforcement (owner-led): the real Envoy configuration, certificates per host, rules and connections ConfigMaps, run tokens, forcing workers through the gateway, and what a new connection type must trigger there.
  2. A way to rename a connection, and which component writes display metadata such as an account label when a provider connects.
  3. Whether the registry's editor-time Nango check should keep reading integration credentials (it needs a credential-reading scope only to see an integration's OAuth scopes).
  4. How to keep publish-1 the only writer of tuples in Janus's OpenFGA (mesh identity with an AuthorizationPolicy, a read-only proxy, or both).
  5. The typed publish capabilities in nainai and events-cluster that the publication registry's saga calls. The registry is the Mission registry (mission-registry-1); its saga calls registerPublication here, with the worker identity of D72.
  6. How the DT and its DT manager are identified in Janus's OpenFGA, and the later flow for moving connections between providers.
  7. Stage and prod rollout: the secrets, the Janus Vault bootstrap, the RDS security group and ECR access must exist before promotion.
