docs.title: Pit Crew Cluster — High Level Design
docs.text: Draft. Decisions the owner has taken are in the Design Decisions Log. Everything marked proposed here, and every item under Open Questions, is not decided. Components, task queues and capability names follow the cluster standard and are provisional until the first component ships.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
pitcrew-cluster-1 is Agent Success's ticket and approval service. Other clusters hand it a ticket under a named procedure (an SOP). It checks the request, answers accept or reject at once, then drives the ticket through the SOP's steps: an AI reviewer, a person, or an automated action at each step. It owns the tickets and their history in its own PostgreSQL database, and gives Agent Success staff one console to work them. This replaces the Jira Service Desk review path of the Mark 2 build and the cluster-specific approval screens.

It is a Nexus-first cluster like the others: one Nexus endpoint, service PitcrewServiceV1, the two fixed operations Execute and DescribeCapabilities, a generic gateway-1 that authenticates and validates, and components behind it. Its distinguishing pattern is that the workflow is an interpreter and the procedure is data. One Temporal workflow type loops over steps read from a versioned SOP (a Kubernetes custom resource), runs the actor the step names, applies the outcome and moves on. Changing how Agent Success handles a kind of ticket is a new SOP version, not a code deploy.

Two speeds are kept apart. Accepting or rejecting a ticket is a short call that returns a ticket ID. Resolving it can take hours, so the requester collects the result with a second, long-running call, or fetches it later. The console reads the queue from PostgreSQL for speed and sends every change through the gateway as the person acting, under a session they have deliberately assumed.

docs.title: Architecture Diagram
docs.text:
requesting service (other clusters)                 Agent Success staff (browser)
   │ Nexus Execute: submitTicket, awaitTicket              │ sign in: platform portal (Dex, Google groups)
   ▼                                                       ▼ STS handoff: system-scope session
 ┌─ pitcrew namespace ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  gateway-1  (STS token, payload schema, coarse authorize)                             │
 │     │ child workflow                                                                  │
 │     ▼                                                                                 │
 │  ticket-engine-1  (Temporal worker, Pinned)             console-1  (SPA + BFF)        │
 │   entrypoint workflow ── submitTicket ─▶ starts TicketWorkflowV1 (independent run)    │
 │   TicketWorkflowV1: load SOP ▶ run step actor ▶ transition ▶ repeat                   │
 │   activities: register, load-sop, run-ai-step, assign-human, transition, notify       │
 │        │  ▲ Updates (human actions)                       │ queue reads: read role     │
 │        │  └───────────────────── via gateway-1 ◀──────────┘ changes: Execute as user   │
 └────────┼───────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
          ▼               ▼                      ▼                 ▼
    PostgreSQL       Kubernetes API         LLM router         notifications
  ob1-pitcrew-db-1  SOP and prompt CRs   (Nexus, AI steps)   (Slack, email)

External systems: the auth cluster (STS for tokens and session exchange, OpenFGA for permissions), Temporal, PostgreSQL (Vault-issued credentials), the Kubernetes API, the platform's LLM router, and a notification channel.

docs.title: Core Interfaces
docs.text:
Architectural contracts, not implementation types:

  • SOP source. Returns the immutable definition of a named version (steps, outcomes, time limits, input and result schemas) and whether it is active, deprecated or retired. Backed by a Kubernetes cache that is loaded at start and kept current by a watch. Versions never change once published, so a stale cache can only miss a new version or a lifecycle change.
  • Actor. What a step runs. Three kinds: agent (an AI step with a prompt, a tool allow-list and an output schema), human (a queue and the actions people may take) and system (an automated call). A fourth kind, wait, holds the ticket for a timer or an outside event. Each returns one outcome from the closed set its step declares.
  • Ticket store. Writes a transition and its event in one transaction, idempotently, and serves the console's read model. The only writer of ticket state.
  • Authorizer. Answers permission questions against the Pit Crew OpenFGA model through go/authz with the identity the token fixed. Fail closed: a deny and an outage are different results and neither is an allow.
  • Notifier. Sends escalations and reminders to the Agent Success channel and owners.

docs.title: Ticket
docs.text:
Field Meaning ticketId tkt_<ULID>. The handle callers hold. Equal to the ticket workflow's ID. tenantId From the verified token of the submitter, never from the request. The tenant the subject content belongs to. requester The submitting service or user identity from the token sop {name, version, digest}. Pinned at acceptance. The digest is a hash of the definition used. state, step, attempt Current lifecycle state, the step being worked and the attempt count at that step owner Who must act next: agent, human:<queue>, system or requester priority, dueAt From the SOP's time limit for the current step result Set when final: the SOP's declared result schema createdAt, resolvedAt Timestamps

Lifecycle states: accepted, in_progress, waiting, resolved, rejected, cancelled, expired. The last four are final.

docs.title: Ticket event (append-only)
docs.text: seq, type (accepted, step_started, ai_decision, human_action, content_opened, sla_breached, escalated, transitioned, comment, resolved), actor (kind and ID, with the assumed session where there was one), step, payload, at. Every change to a ticket is an event; the ticket row is a projection of them.

docs.title: Subject content
docs.text: The thing being reviewed (the draft message, the proposed skill, the error report) is stored apart from the ticket row, in its own table keyed by tenant and ticket. Large artifacts stay where they live and are referenced by ID. The console's queue role has no access to this table.

docs.title: SOP (Kubernetes custom resource PTSOP)
docs.text:
apiVersion: pitcrew.budy.bot/v1alpha1
kind: PTSOP
metadata:
  name: content-approval-v1        # <sop>-v<version>; one object per version
spec:
  sop: content-approval
  version: 1
  lifecycle: active                # active | deprecated | retired. The only mutable field.
  input:  { schema: { ... } }      # JSON Schema the requester's input must satisfy
  result: { schema: { ... } }      # JSON Schema of the outcome returned to the requester
  start: auto_review
  steps:
    auto_review:
      type: agent
      prompt: { model: default-reasoning, system: "...", template: "...", outputSchema: { ... } }   # inline
      maxAttempts: 2
      sla: 2m
      outcomes: { approve: resolved, reject: rejected, unsure: human_review, failed: human_review }
    human_review:
      uses: human-approval         # shared step template: approve, reject, edit and approve, send back
      queue: agent-success
      session: editor              # tenant session boundary needed to act on this step
      sla: 4h
      onSlaBreach: { escalateTo: agent-success-lead }
      outcomes: { approve: resolved, reject: rejected, send_back: auto_review }

Annotations: spec is immutable once created (the CRD carries a transition rule that it equals its old value), apart from lifecycle. Every outcome target must name an existing step or a final state (a CRD validation rule). Reachability and dead ends are checked by a lint in CI. uses names a step template shipped with the cluster, which supplies the standard actions and outcomes for that actor kind so SOPs do not repeat them. A subflow step type is reserved for later nesting and is not accepted in Phase 1.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text: In Phase 1 a prompt is inline in its step: the template, model hint and the JSON Schema its output must satisfy. It is immutable with the SOP version, so a prompt change is a new SOP version. A separate prompt resource is deferred until prompts need to change faster than flows. The full CRD and two sample SOPs are in the TRD.

docs.title: gateway-1
docs.text: Generic and already present. It authenticates the STS token, checks the capability's JSON Schema and the coarse authorize check from the manifest, and starts the component's workflow as a child. It holds no state and no Pit Crew logic.

docs.title: ticket-engine-1
docs.text:
Entrypoint workflow. One workflow type, switching on capability, as the standard requires. submitTicket runs a short path: check the SOP is active, check the input against the SOP's input schema, register the ticket, start the ticket workflow as an independent run (not as a child of the call), and return the ticket ID or a typed error. Other capabilities read a ticket, or deliver a human action to a running ticket.

TicketWorkflowV1. The interpreter. State carried in the workflow is only the ticket ID, the SOP reference with digest, the current step and attempt counters. Everything else is in PostgreSQL. Each turn:

  1. Load the pinned SOP version through an activity, so the result is recorded in history and replay never reads live cluster state.
  2. Run the step's actor: an AI activity for agent; for human, create the queue entry and wait for an Update or the time limit; an activity for system; a timer or event for wait.
  3. Apply the outcome in one transaction (ticket row, event, queue entry), idempotently.
  4. Go to the step the outcome names, or finish if it names a final state.

Human actions arrive as Updates. The Update's validator rejects an action when the ticket is not at a human step, the caller does not hold the ticket, the action is not allowed at that step, or the ticket has moved on. The caller gets that answer straight away.

Each step's time limit is a workflow timer. A breach runs the step's onSlaBreach, records an event and sends a notification. Fleet-level alerting (queue age, breach rate) comes from metrics the worker exports, which the shared Alertmanager rules consume.

Search attributes on every run: ticket ID, tenant, SOP name and version, step and state, so a run can be found in Temporal without the database.

docs.title: console-1
docs.text: The operator console, one container. It signs staff in through the platform portal, reads the queue and ticket metadata from the read model, and sends every change through gateway-1 using the staff member's own token. It never writes to PostgreSQL. See Identity, Roles and Sessions.

docs.title: Submit and accept
docs.text:
service ──Execute submitTicket {sop, input, callback?}──▶ gateway-1 ──▶ ticket-engine-1 entrypoint
          (idempotencyKey, STS token: tenant and user fixed from the token)
                                                           │ SOP active? input valid? (typed errors if not)
                                                           │ insert ticket + accepted event (unique on tenant, requester, key)
                                                           │ start TicketWorkflowV1 (workflow ID = ticketId)
service ◀──{ticketId}─────────────────────────────────────┘   (a repeat call returns the same ticketId)

docs.title: Wait for the result
docs.text:
service ──Execute awaitTicket {ticketId}──▶ gateway-1 ──▶ ticket-engine-1 ──waits on the ticket workflow
service ◀─────────────────────────────── {state, result} once the ticket is final
(if the service is not waiting, getTicket returns the same result later)

docs.title: AI first, then a person
docs.text:
TicketWorkflowV1: step auto_review (agent)
   ├─ activity: prompt v4 via LLM router, output validated against the prompt's schema
   ├─ outcome approve ─────────────────────────────▶ resolved  (event ai_decision, prompt version, reasoning)
   └─ outcome unsure, or invalid output after maxAttempts ─▶ step human_review
step human_review (human): queue entry created, owner = human:agent-success, timer = 4h
   ├─ Update {action: approve} from staff ───────────▶ resolved
   └─ timer fires ─▶ onSlaBreach: escalate, notify, event sla_breached

docs.title: Staff open a ticket
docs.text:
staff ──browser──▶ console-1: queue from read model (summaries only; system-scope session)
staff clicks a ticket ──▶ console-1 asks for a tenant session for ticket.tenantId at the step's boundary
                          (a deliberate, recorded assume step; viewer to read, editor to act)
console-1 ──Execute getTicket (tenant session)──▶ gateway-1 ──▶ content returned, event content_opened
staff ──Execute resolveTicket {action} (tenant session)──▶ gateway-1 ──▶ Update on the ticket workflow

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text: Staff reach the console from the platform portal. The portal signs them in through the shared Dex with Google, reads their Google groups, and exchanges the Dex token at the STS for a session. A new Google group for Agent Success (name to agree) is added to the portal's access groups with a session-boundary cap, and as the visibility group of the Pit Crew console route. The portal hands a one-time handoff to the console, which redeems it into a host-only cookie; the browser never holds a token. This is the existing mechanism, used unchanged.

docs.title: Platform role
docs.text: A new platform role, agent success, is added to the platform authorization model beside the existing platform roles. It is stored on the platform object, limited to internal users like every platform role, and is deliberately not implied by platform admin, support or viewer. Agent Success operators are granted it by name. The STS maps the role to the session boundary it makes a person eligible for on the platform; that mapping lives in the auth service, alongside the existing platform boundary mappings.

docs.title: Two layers of access
docs.text:
Layer What it holds Who can reach it Envelope Ticket ID, tenant, SOP, state, step, owner, due time, queue A system-scope session with the agent success role: the queue and assignment actions Subject content The material under review, and acting on it A tenant-scope session for the ticket's tenant, assumed deliberately when a ticket is opened, at the boundary the SOP step declares

The ticket's tenant is fixed from the submitter's token. Operators do not carry a tenant of their own; they assume the ticket's tenant for the time they work on it, and the assumption is an event on the ticket. The AI step is an internal service identity that does the same: it obtains its own session for the ticket's tenant and never stores or reuses the requester's token, which expires before a ticket does.

docs.title: Permissions model
docs.text: A new pitcrew model module in the authorization config repository defines two object types, following the artifact-store precedent of putting the tenant in the object ID: the SOP (which services may submit it, and which outputs they may read) and the ticket (pitcrew_ticket_1:{tenantId}/{ticketId}, with permissions that extend from the platform's session tiers rather than from stored roles alone). The Nexus service and its operations are registered in the topology file, and tenant admission is added, as for the other clusters.

docs.title: PostgreSQL (ob1-pitcrew-db-1)
docs.text:
Table Purpose Notes tickets One row per ticket; a projection of its events Unique on tenant, requester and idempotency key ticket_events Append-only history The audit record; never updated ticket_content Subject content and large inputs Separate table and database role; not readable by the console's queue role queue_entries Open human work: queue, claim, due time Drives the queue view comments Staff notes on a ticket Events of type comment ticket_queue_v (view) Envelope fields only, for the console The only object the console's read role can select

Credentials are issued by Vault. Schema changes run as a migration Job under a separate role, as in the other clusters. Retention periods for content and events are an open question.

docs.title: Temporal
docs.text: Workflow history is kept for the namespace's retention period (7 days is the intended setting). History is not the record: the database is. Ticket workflows have a maximum run time that ends the ticket as expired, so an unattended ticket cannot live forever.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: SOP and prompt custom resources, read through a cache with a watch. The worker needs read access to those resources in its own namespace and network egress to the Kubernetes API.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Dependency How used Temporal Workflows, Updates, timers, Nexus endpoint, Worker Deployment Versioning (Pinned) Auth cluster, STS Token verification (JWKS) at the gateway; session exchange for the console and the AI step Auth cluster, OpenFGA via go/authz Permission checks on tickets and SOPs Kubernetes API SOP and prompt resources PostgreSQL The ticket store LLM router (Nexus) AI step prompts with structured output Platform UI, Dex Staff sign-in and session handoff Notification channel Escalations to the Agent Success channel (provider open) Requesting clusters Callers of the Pit Crew contract; no calls out from Pit Crew to them in Phase 1

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. The ticket is data; the workflow is an interpreter. Procedures change without code changes.
  2. PostgreSQL owns the ticket; Temporal owns the waiting. One source of truth for state, one for time.
  3. A ticket runs under one immutable SOP version for life. Open tickets are never changed by a new version.
  4. Identity comes from the token only. Nothing the caller says about tenant or user is read.
  5. Seeing customer content is a deliberate, recorded act. The queue shows envelopes; content needs an assumed tenant session.
  6. Answer fast, resolve slowly. Accept or reject in one short call; deliver the outcome through a separate waiting call.
  7. Every automated decision is explainable after the fact. The prompt version, input and output are on the ticket's events.
  8. Changes go through the gateway as the person acting. The console reads for speed and never writes.

docs.title: Design Decisions Log
docs.text: Question Resolution Does Pit Crew own state or only view other systems' state? It owns tickets and their history in its own PostgreSQL database. It is the system of record for Agent Success work. One workflow per ticket kind, or a generic one? One generic interpreter workflow; a ticket's kind is an SOP. Steps are actors (AI, person, system, wait), and flow and limits are configuration. Where do SOPs live? As Kubernetes custom resources with a published CRD and no operator. Immutable per version, with a lifecycle flag. Read through a cache with a watch. Can a request be accepted before it is valid? No. Intake checks that the SOP is active and the input matches before accepting. A bad request is rejected at once and no ticket exists. How does a caller learn the result? submitTicket returns the ticket ID at once. awaitTicket is a long-running call the caller waits on. getTicket fetches it later. The Nexus call carries the result, so callers need no callback service and no workflow signal across namespaces. What is the caller's handle? The ticket ID, equal to the ticket workflow ID. A run ID is a trace field only. Who sets the ticket's tenant? The submitter's verified token. The payload cannot assert it. How is operator access shaped? Two layers. The queue is a platform-scope view of envelopes. Opening content is a deliberate assume into the ticket's tenant, recorded as an event. No separate Pit Crew tenant. How do staff get access? A new platform role for Agent Success, separate from and not implied by the other platform roles. Sign-in is the platform portal with a Google group for Agent Success. How long do tickets live? Designed to resolve within 24 hours. A maximum run time (initial value 72 hours) ends the ticket as expired. Temporal history is kept 7 days; the database is the record. Is continue-as-new used? Not in Phase 1. A ticket is short enough that history growth is not a concern. What happens when a ticket "comes back"? It becomes a new ticket linked to the earlier one. Grouping into a case is deferred. Where does the console read the queue from? PostgreSQL, through a SELECT-only role (pitcrew_meta_read) on the meta schema, behind a verified system-scope token that carries the agent success role. Subject content is in a separate content schema the role cannot read, and is fetched through the gateway. How is the SOP kind named and where do prompts live? The custom resource kind is PTSOP (group pitcrew.budy.bot). Prompts are inline in the step in Phase 1. How are SLA breaches alerted? A SQL exporter reads breach rows from meta with the console's credential; ServiceMonitor and PrometheusRule resources feed the existing Prometheus operator and Alertmanager (team agent-success). How does content access work in Phase 1? A platform-scope token plus a fail-closed Pit Crew authorization check, recorded as content_opened. A true tenant assume needs a platform feature and is a Phase 2 dependency. One worker or several? One standard worker, ticket-engine-1, with the entrypoint and ticket workflows. Does the console write to PostgreSQL? No. Every change goes through the gateway as the user, which applies the correct permissions. What goes through Temporal and what does not? Only client-specific data and changes: opening a ticket's content, acting on a ticket, claiming, releasing, assigning and commenting. The queue, its filters, the stats and a ticket's history are database reads of the meta schema through the read role, so listing and filtering never load Temporal. How does the console read the result of a gateway call? Temporal's Nexus HTTP endpoint answers asynchronously, so the console passes an in-cluster callback URL and waits for Temporal to post the result. The console therefore runs one replica and the platform allows Temporal to reach its callback port (see the TRD, "As built"). How does the console know the caller is Agent Success staff? It asks the OpenFGA read-only proxy before every query and gateway call (may_view_pitcrew_queue, may_work_pitcrew_queue) and fails closed. A role claim in the STS token would replace this check; the platform owners confirm which they want.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
Resolved by the design decisions above: console read path, platform-scope callers for envelope capabilities, procedure and prompt publishing, cross-repository changes (the pull requests are linked from the service document), and the names ticket-engine-1 and console-1. Still open:

  1. Assume mechanism. The STS exchanges a system session for a tenant session through the portal's auth-code flow; a console cannot call it directly. Phase 1 uses a fail-closed check instead (see TRD). Decide whether the platform gets a console-callable exchange.
  2. Delegation authority. Give the agent success role the matching delegation rungs, or write a time-bounded grant per ticket on claim. The second is tighter and needs the authorization manager to write grants for Pit Crew.
  3. Long waits through Nexus. awaitTicket is bounded (default 30 minutes, maximum 60) and callers re-call. Confirm this is acceptable and the endpoint's timeout.
  4. Worker versioning for 72-hour tickets. Confirm that the ceiling is acceptable for deploys, or set a shorter one.
  5. Guards. Phase 1 uses closed outcome sets only. If an expression language is needed, decide before the CRD is published beyond v1alpha1.
  6. AI step plumbing. Which LLM router operation supports structured output with a schema, who owns prompt evaluation, and the per-ticket budget.
  7. Notification provider. Slack through the communications gateway or directly, and who maintains the on-call roster.
  8. Retention. How long to keep content, events and queue history.
  9. Jira. Whether Mark 2's Jira path is replaced at once or runs alongside, and who migrates open tickets.
  10. Phase 2. Raising a ticket from the console (see the TRD, "As built (Phase 1)").

docs.title: pitcrew-cluster-1
docs.text:
pitcrew-cluster-1 is Agent Success's ticket and approval service. Platform services hand it a ticket under a named procedure (an SOP); it accepts or rejects the request at once, then drives the ticket through the SOP's steps (an AI reviewer, a person, or an automated action) and returns the outcome. Agent Success staff work every ticket from one console. It covers escalations, PR reviews, code feedback, and content, skill and context-change approvals, and reduces the fragmented approval workflows spread across Jira and cluster-specific UIs.

Status: Phase 1 built, in review (November 2026). ticket-engine-1, the PTSOP CRD, the SQL exporter and the console are written and open as draft pull requests in this repository and in the platform repositories they touch; nothing is released or deployed. The PRD, HLD, TRD and Nexus contracts describe what was built, with the deviations from the first design recorded in the TRD's "As built" section. The owner has decided the core shape (a ticket system of record in PostgreSQL, SOPs as data, a deliberate tenant-assume step for customer content, and a dedicated Agent Success platform role); the HLD's Design Decisions Log lists what is settled and its Open Questions lists what is not.

docs.title: Boundary
docs.text:
Owns Does not own Tickets and their history, in this cluster's PostgreSQL database The systems that originate the work (DT reviewer in dt-manager-1, context review gate in context-cluster, PR hosts) and their decision logic SOP execution: steps, AI and human actors, time limits, escalation Identity, roles and permissions (auth cluster) The Agent Success operator console: queue, ticket history, review and approval screens Delivering approved messages to customers (the communications services) Per-ticket audit: who decided what, under which SOP version, and who opened which customer's content Manager approval of report changes

It is a callee of other clusters through its own Nexus contract (PitcrewServiceV1) and publishes nothing to them in Phase 1.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
Repository type Nexus-first (gateway + component) plus a non-Nexus console Components gateway-1 (exists), ticket-engine-1 (built, in review: intake and the SOP-driven ticket workflow), console-1 (built, in review: React single-page app and Node BFF in one container, per the platform console standard) Precedent the platform console standard and the nainai console for the UI; studio-services-cluster-1 for a Nexus-first cluster with a PostgreSQL store Product context the Agent Success Rep persona and dashboards/queues in the Mark 2 PRD

The rest of the standard applies unchanged: Go monorepo for services, component catalog (the console is a component with validation.kind: node), thin entry-workflow callers, umbrella plus sub-charts, README, changesets.

First pass (October 2026): the gateway only (gateway-1), like nainai-cluster-1; the components above are added one at a time afterwards, each as a catalog entry.

docs.title: Names (derived from the standard)
docs.text: Kubernetes namespace ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-pitcrew-1-ns-1 Nexus service (decided) PitcrewServiceV1 Gateway component, task queue gateway-1, pitcrew-cluster-1-gateway-1-tq Netpol label, Vault Transit role budybot.io/netpol: pitcrew-gateway-1, ob1_crossplane_vault_transit_pitcrew_gateway_1 Umbrella chart pitcrew-cluster-1-repo-1 Image repository ob1-ecr-repo-v2/ob1_tf_aws_ecr_pitcrew-cluster-1_repo-1 Helm repository ob1-helm-chart-repo-v1/pitcrew-cluster-1-repo-1

docs.title: Callers (assumed, unconfirmed)
docs.text: Callers submit tickets through the Pit Crew Nexus contract. Expected first callers: the DT reviewer in dt-manager-1 (the requestContextReviewV2 flow and package or code review), the context review gate in context-cluster, the DT consulting service (errors and code errors), the Digital Teammates themselves (communication, skill and tool approvals, client emails), and the PR host for PR reviews and code feedback (GitHub and/or gitjib). Each needs an SOP and, for tenant data, a tenant-scoped token. Jira: Mark 2 uses Jira Service Desk today; Pit Crew replaces that path, and the cut-over is an open question in the HLD.

docs.title: Settled and open
docs.text:
Settled by the owner (full list in the HLD Design Decisions Log): Pit Crew is the system of record for tickets (PostgreSQL, ob1-pitcrew-db-1); the workflow is a generic interpreter and SOPs are versioned Kubernetes resources; a request is accepted or rejected immediately and the outcome is collected by a separate call; the console reads for speed but changes go through the gateway as the person; customer content is reached only by a deliberate, recorded tenant assume; staff hold a dedicated Agent Success platform role and sign in through the platform portal.

Resolved in the Phase 1 build (see the TRD, "As built"): the console's read path (database reads of the meta schema, changes through the gateway), platform-scope access to ticket envelopes (the read role), the SOP publishing path (PTSOP resources), and the cross-repository changes (the build PRs below).

Still open (HLD Open Questions): how the console assumes a tenant session (Phase 1 uses an OpenFGA check and fails closed until the platform provides an exchange), delegation scope, long-wait limits, guard language, AI step plumbing, notification provider, retention, and the Jira cut-over.

docs.title: Pit Crew Cluster — Nexus Contracts
docs.text: How other clusters, and the Pit Crew console, call the cluster. This is a design-stage contract: capability names and payloads are proposed and become authoritative in the contract module of pitcrew-cluster-1_repo-1 (shared/contract) when the first component ships. The JSON Schemas the gateway enforces will live in charts/gateway-1/files/capabilities/ticket-engine-1.yaml.

docs.title: Endpoint and operations
docs.text:
Nexus endpoint ob1-nexus-pitcrew-cluster-1-endpoint-1 (never versioned) Service PitcrewServiceV1 Operations Execute and DescribeCapabilities STS audience urn:budy:nexus:ob1-nexus-pitcrew-cluster-1-endpoint-1:PitcrewServiceV1 Component ticket-engine-1 (provisional)

Execute takes {component, capability, payload, idempotencyKey?, auth: {token}} and returns {ok, data?, error?: {code, message}}. The caller's tenant, user and session boundary come only from the STS token; anything the payload says about them is ignored. Mutating capabilities require idempotencyKey.

DescribeCapabilities returns the capability list and, with includeSchemas, each capability's JSON Schema. It needs a valid token and nothing else. It does not list SOPs; use describeSops.

docs.title: Scope and session rules
docs.text:
Kind Token scope Session boundary Capabilities Requester Tenant any describeSops, submitTicket, awaitTicket, getTicket, cancelTicket Envelope (staff) Platform, with the agent success role editor listTickets, claimTicket, releaseTicket, assignTicket Content (staff) Tenant, assumed for the ticket's tenant viewer to read, the step's boundary to act getTicketContent, listTicketEvents, resolveTicket, addComment

Envelope capabilities return and change only the ticket's envelope: ID, tenant, SOP, state, step, owner, queue and due time, plus the requester's short summary. They never return subject content. Requesters should treat summary as visible to all Agent Success staff and keep sensitive material in input.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Every call is Execute with component: "ticket-engine-1". A ticket ID has the form tkt_<ULID>.

Capability Payload Result describeSops sop? (name) sops[]: name, version, lifecycle, inputSchema, resultSchema. Only SOPs the caller may submit. submitTicket sop ({name, version}), input, summary? (up to 140 characters), priority? ticketId, state, sop, dueAt?. A repeat with the same key returns the same ticket. awaitTicket ticketId, waitUpTo? (seconds, default 1800, maximum 3600) ticketId, final (boolean), state, and when final: result, resolvedAt. When the wait ends first, final is false and the caller calls again. getTicket ticketId Envelope, and result when final. For the requester, its own tickets only. cancelTicket ticketId, reason? ticketId, state (cancelled). Idempotent. Refused once final. listTickets queue?, state?, owner?, sop?, dueBefore?, limit? (1 to 200), cursor? tickets[] (envelopes), nextCursor? claimTicket ticketId Envelope. Refused if another person holds it. releaseTicket ticketId Envelope assignTicket ticketId, assignee Envelope getTicketContent ticketId input and the subject content. Records a content_opened event for the caller. listTicketEvents ticketId, limit?, cursor? events[] (oldest first), nextCursor? resolveTicket ticketId, action, expectedStep, comment?, edits? or input? New state and step. addComment ticketId, text The new event

action is one of the actions the current step allows. The standard human step offers approve, reject, edit_approve, send_back and update_input. expectedStep is the step the caller saw; if the ticket has moved, the call is refused rather than applied.

submitTicket is validated twice. The gateway checks the envelope against the capability's schema. The component then checks input against the named SOP version's input schema and refuses the call, creating no ticket, if the SOP is unknown, deprecated or retired, or the input does not match.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Failures return as ok: false with a code from the shared envelope. Where a caller needs to tell two causes apart, the message begins with a stable reason token (proposed, until the shared envelope gains more codes).

Reason Code Retry SOP_UNKNOWN NOT_FOUND No SOP_DEPRECATED, SOP_RETIRED INVALID_ARGUMENT No; choose a newer version INPUT_INVALID (fields listed) INVALID_ARGUMENT No TICKET_NOT_FOUND NOT_FOUND No CONFLICT (ticket moved on, held by someone else, or action not allowed at this step) INVALID_ARGUMENT Only after re-reading the ticket NOT_PERMITTED PERMISSION_DENIED No Token missing, expired or wrong audience UNAUTHORIZED No; get a new token Dependency down UNAVAILABLE Yes, with backoff Anything else INTERNAL Yes, a limited number of times

nonRetryableErrorTypes for callers: INVALID_ARGUMENT, NOT_FOUND, PERMISSION_DENIED, UNAUTHORIZED.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text: Capability Timeout Notes submitTicket, cancelTicket, getTicket, describeSops 15 s Accept or reject target: p99 under 5 s (PRD) Envelope capabilities and resolveTicket, addComment, getTicketContent, listTicketEvents 15 s The action is applied or refused in this window awaitTicket 1 h 1 m (the longest waitUpTo plus margin) Bounded so no Nexus call lives for the ticket's whole life; the caller re-calls until final is true

docs.title: Caller guidance
docs.text:
A workflow in another cluster submits, then waits. This is a sketch, not the typed binding.

nc := workflow.NewNexusClient(contract.NexusEndpoint, contract.ServiceName)

// 1. Submit: short call; accepted or rejected now.
var sub contract.ExecuteResponse
fut := nc.ExecuteOperation(ctx, contract.OperationExecute, submitRequest, workflow.NexusOperationOptions{})
if err := fut.Get(ctx, &sub); err != nil { return err }
if !sub.OK { return nonRetryable(sub.Error) } // rejected: no ticket exists

// 2. Wait: repeat until the ticket is final.
for {
    var res contract.ExecuteResponse
    f := nc.ExecuteOperation(ctx, contract.OperationExecute, awaitRequest(ticketID), workflow.NexusOperationOptions{})
    if err := f.Get(ctx, &res); err != nil { return err }
    if awaited(res).Final { return awaited(res).Result }
}

Guidance:

  • Always send an idempotencyKey on submitTicket. Reuse the same key when retrying so a retry returns the same ticket.
  • Store the ticketId. It is the only handle.
  • Do not keep the caller's token waiting on a ticket. Each call carries a fresh token.
  • Pin the SOP version in the request. Use describeSops at build or deploy time to see which versions are active and what input they expect.
  • Treat final: false as normal, not as an error.

docs.title: Versioning policy
docs.text:
• The service version covers the whole contract. A breaking change to a capability's payload or meaning adds PitcrewServiceV2 beside V1; V1 is never edited incompatibly.
  • New capabilities and new optional fields are additive and do not change the version.
  • An SOP version's input and result schemas are part of that SOP version, not of the service. Changing them means publishing a new SOP version. Old versions keep working until retired.

docs.title: Pit Crew Cluster — Product Requirements
docs.text: Draft. Targets marked proposed are starting points to confirm with Agent Success. Anything the owner has decided is recorded in the HLD Design Decisions Log, not here.

docs.title: Why This Exists
docs.text: Agent Success staff approve and resolve work that Digital Teammates (DTs) and platform services cannot, or should not, finish alone: a drafted customer message, a new skill or tool, an error in a consulting engagement, a client email that needs a human decision. Today these requests are spread across Jira Service Desk tickets, email and cluster-specific screens. No single place shows what is waiting, who owns it or what was decided. Without one queue, work waits unseen, decisions are recorded in different shapes (or not at all), and every new kind of approval means another one-off tool.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Any platform service can hand Pit Crew a request for review, called a ticket, under a named procedure (an SOP). Pit Crew checks the request immediately and either accepts it or rejects it with a reason. An accepted ticket then moves through the steps its procedure defines: an AI reviewer may try first, a person may decide, or both, in the order the procedure says. Agent Success staff work from one console that shows every open ticket, what happens next and the full history. When the ticket is resolved, the requesting service gets the outcome back.

docs.title: Request types
docs.text:
Which procedure handles a request is decided by the requester naming it. The list below is what the first procedures are expected to cover.

Request type Example Typical outcome Communication and content approvals A DT's drafted message or report change waiting for review before it reaches a customer Approve, send back with feedback, or reject Context-change approvals A proposed change to stored context that must pass the review gate Approve or reject Platform approvals A DT creating a new skill or tool, which must follow the platform's internal schemas Approve, or request changes Engineering escalations The DT consulting service reports an error or a code error it cannot resolve Guidance to retry, a fix, or a hand-off to engineering PR reviews and code feedback Review status and feedback on a proposed code change Approve, or send feedback Client emails to a DT A client's email that the DT should not answer alone Reply approved, edited, or escalated

docs.title: Intake Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Accept a request from an authenticated platform service and answer right away: accepted (with a ticket reference) or rejected (with the reason).
  • Reject a request that names an unknown, retired or deprecated procedure, or whose content does not match what the procedure expects.
  • Treat a repeated submission of the same request as the same ticket.
  • Let the requester wait for the final outcome, or collect it later.

docs.title: Procedure Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Run each ticket under exactly one named procedure version for its whole life.
  • Let a procedure say, for each step, whether an AI reviewer, a person or an automated action acts, what the person may do, how long it may take and where each outcome leads.
  • Make a new procedure version available without disturbing tickets already open.

docs.title: Work Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Run the AI reviewer where the procedure says, record what it decided and why, and fall back to a person as the procedure directs.
  • Put tickets that need a person into a queue, show who owns the next action and track the time limit.
  • Escalate when a time limit is missed, and notify the Agent Success channel.
  • Give staff the actions the procedure allows, such as approve, reject, edit and approve, send back, or update the input.

docs.title: Console Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Show every open ticket in one queue, filterable by request type, owner, state and due time, without showing customer content.
  • Require a deliberate step to open a ticket's content, and record who opened what and when.
  • Show each ticket's full history: every step, actor, decision and procedure version.
  • Let staff act on a ticket only through the actions its current step allows.

docs.title: What Pit Crew Is NOT Responsible For
docs.text:
• The decision logic of the originating system: the DT, the DT reviewer, the consulting service and the PR host own what they ask for and what they do with the answer.
  • Who a person is and what they may do: the auth cluster owns identity, roles and permissions. Pit Crew uses them.
  • Delivering messages to customers: the communications services deliver, after Pit Crew has approved.
  • Manager approval of report changes: managers still approve their own report changes. Pit Crew covers the Agent Success review step.
  • Live conversation between a DT and staff: tickets are asynchronous in Phase 1.
  • Long-running customer cases: a ticket is one decision. Threads that span many exchanges are Phase 2.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
All targets are proposed.

Metric Target Accept or reject answer to a requester p50 under 1 second, p99 under 5 seconds Tickets reaching a final state within 24 hours At least 95% Tickets reaching a final state within 72 hours 100% (an unresolved ticket ends as expired and escalated, never silently open) Tickets lost or decided twice because of a restart or failure 0 Automated decisions that record the procedure version, prompt version and reasoning 100% Views of customer content that are recorded with who, when and which customer 100% Console queue load with 500 open tickets p95 under 1.5 seconds

docs.title: Phase 1 UAT Acceptance Criteria
docs.text: # Scenario Pass condition 1 A service submits a valid request under an active procedure It gets an acceptance with a ticket reference within the target time, and the ticket appears in the console queue 2 A service submits a request naming an unknown procedure The request is rejected with a clear reason and no ticket exists 3 A service submits a request under a deprecated procedure version It is rejected for the new ticket; tickets already open under that version carry on 4 A service submits content that does not match what the procedure expects It is rejected with the offending fields named and no ticket exists 5 A service submits the same request twice (same request key) Both calls return the same ticket and only one ticket exists 6 The procedure has the AI reviewer decide first and it approves The ticket resolves without a person, the decision, reasoning and prompt version are on the ticket, and the requester receives the outcome 7 The AI reviewer fails or is unsure The ticket moves to the person queue the procedure names, and the staff member sees the AI's recommendation 8 A staff member approves a ticket The requester receives the outcome, and the history shows who, when and under which procedure version 9 A staff member edits and approves, or sends a ticket back with feedback The ticket goes to the step the procedure names, the revision is counted and the edit is in the history 10 Two staff members act on the same ticket at once The first action counts, the second is told the ticket was already handled, and no action is applied twice 11 A staff member opens a ticket's content An explicit access step is required, and the history records who opened content of which customer and when 12 A person without the Agent Success role tries to use the console They cannot see the queue or any ticket 13 The queue is open It shows ticket summaries only, with no customer content, until a ticket is deliberately opened 14 A step's time limit is missed The ticket is flagged and escalated as the procedure says, the Agent Success channel is notified, and the console shows the breach 15 A ticket reaches its maximum age without resolution It ends as expired, is escalated and stays visible in history 16 A new procedure version is published while tickets are open Open tickets finish under their original version and new tickets use the new one 17 The service restarts while tickets are mid-step No ticket is lost, and no decision is recorded twice 18 A requester waits for the outcome, or comes back later A waiting requester is told when the ticket finishes; a returning requester can fetch the outcome

docs.title: Phase 2 / Deferred Scope
docs.text:
• Customer support threads and cases: tickets that come back and forth with a customer need a case that groups many tickets. Deferred until Agent Success decides to take customer support.
  • Procedures inside procedures: a step that runs another procedure. Phase 1 procedures are flat, with shared step templates.
  • A procedure editor in the console: procedures are written and reviewed as code in Phase 1.
  • Importing Jira history: new tickets start in Pit Crew. Whether old ones are migrated is open.
  • Several AI reviewers working on one ticket: Phase 1 has at most one AI actor per step.
  • Reporting beyond the console: queue and flow dashboards are in scope; deeper analytics are not.

docs.title: Pit Crew Cluster — TRD
docs.text:
Technical requirements for Phase 1 of pitcrew-cluster-1: what to build, with the exact shapes. Product intent is in the PRD, architecture in the HLD, the caller contract in nexus-contracts, and how it was built in the "As built" section at the end.

Names below follow the existing cluster conventions and are checked against the reference repositories (studio-services-cluster-1, the nainai console and the platform console standard). Where a name is derived from a pattern rather than copied, it is marked derive, and the implementer confirms it against the repository before use.

docs.title: Data Model (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
Two schemas separate what the console may read from what only the worker and the user's own session may read.

Schema Holds Readable by meta Envelope data: no tenant content, nothing a requester typed worker role, meta_read role (console BFF, exporter) content Subject content, comments, event payloads worker role only

docs.title: DDL (migration 0001_init.sql)
docs.text:
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS meta;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS content;

CREATE TABLE meta.tickets (
  ticket_id        text PRIMARY KEY,                      -- tkt_<ULID>
  tenant_id        text NOT NULL,
  requester        text NOT NULL,                         -- identity from token
  idempotency_key  text NOT NULL,
  sop_name         text NOT NULL,
  sop_version      int  NOT NULL,
  sop_digest       text NOT NULL,
  state            text NOT NULL CHECK (state IN
                   ('accepted','in_progress','waiting','resolved','rejected','cancelled','expired')),
  step             text NOT NULL,
  attempt          int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  owner_kind       text NOT NULL CHECK (owner_kind IN ('agent','human','system','requester')),
  owner_queue      text,
  assignee         text,
  priority         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal' CHECK (priority IN ('low','normal','high','urgent')),
  summary          text,                                  -- up to 140 chars, visible to all staff
  due_at           timestamptz,
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  resolved_at      timestamptz,
  result_state     text,                                  -- final state label only; result body is in content
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, requester, idempotency_key)
);
CREATE INDEX tickets_open_idx ON meta.tickets (owner_queue, due_at) WHERE state IN ('accepted','in_progress','waiting');
CREATE INDEX tickets_tenant_idx ON meta.tickets (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE meta.ticket_events (
  ticket_id   text NOT NULL REFERENCES meta.tickets(ticket_id),
  seq         int  NOT NULL,
  type        text NOT NULL,                              -- accepted, step_started, ai_decision, human_action,
                                                          -- content_opened, sla_breached, escalated, transitioned, comment, resolved
  actor_kind  text NOT NULL,                              -- user, service, agent, system
  actor_id    text NOT NULL,
  assumed_tenant text,                                    -- set when the actor acted in an assumed tenant session
  step        text,
  at          timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (ticket_id, seq)
);

CREATE TABLE meta.queue_entries (
  ticket_id    text PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES meta.tickets(ticket_id),
  queue        text NOT NULL,
  step         text NOT NULL,
  claimed_by   text,
  claimed_at   timestamptz,
  due_at       timestamptz NOT NULL,
  breached_at  timestamptz,                               -- set once by the worker timer; exporter counts these
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX queue_due_idx ON meta.queue_entries (due_at) WHERE breached_at IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE content.ticket_content (
  ticket_id   text PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES meta.tickets(ticket_id),
  tenant_id   text NOT NULL,
  input       jsonb NOT NULL,                             -- requester's validated input
  subject     jsonb,                                      -- material under review, or an artifact reference
  result      jsonb                                       -- SOP result body when final
);

CREATE TABLE content.event_payloads (
  ticket_id   text NOT NULL,
  seq         int  NOT NULL,
  payload     jsonb NOT NULL,                             -- AI reasoning, human edits, comment text
  PRIMARY KEY (ticket_id, seq),
  FOREIGN KEY (ticket_id, seq) REFERENCES meta.ticket_events(ticket_id, seq)
);

CREATE VIEW meta.ticket_queue_v AS
  SELECT t.ticket_id, t.tenant_id, t.sop_name, t.sop_version, t.state, t.step, t.owner_kind,
         t.owner_queue, t.assignee, t.priority, t.summary, t.due_at, t.created_at, t.updated_at,
         q.claimed_by, q.breached_at
    FROM meta.tickets t LEFT JOIN meta.queue_entries q USING (ticket_id);

summary is requester-written and is shown to every staff member who can see the queue. The capability contract tells requesters to keep sensitive material in input.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Standard roles (-admin, -user, -read-role) and standard grants on public come from the existing database provisioning and are not changed. Migration objects live in meta and content, so the standard -read-role does not apply to them. The custom grants file ob1-pitcrew-db-1.sql in the EKS stack's postgres-objs jobs (the per-database custom grants location) adds:

-- Console metadata read role: the BFF and the exporter use this and nothing else.
DO $$ BEGIN
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'pitcrew_meta_read') THEN
    CREATE ROLE pitcrew_meta_read NOLOGIN;
  END IF;
END $$;

GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA meta TO pitcrew_meta_read;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA meta TO pitcrew_meta_read;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA meta GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO pitcrew_meta_read;
REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA content FROM pitcrew_meta_read;

-- Worker role: full DML on both schemas.
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA meta, content TO "ob1-pitcrew-db-1-user";    -- role name: derive from the standard
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA meta, content TO "ob1-pitcrew-db-1-user";
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA meta, content GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO "ob1-pitcrew-db-1-user";
GRANT USAGE ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA meta, content TO "ob1-pitcrew-db-1-user";

The Vault database engine (db-eng-1) gets a precreated role for the console, with creation statements that GRANT pitcrew_meta_read TO "{{name}}". Its name follows <service>_<suffix>_vault_pg_role_1 with suffix meta_read (derive). The worker's dynamic role uses the standard -user suffix. The migration Job uses the static admin role, as in the other clusters.

ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES applies to objects created by the role that runs it. The migration runs as the static admin, so the grants job must run ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE <admin> (derive), or the migration must re-grant at its end. The implementer verifies with a test that a new table created by migration is readable by pitcrew_meta_read and, for content, is not.

docs.title: PTSOP Custom Resource
docs.text:
Property Value Group, version pitcrew.budy.bot/v1alpha1 Kind, plural, short name PTSOP, ptsops, ptsop Scope Namespaced (the Pit Crew namespace) Immutability spec equals its old value, except spec.lifecycle, enforced by a CEL transition rule Prompts Inline in the step; there is no separate prompt kind in Phase 1

CRD validation rules (CEL): every value in a step's outcomes is a step name or one of resolved, rejected; start is a step name; a step has exactly one of type: agent|human|system|wait; uses is one of the shipped templates; sla and timeout match a duration pattern.

Schema (abridged to the fields the worker reads):

spec:
  sop: string                    # name, e.g. content-approval
  version: int                   # >= 1
  lifecycle: active|deprecated|retired
  maxRuntime: 72h
  input:  { schema: <JSON Schema> }
  result: { schema: <JSON Schema> }
  start: string
  steps:
    <name>:
      type: agent|human|system|wait
      uses: human-approval       # human steps only
      queue: string              # human steps
      session: viewer|editor     # tenant session boundary to act
      sla: duration
      onSlaBreach: { escalateTo: string }
      maxAttempts: int           # agent steps
      prompt:                    # agent steps
        model: string            # hint passed to the LLM router
        system: string
        template: string         # Go text/template over {input, subject}
        outputSchema: <JSON Schema>   # must include `outcome` (enum of the step's outcome keys)
      action: { capability: string }  # system steps
      wait: { for: duration }         # wait steps
      outcomes: { <outcome>: <step|resolved|rejected> }

docs.title: Sample 1: content-approval-v1
docs.text:
An AI reviewer approves or rejects a draft message; unsure or invalid output goes to a person.

apiVersion: pitcrew.budy.bot/v1alpha1
kind: PTSOP
metadata:
  name: content-approval-v1
spec:
  sop: content-approval
  version: 1
  lifecycle: active
  maxRuntime: 72h
  input:
    schema:
      type: object
      required: [channel, draft]
      properties:
        channel: { type: string, enum: [email, sms, whatsapp] }
        draft:   { type: string, minLength: 1, maxLength: 4000 }
        context: { type: string }
  result:
    schema:
      type: object
      required: [decision]
      properties:
        decision: { type: string, enum: [approved, rejected] }
        editedDraft: { type: string }
        reason: { type: string }
  start: auto_review
  steps:
    auto_review:
      type: agent
      maxAttempts: 2
      sla: 2m
      prompt:
        model: default-reasoning
        system: >-
          You review outbound customer messages for policy, tone and accuracy.
          Return approve only when the message is safe to send unchanged.
        template: |
          Channel: {{.input.channel}}
          Draft: {{.input.draft}}
          Context: {{.input.context}}
        outputSchema:
          type: object
          required: [outcome, reasoning]
          properties:
            outcome: { type: string, enum: [approve, reject, unsure] }
            reasoning: { type: string }
      outcomes: { approve: resolved, reject: rejected, unsure: human_review, failed: human_review }
    human_review:
      type: human
      uses: human-approval
      queue: agent-success
      session: editor
      sla: 4h
      onSlaBreach: { escalateTo: agent-success-lead }
      outcomes: { approve: resolved, edit_approve: resolved, reject: rejected, send_back: auto_review }

docs.title: Sample 2: skill-publish-review-v1
docs.text:
A person always reviews; a system step then publishes. Shows a system actor and a non-AI path.

apiVersion: pitcrew.budy.bot/v1alpha1
kind: PTSOP
metadata:
  name: skill-publish-review-v1
spec:
  sop: skill-publish-review
  version: 1
  lifecycle: active
  maxRuntime: 72h
  input:
    schema:
      type: object
      required: [skillId, skillVersion]
      properties:
        skillId: { type: string }
        skillVersion: { type: string }
        changeNote: { type: string }
  result:
    schema:
      type: object
      required: [decision]
      properties:
        decision: { type: string, enum: [published, rejected] }
        reason: { type: string }
  start: triage
  steps:
    triage:
      type: human
      uses: human-approval
      queue: agent-success
      session: editor
      sla: 8h
      onSlaBreach: { escalateTo: agent-success-lead }
      outcomes: { approve: publish, reject: rejected, send_back: triage }
    publish:
      type: system
      sla: 5m
      action: { capability: publishSkill }
      outcomes: { done: resolved, failed: triage }

In Phase 1 the publishSkill system action is a stub that records an event and returns done, because the target capability belongs to another cluster. The real binding is a later change to the SOP version.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
The contract is in nexus-contracts. The component manifest charts/gateway-1/files/capabilities/ticket-engine-1.yaml has this shape (one entry shown; the others follow the contract table):

apiVersion: capabilities.budy.bot/v1
kind: ComponentCapabilities
component: ticket-engine-1
taskQueue: pitcrew-ticket-engine-1
workflowType: TicketEngineEntryV1
defaults: { timeout: 10s }
capabilities:
  - name: submitTicket
    mutating: true
    scope: tenant
    schema:
      type: object
      required: [sop, input]
      additionalProperties: false
      properties:
        sop:      { type: object, required: [name, version], properties: { name: {type: string}, version: {type: integer, minimum: 1} } }
        input:    { type: object }
        summary:  { type: string, maxLength: 140 }
        priority: { type: string, enum: [low, normal, high, urgent] }

The capabilitytest.Verify conformance test runs against the manifest and the registered handlers, as in engagement-manager-1.

docs.title: Workflows and Activities
docs.text:
Workflow Registered as Notes TicketEngineEntryV1 Pinned entry workflow, switch on capability Short path for submitTicket, getTicket, cancelTicket, describeSops, awaitTicket; envelope and content capabilities query the database or send an Update TicketWorkflowV1 Pinned, workflow ID = ticket ID, started as an independent run Interpreter; carries only ticket ID, SOP reference and digest, step, attempt Lifecycle workflow AutoUpgrade, as in engagement-manager-1 Per the standard Activity Retries Notes RegisterTicket Default One transaction: insert ticket, accepted event, content row; unique on (tenant, requester, key); a repeat returns the same ticket LoadSOP Default Reads the pinned name, version and digest from the cache; result recorded in history RunAIStep 2 attempts plus the step's maxAttempts; non-retryable on schema failure after the last attempt Renders the template, calls the LLM router, validates against outputSchema; failed outcome on exhaustion AssignHuman Default Inserts the queue_entries row, sets owner Transition Default Applies an outcome in one transaction (ticket, event, queue entry); idempotent on (ticket, seq) NotifyBreach Limited Phase 1 writes an event and logs; provider integration is later ExpireTicket Default Ends the ticket as expired at maxRuntime

Updates on TicketWorkflowV1: HumanAction{action, expectedStep, edits, comment, actor}, with a validator that rejects when the ticket is not at a human step, the step differs from expectedStep, or the action is not allowed. Queries: none; state is read from PostgreSQL.

Search attributes: TicketId, TenantId, SopName, SopVersion, Step, TicketState.

docs.title: BFF API
docs.text:
The BFF runs on @budybot/console-kit with a user adapter (the signed-in staff member) and a pod adapter limited to system scope. All routes require a valid session cookie. All write routes are same-origin JSON with a CSRF guard, as in the reference console.

Route Source Behaviour GET /api/queue meta.ticket_queue_v via meta_read Filters: queue, state, sop, owner; keyset pagination on (due_at, ticket_id); no tenant filter beyond the token (see below) GET /api/stats meta aggregates Open, breached, due within 1 hour, resolved today GET /api/tickets/:id meta.tickets, meta.ticket_events via meta_read Envelope and event list without payloads GET /api/tickets/:id/content Gateway getTicketContent Needs a tenant session (below); records content_opened POST /api/tickets/:id/claim Gateway claimTicket System-scope user token POST /api/tickets/:id/release Gateway releaseTicket POST /api/tickets/:id/resolve Gateway resolveTicket Body {action, expectedStep, comment?, edits?}; tenant session POST /api/tickets/:id/comment Gateway addComment Tenant session GET /healthz, GET /readyz Readiness checks the pool

docs.title: Read access
docs.text: The BFF holds a Vault-issued credential for pitcrew_meta_read. This is an own-store read of envelope data, behind a verified system-scope user token whose session carries the agent success role. The BFF checks the role before every query and refuses (fail closed) on a missing or unverifiable token. The queue is a platform-wide view by design for this role.

docs.title: Content access
docs.text:
Opening or acting on content needs a session for the ticket's tenant. Phase 1 behaviour:

  1. The BFF calls getTicketContent or resolveTicket through the gateway with the staff member's token.
  2. The component authorizes with the Pit Crew OpenFGA model: the caller must hold the agent success role on the platform and the ticket must be open at a step whose session boundary the caller's role grants.
  3. The component records content_opened with the caller and, where present, the assumed tenant.

A true tenant assume (the STS exchanging a system session for a tenant session for a chosen tenant) is the intended end state. The portal performs it at launch through the auth-code flow, and the BFF cannot mint it. Until the platform provides a console-callable exchange, Phase 1 uses the check above and fails closed if the Pit Crew model denies. It is a platform dependency, not a Pit Crew change.

docs.title: Exporter Metrics and Alerts
docs.text:
sql_exporter runs with the meta_read credential (the same Vault role the BFF uses, a separate VaultDynamicSecret in the exporter's own chart). Collector queries:

Metric Type Query pitcrew_sla_breached_open gauge SELECT count(*) FROM meta.queue_entries q JOIN meta.tickets t USING (ticket_id) WHERE q.breached_at IS NOT NULL AND t.state IN ('accepted','in_progress','waiting') pitcrew_queue_depth gauge, labels queue, sop open entries grouped by queue and SOP pitcrew_oldest_open_age_seconds gauge, label queue max(extract(epoch from now() - created_at)) per queue pitcrew_due_unbreached_overdue gauge entries with due_at < now() and breached_at IS NULL (the worker timer is late) pitcrew_tickets_by_state gauge, label state counts by state

Rules (PrometheusRule, in the EKS stack under the agent-success/ rules directory, evaluator label thanos-ruler, Alertmanager label team: agent-success):

Alert Condition For Severity PitcrewSlaBreached pitcrew_sla_breached_open > 0 5m warning PitcrewSlaBreachedMany pitcrew_sla_breached_open > 10 10m critical PitcrewWorkerTimerLate pitcrew_due_unbreached_overdue > 0 10m warning PitcrewExporterDown up{job="pitcrew-sql-exporter"} == 0 5m critical

The ServiceMonitor lives in the exporter's chart so prometheus-obs-1 scrapes it, and carries the labels that instance selects on (derive from an existing ServiceMonitor in the EKS stack).

docs.title: Seed Job (dev only)
docs.text:
pitcrew-seed-1 is a CronJob (suspended by default, enabled only in the dev values file through GitOps). It runs cmd/seed, which uses the worker role to insert tickets through the same RegisterTicket path and starts workflows, so seeded tickets behave like real ones.
