docs.title: As built (Phase 1)
docs.text: The sections above are the design. This section records where the build differs from them, and why. Nothing here is released or deployed, and nothing has been run against a real Temporal, OpenFGA, Vault or cluster.

docs.title: Layout and names
docs.text: Design Built Why ticket-engine-1/ at the repository root components/ticket-engine-1/, module github.com/Budybot/pitcrew-cluster-1_repo-1/components/ticket-engine-1 The repository standard puts every component under components/, and the catalog, go.work and the shared Dockerfile expect it. cmd/seed in its own binary and chart pitcrew-seed-1 A seed mode of the worker binary (worker seed, like migrate) and a CronJob template in the ticket-engine-1 chart The shared Dockerfile builds one binary per image, and the seed must run the same build as the worker. The job has its own service account pitcrew-seed-1, its own Vault role and the netpol label pitcrew-seed-1. Two sample SOPs Three: content-approval, skill-publish-review and demo-triage demo-triage has a two-minute time limit, so the dev seed can exercise a breach and its alert within minutes; a step's due time is set when the ticket enters it, so a seed cannot back-date it. Task queue pitcrew-ticket-engine-1 pitcrew-cluster-1-ticket-engine-1-tq The standard derives <cluster>-<component>-tq; the chart's shared task-queue ConfigMap sets it. console-1 and sql-exporter-1 charts Both are standalone charts like the reference consoles, off by default They are not Temporal workers. The exporter stays off until the sql_exporter image is mirrored into the platform registry.

docs.title: Database and Vault
docs.text:
• No pitcrew_meta_read role. The Vault catalog only grants the standard group roles, so the console and the exporter use ob1-pitcrew-db-1-read-role, limited to the meta schema by the custom grants file in the EKS stack. The worker uses ob1-pitcrew-db-1-user-role and the migration Job ob1-pitcrew-db-1-admin-role.
  • The migration role cannot CREATE SCHEMA (the standard grants give it no CREATE on the database, even for IF NOT EXISTS). The grants file creates meta and content, owned by the admin role, and sets default privileges FOR ROLE the admin. 0001_init.sql creates a schema only when it is missing (local and test databases) and re-grants at its end as a safety net.
  • Events carry a dedupe_key. meta.ticket_events has a dedupe_key column with a unique index per ticket, so a retried activity writes its event once. The design's "idempotent on (ticket, seq)" could not do that, because the sequence number is allocated by the database.
  • Vault names are the platform catalog's, not pitcrew_<suffix>_vault_pg_role_1: auth roles ob1_tf_vault_pitcrew-cluster-1-<service>_role_1, database paths creds/pitcrew-cluster-1-<service>_readwrite_vault_pg_role_1 (worker, seed) and ..._readonly_... (console, exporter), and the migration's static credentials. The console session key is sessionSecret at v1/de-v2/ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-pitcrew-1-ns-1/pitcrew-cluster-1-console-1/session. Service accounts are fixed in the chart defaults (ticket-engine-1, ticket-engine-1-migrate, pitcrew-seed-1, console-1, sql-exporter-1) because the Vault roles bind to exact names.

docs.title: PTSOP
docs.text:
• results per step. The design never said how an outcome becomes the result the requester receives. A step now declares results: {<outcome>: <JSON object>} for every outcome whose target is resolved or rejected. Each body must satisfy the SOP's result schema (validated when the resource is loaded). When a person resolves a ticket, their edits (a JSON object) are merged over the body key by key and their comment is added as reason if the result schema has that property; the merged result is checked against the schema, and an edit that breaks it is refused before the Update is accepted.
  • Admission. The CRD's CEL rules (start names a step, every outcome leads to a step, resolved or rejected, step shape per type, spec immutable except lifecycle) are checked in the repository's tests with the API server's own CRD validation and admission code, so the CEL compiles and stays inside the cost budget. The worker's validator adds what CEL cannot: reachability, dead ends, the model's outcome enum against the step's outcomes, and the results. A resource that fails the validator is kept out of the cache and counted, and does not affect other SOPs.
  • Scope of the CRD whitelist. A CRD is cluster-scoped, so the AppProject whitelist is by CRD name (ptsops.pitcrew.budy.bot), not by namespace.

docs.title: Capabilities and the gateway manifest
docs.text:
• The manifest format is a map keyed by capability name with a description, an optional timeout and a schema. It has no scope or mutating field, so the scope of a capability (tenant for requesters, platform for staff) is asserted by ticket-engine-1 as the first thing every call does, before any authorization call. awaitTicket has a one-hour-one-minute timeout; every other capability inherits 15 seconds.
  • listTicketEvents returns event payloads (AI reasoning, edits, comments), so it is content access: it needs the same permission as getTicketContent and records a content_opened event. With the Phase 1 fail-closed check this means history with payloads is readable only while a ticket waits at a human step; the console shows event metadata for every ticket from the database.

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text:
• Human actions are Updates sent from an activity. A workflow cannot send an Update to another workflow, so resolveTicket runs in the Execute activity, which checks authorization and the ticket's state, then sends the Update through the worker's own client (activity.GetClient). The validator refuses an action at once when the ticket is not at a human step, the step moved, the action is not offered, an action is already being applied, or the result it would produce breaks the schema. The handler applies the transition, so the caller learns the outcome and the first of two concurrent actions wins.
  • awaitTicket is a polling activity with heartbeats, bounded by waitUpTo (default 1800 seconds, maximum 3600); when it ends first the answer is final: false.
  • A ticket never stays silently open. If the workflow fails for any reason except cancellation or a conflict, it ends the ticket as expired and escalated, then reports the failure.
  • Search attributes are off by default (engine.searchAttributes), because upserting an attribute that is not registered on the Temporal namespace fails every workflow task. Registering TicketId, TenantId, SopName, SopVersion, Step and TicketState is a platform step; then the flag is turned on.
  • The AI step is behind an interface with a refusing default. Until the router's structured-output operation is confirmed, the default runner is not configured, so an agent step ends in its failed outcome after its attempts, which the sample SOPs route to a person. It never approves anything. System steps are labelled stubs (publishSkill records the call and succeeds).
  • A time limit that passes escalates (an sla_breached and an escalated event, a log line) and keeps waiting; Phase 1 has no notification provider.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: The model is models/pitcrew.fga in the authorization config. ticket-engine-1 supplies the contextual edges from its own record of the ticket and the verified token: the ticket's tenant (owning_tenant), its requester, its SOP, the platform (owning_platform) and, only while the ticket waits at a human step, the boundary that step declares (viewer_step_platform or editor_step_platform). A ticket that is not at a human step has neither edge, so no content permission holds. The platform object is platform:budy; the live session is stated as user session_<boundary> platform:budy for staff and ... tenant:<t> for requesters. agent_success is eligible for the viewer and editor boundaries only, through a new assumable_platform_editor union in the platform model; the STS needed no new Go mapping beyond using it.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
• Results through Nexus callbacks. The console fires Execute and getTicketContent, resolveTicket and the other gateway calls need their result, so the backend passes ?callback=<in-cluster URL> to Temporal's Nexus HTTP endpoint and resolves a pending promise when Temporal posts the completion (a 200 is a synchronous result, a 201 waits for the callback). This is the context-cluster control plane's pattern. Consequences: the chart runs one replica and refuses any other value (a callback lands on one pod, and a rollout loses in-flight results); the callback is served on a second port (3001) with its own Service, not on the public app; its only protection is a random one-time id in the path plus network isolation; and two platform changes are needed outside this repository: Temporal's callback allow-list must include console-1-callback.ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-pitcrew-1-ns-1.svc.cluster.local:3001, and a network policy must admit Temporal's history pods to that port.
  • How the backend knows the caller is staff. A platform-scope token does not by itself prove the agent_success role, and no repository shows how other system-scope consoles authorize staff. The backend asks the OpenFGA read-only proxy before every query and gateway call (may_view_pitcrew_queue for reads, may_work_pitcrew_queue with an editor or admin session for actions), using the wire format of go/authz, failing closed (deny is 403, an outage is 503) with a short cache. This is an assumption the platform owners must confirm.
  • Reads are the three pod adapters (queue, stats, ticket) over meta as the read role; the content route also needs an x-pitcrew-intent: open-content header and a same-origin request, because it has a recorded side effect. The content gate has no "assume tenant and reason" step, because Phase 1 has no tenant assume and getTicketContent takes no reason.
  • Kit version and npm setup. The console pins @budybot/console-kit 0.4.0. Because console-1 is a root workspace, npm uses the root .npmrc (the @budybot scope mapping and the supply-chain settings) and the root lockfile; the image build uses the component's own .npmrc and lockfile. Both lockfiles must be committed.
  • Not verified. The typecheck and an end-to-end read test ran against a build of kit 0.4.0 made from its source, not the published package. The Docker image, a live callback and a browser or accessibility audit were not run.

docs.title: Observability and alerts
docs.text: The exporter's Service is named pitcrew-sql-exporter, because the Prometheus job label is the Service name and PitcrewExporterDown matches job="pitcrew-sql-exporter". prometheus-obs-1 selects every ServiceMonitor, so none needs a selector label. The agent-success rules directory is included in the prod profile only, so the Pit Crew alerts do not evaluate in dev until the directory is added to the dev profile.

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text: No Docker daemon, so the images were never built. golangci-lint was not run (its binary was built with an older Go than the modules). The helm checks used the library charts resolved from file:// in the helm charts repository. The OpenFGA model was not validated with fga model validate. Nothing was exercised against Temporal's Nexus endpoint, the STS, Vault or a cluster.

docs.title: Studio Services Cluster — High Level Design
Overview
docs.text:
The Studio Services Cluster (studio-services-cluster-1) is where artifacts are created. An artifact is a typed, versioned piece of work product that Digital Teammates (DTs), workflows and people produce and read together. Two types exist: doc (Markdown) and dashboard (a declarative spec whose data is pushed in separately). The cluster stores artifacts, keeps their revisions, controls who may read them and renders them as web pages.

It is a Nexus-first cluster. DTs and workflows in other clusters call a generic gateway (gateway-1) that authenticates the STS token, validates the payload against a capability schema and starts a child workflow on the component's task queue; the component, artifact-store-1, owns every write. A second component, artifact-web-1, is a read-only HTTP service for people: it authenticates a reader, reads the artifact straight from the store and renders HTML. Both components use the same store library, so "latest", validation, tenancy and share checks exist once.

Artifact content is written to one S3 object per revision; metadata (artifacts, revisions, dashboard input updates, shares, idempotency records) lives in PostgreSQL. Revisions are immutable, a dashboard's spec (design) is separate from its inputs (data), and readers without a platform identity get access through link or basic-auth shares.

docs.title: Architecture Diagram
docs.text:
DT / workflow (other clusters)                     browser, customer
        │ Nexus Execute                                    │ https://artifacts.budybot.ai
        ▼                                                  ▼
 ┌─ studio-services namespace ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  gateway-1                                         artifact-web-1  (HTTP, read-only)     │
 │   1 STS token (JWKS)                                 /a/<id>  /s/<token>  /session       │
 │   2 payload schema                                   auth: STS bearer or cookie, link,   │
 │   3 child workflow                                   basic share; rendering              │
 │        │                                                   │                              │
 │        ▼                                                   │                              │
 │  artifact-store-1  (Temporal worker)                       │                              │
 │   ArtifactStoreWorkflowV1 → Execute activity               │                              │
 │        │                                                   │                              │
 │        └──────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────┘                              │
 │                           ▼        ▼                                                      │
 │                       shared store library (tenancy, revisions, types, shares)            │
 └────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ▼                     ▼
                  RDS PostgreSQL (metadata)   S3 bucket (content, one object per revision)

External systems: the auth cluster's STS (token verification over JWKS), Temporal, RDS, S3, Vault (database credentials).

docs.title: Deployment Model
docs.text: Property Value Type Umbrella chart studio-services-cluster-1-repo-1 in namespace ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-studio-services-1-ns-1; sub-charts per component Language Go gateway-1 Temporal worker with the Nexus service; reads the capability manifests from a ConfigMap artifact-store-1 Temporal worker, Pinned worker versioning; also runs as a pre-upgrade migration Job and a daily purge CronJob (same image, different argument) artifact-web-1 Deployment with a ClusterIP Service behind the Istio ingress at artifacts.budybot.ai; health on port 3000 Storage One RDS PostgreSQL database and one S3 bucket for this cluster Disabled by default outside dev Stage and prod ship switched off until promoted

docs.title: Core Interfaces
docs.text:
Architectural contracts, not implementation types:

  • Artifact type. A type version turns the JSON form callers send into stored bytes (validating it), turns stored bytes back into JSON, applies typed patch operations, and, for types with inputs, declares and validates inputs. A registry holds the type versions a build knows and exactly one active version per type.
  • Object store. Put, get and delete of immutable content objects by key.
  • Authorizer. Decides whether an identity may read, write, share or archive an artifact in its own tenant. Everyone is checked, the owner included, against the OpenFGA model artifact-store-1 through go/authz (fail closed: a deny is a deny, an outage is UNAVAILABLE, never an allow). The store's record of the creator is handed to the model as a contextual owner tuple (until authz-manager-1 can persist owner tuples), and every check carries the token's session boundary as the contextual session_<boundary> tuple, so each permission extends from the platform's active_* session tiers: a viewer-boundary session can read and cannot write, share or archive, and a token without a boundary holds no tier. The seed job is the one exception: an operator-run job with no session that uses an owner-only authorizer. One implementation, storeauthz, serves both components.
  • Share evaluation. Resolves a token or a username and password to a live share (not revoked, not expired, artifact not archived), enforces password attempt limits and counts views.

docs.title: Artifact
docs.text: Field Meaning id art_<ULID>; time-sortable and opaque tenantId, owner From the verified token; every query filters by tenant type, typeVersion Pinned at creation; a new type version never changes existing artifacts title Free text, up to 200 characters latestRevision, createdAt, updatedAt, archivedAt Revision pointer and lifecycle

docs.title: Revision
docs.text: Immutable. revision (1..n), a content hash and size, the type version it was validated against, who wrote it and an optional message. The content itself is the S3 object. A revision also records the type's declaration of the inputs it accepts, so pushing inputs never reads S3.

docs.title: Dashboard spec (dashboard@1)
docs.text: Field Meaning defaultRefreshSeconds Page refresh: 0 (off) or 30 to 86400; default 300 layout.columns 1 to 24, default 12 inputs Named inputs of type number, string, boolean, table (ordered, typed columns) or series (points of time and number); each may have a label and a unit widgets stat, table, chart (line or bar) or markdown, each placed by column and height, each bound to one declared input of a type it can show

docs.title: Input update
docs.text: seq, the merged value set, an optional caller-supplied asOf, updatedAt, updatedBy. The store keeps the five newest per artifact. A push validates its keys against the latest revision's declaration, merges onto the previous values and records the full result.

docs.title: Share
docs.text: auth is link (a 256-bit token in the URL, stored hashed), basic (username and generated password at the artifact URL) or link+basic. Shares give the view role only, may pin a revision, expire and be revoked. Secrets are returned once.

docs.title: Component Breakdown
docs.text:
• gateway-1. Generic: authenticates, validates, routes. No business logic, no state; it learns components and capabilities from manifests.
  • artifact-store-1. One workflow and one activity. The activity's first act is to assert the tenant; it then dispatches the capability to the store, maps store errors to typed responses (infrastructure detail never reaches callers) and lets the workflow retry only unavailable dependencies.
  • artifact-web-1. Authenticates a reader, asks the store for content, renders. Documents go through a CommonMark renderer with raw HTML disabled and a sanitiser on its output. Dashboards are server-rendered pages that load two vendored libraries (a chart library and a small AJAX/refresh library) and fetch their own URL again on an interval to swap the dashboard in place. Strict security headers, rate limiting, structured view logs.
  • Store library. Types, revisions, inputs, shares, idempotency, purge; owns the PostgreSQL schema and the S3 layout.

docs.title: A DT creates and shares a dashboard
docs.text:
DT ──Execute createArtifact──▶ gateway-1 ──child workflow──▶ artifact-store-1
                                                              │ assert tenant, validate spec
                                                              │ write S3 object r1, insert artifact + revision (one transaction)
DT ◀──{artifact, revision}─────────────────────────────────────┘
DT ──Execute createShare (link)──▶ … ──▶ store: random token, hash stored ──▶ DT gets URL + token once
workflow ──Execute setInputs──▶ … ──▶ store: validate against declaration, merge, keep last 5

docs.title: A customer opens a share link
docs.text:
browser ──GET /s/<token>──▶ artifact-web-1
                              │ token → share (live? pinned revision?) ; basic password if required
                              │ read content from store, render HTML ; count view
browser ◀──page (CSP, no-store)─┘
browser ──GET /s/<token> every N seconds (refresh)──▶ dashboard element swapped in place

docs.title: Concurrent writers
docs.text: Two writers holding the same baseRevision: the artifact row is locked while the next revision is written, so one write wins and the other gets CONFLICT, re-reads and decides whether to reapply.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Store What Notes PostgreSQL artifacts, revisions, type versions, input updates, shares, idempotency records Credentials issued by Vault and mounted as files; re-read per connection and connections recycled so rotation needs no restart; schema applied by a migration Job as a separate role S3 one immutable object per revision, tenants/<tenant>/artifacts/<id>/revisions/<n> Versioning on as a safety net with a 30-day lifecycle rule on non-current versions; never the revision model

Retention: archiving hides an artifact and switches its shares off immediately; a daily job hard-deletes artifacts archived for more than 30 days (with their objects), shares revoked or expired for more than 90 days and idempotency records older than 7 days.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Dependency Use Auth cluster STS Verifies bearer tokens over HTTP (JWKS); issues tokens with the artifact-web-1 audience for the browser flow Temporal Gateway to component dispatch RDS PostgreSQL, S3 Storage Vault Database credentials Istio ingress, DNS artifacts.budybot.ai OpenFGA read-only proxy (component listener, 8082) Per-object checks of both components; model module artifact-store-1 in auth-store-2. authz-manager-1 writes the share tuples later

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. One store library, two front doors. Writes and DT reads go through Temporal; reads for people go straight to the store. Neither bypasses tenancy or share checks.
  2. Tenancy twice. The gateway fixes the identity from the token; the component and the store assert the tenant again before touching data. Another tenant's artifact is "not found".
  3. Revisions are immutable; latest is a pointer. Writers state the revision they started from.
  4. Spec and data are separate. A dashboard's design is versioned content; its data is a latest-only channel.
  5. Types are versioned and pinned. A breaking change is a new type version, never an edit.
  6. Nothing untrusted runs. No author-supplied script; documents are sanitised; pages load scripts only from their own origin.
  7. Secrets are never stored in clear. Share tokens are hashed, passwords use argon2id, both are shown once.
  8. Defaults in code, limits in configuration. Size limits and retention are environment settings changed by deployment values.

docs.title: Design Decisions Log
docs.text: Question Resolution Where does content live? This cluster's own S3 bucket; not the object storage cluster. Postgres for content or JSON? No. Content is always S3; only small, bounded dashboard input updates are JSON in PostgreSQL. S3 bucket versioning as the revision model? No: opaque ids, no author or message, no concurrency control. Revisions are explicit objects and rows; bucket versioning is a safety net. Who renders? This cluster, in Go. First types doc and dashboard; a webpage type (arbitrary HTML and JavaScript) needs a sandbox origin and comes later. Dashboard data Pushed by workflows as structured inputs; the page never queries data sources. The last five updates are kept; the page refreshes every five minutes by default. Update modes Replace the content, apply typed patch operations, or push inputs. Share types Link, basic and both; view only. Browser identity The internal STS token as a bearer header or, for navigations, a host-only session cookie created by POST /session. Cross-tenant access None. Authenticated readers are in the artifact's tenant. Per-object authorization OpenFGA through go/authz with our own model, extending from the platform's active_* session tiers; the owner comes from the store's record as a contextual tuple until authz-manager-1 can write owner tuples. Customer editing Not over HTTP in v1. Limits and retention Starting defaults (see the Nexus contracts and Storage); limits are environment settings. Access logs A structured log line per view; a separate S3-based component only if "who viewed what" becomes a feature.

docs.title: Open Questions / TRD Scope
docs.text:
1. Can the internal STS mint tokens with the artifact-web-1 audience for browser users?
  2. A typed authz-manager-1 operation for artifact owner and share tuples for sharing inside a tenant; the authorize: manifest field (platform). The session boundary in ComponentRequest is built (go/capability v0.3.0).
  3. The ingress header that carries the real client address, for rate limiting.
  4. A TRD in the platform format (implementation detail currently lives in the repository's docs/design/).

docs.title: studio-services-cluster-1
docs.text:
The Studio Services Cluster is where artifacts are created. Digital Teammates (DTs) and workflows create, update and share artifacts through the cluster's Nexus contract; people and customers read them as web pages. An artifact has a type, immutable revisions and, for dashboards, structured inputs that workflows push without involving a language model. The first two types are doc (Markdown) and dashboard (a declarative spec with pushed inputs).

Status: implemented, not deployed (October 2026). The repository contains the gateway, the artifact store worker and the web service, with charts and CI. The infrastructure they need (database, bucket, Vault roles, network policy, ingress) is not provisioned yet; see the HLD.

docs.title: Boundary
docs.text: Owns Does not own Artifact records: metadata, revisions, ownership, shares Authentication of callers (the auth cluster's STS) Artifact content, in this cluster's own S3 bucket Tenant membership and platform roles (authz-manager-1) Artifact types, their schemas and typed patching Producing the content (the Digital Teammates and workflows that call it) Rendering artifacts as web pages at artifacts.budybot.ai The application UI and its navigation (the platform UI links to artifact pages) Share links and basic-auth shares for readers without a platform identity Sharing with other users inside a tenant (later, see the HLD) Retention: archive, purge

docs.title: Shape
docs.text: Repository type Nexus-first: gateway + components, plus one HTTP component Components gateway-1 (Nexus), artifact-store-1 (Temporal worker: writes and DT reads), artifact-web-1 (HTTP: page rendering, shares, sessions; read-only) Storage PostgreSQL on RDS for metadata (Vault-issued credentials); one S3 bucket for content Capabilities describeTypes, createArtifact, getArtifact, listArtifacts, listRevisions, updateArtifact, patchArtifact, setInputs, getInputs, archiveArtifact, createShare, listShares, revokeShare (see Nexus contracts) Rendering Go (goldmark and bluemonday for documents, html/template, htmx and Chart.js for dashboards); no Node at build or run time

docs.title: Names (derived from the standard)
docs.text: Kubernetes namespace ob1-tf-eks-de-v2-studio-services-1-ns-1 Nexus endpoint (control surface) ob1-nexus-studio-services-cluster-1-endpoint-1 Nexus service ArtifactServiceV1 Components, task queues gateway-1, artifact-store-1 (studio-services-cluster-1-artifact-store-1-tq), artifact-web-1 Netpol labels budybot.io/netpol: studio-services-gateway-1, studio-services-artifact-store-1, studio-services-artifact-web-1 Umbrella chart studio-services-cluster-1-repo-1 Image repository ob1-ecr-repo-v2/ob1_tf_aws_ecr_studio-services-cluster-1_repo-1 Public host artifacts.budybot.ai (artifact-web-1)

docs.title: Callers and callees
docs.text:
• Inbound: Digital Teammate workers and other clusters' workflows through the Nexus endpoint; people and customers through artifacts.budybot.ai (an STS-authenticated owner, a share link, or basic-auth credentials).
  • Outbound: the auth cluster's STS (JWKS, token verification), PostgreSQL, S3, Temporal. No call to the object storage cluster.

docs.title: Decisions (October 2026)
docs.text:
These resolve the questions the bootstrap version of this page asked.

  1. Artifact model. Typed artifacts with immutable integer revisions and a latest pointer; a type version is immutable and a breaking change is a new version (doc@2). Content is one S3 object per revision.
  2. Storage. This cluster owns its storage: a dedicated bucket for artifact content and RDS for metadata. The object storage cluster is not used.
  3. Collaboration semantics. Writers name the revision they started from (baseRevision); a stale write fails with CONFLICT and the writer re-reads. Dashboard inputs are a separate, latest-only channel (the last five updates are kept) and do not create revisions.
  4. Human access. The cluster renders pages itself. An STS-authenticated owner uses a bearer token or a session cookie; readers without an identity use link or basic-auth shares. Sharing with other people inside a tenant comes later.
  5. Tenancy and authorization. Tenant is enforced at the gateway and again in the store. Per-object authorization follows the Component Authorization Module Standard: both components ask the shared OpenFGA store through go/authz with a model of their own (artifact_1:{tenant}/{id}; owner, editor, viewer for a user or a whole tenant, can_view, can_edit, can_share, can_archive), failing closed. Every permission extends from the platform's session tiers (active_viewer, active_digital_teammate): the components send the token's session boundary with every check. The creator is recorded by the store and handed to the model as a contextual owner tuple; the share relations wait for tuples.
  6. Service name. ArtifactServiceV1 stays.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. The auth cluster must mint STS tokens with the audience artifact-web-1 for the browser flow (or another audience is configured).
  2. Sharing inside a tenant needs a typed operation in authz-manager-1 that writes owner and share tuples. Platform side: the authorize: field in the capability manifest (the session boundary reaches the components already).
  3. Primary owner (tbd).

docs.title: Studio Services Cluster — Nexus Contracts
docs.text: How other clusters and Digital Teammate workflows call the cluster. The Go types are in the contract module of studio-services-cluster-1_repo-1 (shared/contract), which is the authoritative source for payloads; the JSON Schemas the gateway enforces are in charts/gateway-1/files/capabilities/artifact-store-1.yaml.

docs.title: Endpoint and operations
docs.text:
Nexus endpoint ob1-nexus-studio-services-cluster-1-endpoint-1 (never versioned) Service ArtifactServiceV1 Operations Execute and DescribeCapabilities STS audience urn:budy:nexus:ob1-nexus-studio-services-cluster-1-endpoint-1:ArtifactServiceV1 Component artifact-store-1

Execute takes {component, capability, payload, idempotencyKey?, auth: {token}} and returns {ok, data?, error?: {code, message}}. The caller's tenant and user come only from the STS token. A caller-supplied tenant or user is ignored. Platform-scoped tokens (no tenant) are refused with PERMISSION_DENIED.

DescribeCapabilities returns the capability list and, with includeSchemas, each capability's JSON Schema. It needs a valid token and nothing else.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Every call is Execute with component: "artifact-store-1". id is an artifact id of the form art_<ULID>. Every capability acts inside the caller's tenant. Permissions are checked against the authorization model and extend from the caller's session tier, which the token's session boundary sets: reading needs a viewer-boundary session or above, and writing, sharing and archiving an editor-boundary session or above (a digital teammate or an admin). The creator (owner) of an artifact may do anything with it at that tier. Any other user needs a relation granted in the authorization model: read capabilities (getArtifact, listRevisions, getInputs) need can_view (a direct viewer, or the tenant default when it is switched on), updateArtifact, patchArtifact and setInputs need can_edit (editor), createShare, listShares and revokeShare need can_share and archiveArtifact needs can_archive (both owner). listArtifacts lists the caller's own artifacts. Until authz-manager-1 writes per-object tuples only the owner and the tenant default (off by default) apply.

Capability Payload Result describeTypes none types[]: name, version, state, contentSchema, inputs, operations createArtifact type, typeVersion?, title, content, message? artifact, revision getArtifact artifactId, revision? (default latest) artifact, revision, content listArtifacts type?, includeArchived?, limit? (1 to 200), cursor? artifacts[], nextCursor? listRevisions artifactId, limit?, cursor? revisions[] (newest first), nextCursor? updateArtifact artifactId, baseRevision, content, title?, message? artifact, revision patchArtifact artifactId, baseRevision, operations[], message? artifact, revision setInputs artifactId, values{}, asOf? the stored update: seq, values, asOf, updatedAt, updatedBy getInputs artifactId, history? (0 to 4) latest?, history[] archiveArtifact artifactId artifact (hidden, shares off; idempotent) createShare artifactId, auth (link, basic, link+basic), username?, revisionPin?, expiresAt? share, url?, token?, password? (shown once) listShares artifactId shares[] (no secrets) revokeShare artifactId, shareId share (idempotent)

content is the JSON form of the content: a JSON string holding Markdown for doc@1, the spec object for dashboard@1. describeTypes lists the patch operations of each type:

  • doc@1: replaceSection, insertSection, deleteSection (sections are addressed by heading text, with level or occurrence when ambiguous).
  • dashboard@1: setWidget, removeWidget, setRefresh, setLayout, declareInput, removeInput.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Code Meaning Caller action INVALID_ARGUMENT The request or the content violates the schema or a type rule; the message says which. Fix the request. Do not retry unchanged. NOT_FOUND The artifact, revision or share does not exist for this caller (another tenant's artifact looks the same). Do not retry. PERMISSION_DENIED The caller may not do this (no relation that allows the capability on this artifact, or a platform-scoped token). Do not retry. CONFLICT baseRevision is not the latest, or the idempotency key was reused for a different request. Re-read (getArtifact) and retry with the new base. UNAVAILABLE A dependency is down; the component already retried. Retry later. UNIMPLEMENTED, INTERNAL Unknown capability; unexpected failure. Do not retry; report.

Permanent failures are non-retryable application errors inside the cluster; callers only ever see the Response.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: Send an idempotencyKey on every write (createArtifact, updateArtifact, patchArtifact, setInputs). A repeat with the same key and the same request returns the first result; the same key with a different request is CONFLICT. Without a key, a retry inside one workflow execution is still deduplicated, but two separate calls are two writes. createShare is deliberately not idempotent: its token and password are returned once and never stored in clear, so a repeat creates another share.

docs.title: Limits (defaults, set in deployment values)
docs.text: Title 200 characters; revision message 500; doc@1 body 1 MiB; dashboard@1 spec 256 KiB with at most 100 widgets and 100 inputs; one setInputs call and the stored value set 256 KiB; tables 5,000 rows; series 10,000 points; 50 active shares per artifact.

docs.title: Caller guidance
docs.text:
// Create a dashboard, then push data into it from a workflow. Each call is one Execute.
create := contract.CreateArtifactRequest{Type: contract.TypeDashboard, Title: "Support", Content: spec}
// ... Execute(component, contract.CapabilityCreateArtifact, create, idempotencyKey)
set := contract.SetInputsRequest{ArtifactID: id, Values: map[string]json.RawMessage{"open": json.RawMessage(`42`)}}
// ... Execute(component, contract.CapabilitySetInputs, set, idempotencyKey)

On CONFLICT from an update or patch, re-read the artifact and decide whether to reapply the change on the new revision. On INVALID_ARGUMENT from setInputs, the dashboard does not declare that input (or declares a different type): patch the spec with declareInput first.

docs.title: Versioning policy
docs.text: A breaking change to a capability is a new capability name; a breaking change to the service is ArtifactServiceV2; a breaking change to an artifact type is a new type version (doc@2) that sits beside the old one. Published schemas are never changed silently.

docs.title: Reading artifacts (HTTP)
docs.text: Readers use https://artifacts.budybot.ai rather than Nexus: /a/<id> (bearer token or session cookie, or Basic credentials for a basic share), /s/<token> (link share), POST /session (bearer token to cookie). Accept: application/json returns the stored content. See the HLD.

docs.title: BudyDigitalEntity (bde)
docs.text:
platform.budy/v2 · Namespaced (userOrg namespace)

Provisions a Digital Entity instance for a userOrg: a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, a Temporal task queue, and an ArgoCD Application that manages the entity's workload. Each BudyDigitalEntity represents one autonomous agent instance within a userOrg.

Created by: BudyServer (bs) — created automatically when spec.digitalEntities entries are declared on the BudyServer. Can also be applied directly.

Reconciles: DE-specific k8s namespace, Temporal task queue, ArgoCD Application

Field Description spec.userOrgShortName Org identifier — immutable after creation

Status phases: Pending → Provisioning → Ready / Degraded / Deleting

Status also surfaces digitalEntityNamespace, temporalNamespace, temporalQueueName, and applicationName.

apiVersion: platform.budy/v2
kind: BudyDigitalEntity
metadata:
  name: budytestorg-bde-1
  namespace: uo-bpo1-budytestorg-ns-1
spec:
  userOrgShortName: budytestorg

Related: BudyServer (bs), BudyTemporalObject (bto)

docs.title: BudyServer (bs)
docs.text:
platform.budy/v1alpha1 · Namespaced (operator namespace)

Top-level object per userOrg (client tenant). On creation, the operator provisions a dedicated Kubernetes namespace and Temporal namespace for the userOrg, then creates BudyWorkerPool (bwp)s from the referenced BudyServerType (bst) and any BudyDigitalEntity (bde)s declared in spec.

Created by: Platform ops — one per client, applied manually or via GitOps on client onboarding.

Reconciles: userOrg k8s namespace, Temporal namespace, BudyWorkerPool (bwp) CRs, BudyDigitalEntity (bde) CRs

Field Description spec.userOrgShortName Unique org identifier, 2–12 lowercase alphanumeric chars spec.budyServerTypeRef.name The BudyServerType (bst) that defines pool composition spec.digitalEntities Optional list of BudyDigitalEntity (bde)s to create (each needs a name) spec.displayName Human-readable server name

Status phases: Pending → Provisioning → Ready / Degraded / Deleting

Status also surfaces userOrgNamespace, temporalNamespace, createdWorkerPools, and createdDigitalEntities.

apiVersion: platform.budy/v1alpha1
kind: BudyServer
metadata:
  name: budytestorg-server-1
  namespace: ob1-tf-eks-budy-platform-operator-1-ns-1
spec:
  userOrgShortName: budytestorg
  budyServerTypeRef:
    name: t1b-small
  displayName: budytestorg-t1b.small
  digitalEntities:
    - name: budytestorg-bde-1
  internalTags:
    env: production
    userOrgShortName: budytestorg
  externalTags:
    customerName: budytestorg

Related: BudyServerType (bst), BudyWorkerPool (bwp), BudyDigitalEntity (bde)

docs.title: BudyServerType (bst)
docs.text:
platform.budy/v1alpha1 · Cluster-scoped

Cluster-level template that defines a server tier: which BudyWorkerPoolType (bwpt)s are included and how many of each. When a BudyServer (bs) is created, it reads this type to determine which BudyWorkerPool (bwp)s to provision.

Created by: Platform ops — applied once at cluster setup, before any BudyServers.

Field Description spec.serverTypeName Infrastructure name, lowercase + numbers only (e.g. t1bsmall) spec.budyWorkerPoolTypeRefs List of {name, count} — which pool types and how many spec.temporalRetention Default Temporal retention for userOrg namespaces (e.g. 7d) spec.displayName Human-readable name (e.g. t1b.small) spec.description Optional context about this server tier

Status: Conditions only — no phase.

apiVersion: platform.budy/v1alpha1
kind: BudyServerType
metadata:
  name: t1b-small
spec:
  displayName: t1b.small
  serverTypeName: t1bsmall
  description: Small server type with 1 shared small pool and 1 single small pool.
  temporalRetention: 7d
  budyWorkerPoolTypeRefs:
    - name: shared-standard-small
      count: 1
    - name: single-standard-small
      count: 1

Related: BudyServer (bs), BudyWorkerPoolType (bwpt)

docs.title: BudyTemporalObject (bto)
docs.text:
infra.budy/v1 · Cluster-scoped

Manages a single Temporal resource — either a namespace (with optional custom search attributes and retention) or a Nexus endpoint registered against an existing namespace. Exactly one mode must be set per CR. Used by operator controllers to declaratively manage Temporal infrastructure, and can also be applied directly by platform ops for custom endpoints.

Created by: Operator controllers (BudyServer (bs), BudyDigitalEntity (bde)) or platform ops directly for custom Nexus endpoints.

Reconciles: Temporal namespace OR Temporal Nexus endpoint (mutually exclusive per CR)

Field Description spec.namespace.name Temporal namespace to create/manage spec.namespace.retention Workflow retention period (e.g. 7d, 30d) spec.namespace.searchAttributes Custom search attributes to register (name + type) spec.nexusEndpoint.endpointName Nexus endpoint name to register spec.nexusEndpoint.namespace Target Temporal namespace (must already exist) spec.nexusEndpoint.taskQueue Target task queue within the namespace spec.nexusEndpoint.description Optional human-readable description

Status phases: Pending → Provisioning → Ready / Degraded

Status surfaces temporalNamespace (namespace mode) or nexusEndpointId (nexus mode).

Namespace example:

apiVersion: infra.budy/v1
kind: BudyTemporalObject
metadata:
  name: org-budytestorg-namespace
spec:
  namespace:
    name: uo-bpo1-temporal-budytestorg-ns-1
    retention: 7d
    searchAttributes:
      - name: UserOrgShortName
        type: Keyword
      - name: WorkflowVersionId
        type: Keyword

Nexus endpoint example:

apiVersion: infra.budy/v1
kind: BudyTemporalObject
metadata:
  name: budytestorg-payments-nexus
spec:
  nexusEndpoint:
    endpointName: budytestorg-payments
    namespace: uo-bpo1-temporal-budytestorg-ns-1
    taskQueue: payments-handler
    description: Nexus endpoint for the budytestorg payments workflow handler.

Related: BudyServer (bs), BudyDigitalEntity (bde)

docs.title: BudyWorker (bw)
docs.text:
platform.budy/v1alpha1 · Namespaced (userOrg namespace)

Provisions a Temporal worker Deployment and KEDA ScaledObject in the userOrg namespace for a specific workflow version. Each BudyWorker maps to one published workflow automation — either dedicated to a single task queue (Single) or shared across multiple workflows (Shared).

Created by: Publish Consultant Workflow — triggered automatically when a consultant publishes an automation from Design Services.

Reconciles: Deployment, ScaledObject (KEDA)

Field Description spec.workerType Single (dedicated per workflow) or Shared spec.workflowVersionId Temporal task queue name — required when workerType is Single spec.budyWorkerPoolRef.name The BudyWorkerPool (bwp) this worker belongs to spec.image Worker container image spec.replicas Desired replica count when autoscaling is not used (default 1) spec.temporalNamespace Temporal namespace whose task queue KEDA monitors for scaling spec.autoscaling Optional KEDA min/max replica bounds

Status phases: Pending → Provisioning → Ready / Degraded / Deleting

apiVersion: platform.budy/v1alpha1
kind: BudyWorker
metadata:
  name: budytestorg-bw-3h552ty
  namespace: uo-bpo1-budytestorg-ns-1
spec:
  userOrgShortName: budytestorg
  workerType: Single
  workflowVersionId: wfv_v1_5f0bf1c3ae55402caf
  image: 515407373958.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/ob1-ecr-repo-v2/workflow-worker-image_repo-1:wfv_v1_5f0bf1c3ae55402caf
  budyWorkerPoolRef:
    name: budytestorg-server-1-workerpool-single-standard-medium-574453
  temporalNamespace: budytestorg-ns
  autoscaling:
    min: 1
    max: 10

Related: BudyWorkerPool (bwp), BudyWorkerPoolType (bwpt)

docs.title: BudyWorkerPool (bwp)
docs.text:
platform.budy/v1alpha1 · Namespaced (userOrg namespace)

A pool of worker slots within a userOrg namespace, instantiated from a BudyWorkerPoolType (bwpt) template. BudyWorker (bw)s reference this pool to inherit resource bounds and node scheduling rules. For Single pools each slot maps to one BudyWorker; for Shared pools one worker serves all slots.

Created by: BudyServer (bs) — automatically creates one BudyWorkerPool per pool type entry in the referenced BudyServerType (bst).

Field Description spec.budyWorkerPoolTypeRef.name The BudyWorkerPoolType (bwpt) template for this pool spec.slots Number of concurrent worker slots (set by BudyServer from type defaults) spec.resourcesPerSlot CPU/memory per slot (set by BudyServer from type defaults) spec.autoscaling KEDA min/max bounds — Shared pools only spec.replicas Static replica count — Shared pools only, overridden by autoscaling spec.overrides.maxTimeoutMinutes Per-pool timeout override (max 1440 min)

Status phases: Pending → Provisioning → Ready / Degraded / Deleting

Status also surfaces activeWorkers, resolvedConfiguration (effective slots/resources/maxWorkers), and the workers list of attached BudyWorker names.

apiVersion: platform.budy/v1alpha1
kind: BudyWorkerPool
metadata:
  name: budytestorg-server-1-workerpool-single-standard-medium-574453
  namespace: uo-bpo1-budytestorg-ns-1
spec:
  userOrgShortName: budytestorg
  budyWorkerPoolTypeRef:
    name: single-standard-medium
  serverType: t1bsmall
  slots: 4
  resourcesPerSlot:
    cpu:
      maxCPU: 0.4
      reserveCPU: 0.25
    memory:
      maxMemoryMB: 1024
      reserveMemoryMB: 256

Related: BudyServer (bs), BudyWorkerPoolType (bwpt), BudyWorker (bw)

docs.title: BudyWorkerPoolType (bwpt)
docs.text:
platform.budy/v1alpha1 · Cluster-scoped

Cluster-level template that defines compute characteristics for a worker pool: whether it is Single (one worker per slot) or Shared (one worker for all slots), total CPU/memory caps, default slot configuration, and node scheduling rules. Referenced by BudyServerType (bst) and used when BudyServer (bs) creates BudyWorkerPool (bwp)s.

Created by: Platform ops — applied once at cluster setup.

Field Description spec.poolType Single (one worker per slot) or Shared (one worker for all slots) spec.totalCPU / spec.totalMemoryMB Maximum total resources across all slots spec.defaultPoolSpec.defaultSlots Default slot count for new pools of this type spec.defaultPoolSpec.defaultResourcesPerSlot Default CPU/memory per slot spec.defaultPoolSpec.defaultAutoscaling Default KEDA autoscaling bounds (Shared pools only) spec.maxTimeoutMinutes Maximum worker execution time (default 60) spec.nodeScheduling Node selector + taints for Karpenter placement

Status: Conditions + activePoolCount — no phase.

apiVersion: platform.budy/v1alpha1
kind: BudyWorkerPoolType
metadata:
  name: single-standard-medium
spec:
  displayName: Single standard Medium
  description: Single worker per slot, standard compute, medium size (2 CPU, 8 GiB total cap).
  poolType: Single
  totalCPU: 2
  totalMemoryMB: 8192
  maxTimeoutMinutes: 60
  defaultPoolSpec:
    defaultSlots: 4
    defaultResourcesPerSlot:
      cpu:
        maxCPU: 0.4
        reserveCPU: 0.25
      memory:
        maxMemoryMB: 1024
        reserveMemoryMB: 256
  nodeScheduling:
    nodeTaints:
      - key: budy.io/nodepool-required
        value: "true"
        effect: NoSchedule
    nodeSelector:
      budy.io/nodepool: "true"
      budy.io/compute-type: standard
      budy.io/spot-allowed: "true"

Related: BudyServerType (bst), BudyWorkerPool (bwp)

docs.title: Temporal Nexus Service
docs.text:
A Temporal Nexus Service is a service contract built on top of Temporal that exposes durable, distributed operations as callable endpoints — conceptually similar to a REST API, but built for work that is async, long-running, or needs to survive failures.

Where a REST API call is transient (the caller either gets a response or handles a timeout on its own), a Nexus call is durable: if the caller or the service crashes mid-operation, Temporal ensures the work resumes from where it left off. The caller does not need to know whether the underlying implementation is a short-lived function or a multi-day workflow — it just calls the endpoint and Temporal handles the rest.

Why we use it: Almost all services in the de-v2 platform are Temporal workers. Nexus lets those services expose clean, typed contracts to each other without giving up the durability and observability guarantees that Temporal provides. It is our preferred internal service contract wherever REST is not strictly required (e.g., REST remains necessary for inbound webhooks and external-facing APIs).

Example: The Context Service needs to request an LLM review of a proposed memory update before approving it. Rather than making a REST call to the LLM Service — which would be lost if anything crashed mid-review — the Context Service calls the LLM Service's Nexus endpoint. Temporal tracks the in-progress call. If the LLM Service worker restarts during the request, Temporal retries from the last checkpoint. The Context Service does not need to implement its own retry logic or dead-letter queue. Temporal handles it, and the full operation is visible in the Temporal UI from start to finish.

Further reading: Temporal Nexus documentation

docs.title: Dynamo worker
docs.text: A Dynamo worker is a Temporal worker, one per digital teammate (DT) workbench, that runs the DT's deterministic workflows. Those workflows may contain prompts and call external and internal systems. Each DT's worker has its own repository in GitLab (gitjib-cluster-1), created from a template; once an image built to the required spec is pushed, nainai-cluster-1 deploys it. dt-consulting-services-1 is how a DT gets a workflow added or changed.

docs.title: Engagement
docs.text: An engagement is a digital teammate's request to dt-consulting-services-1 to add or change a workflow of its Dynamo worker. It is written like a PRD (outcome, context, audience, do's and don'ts, success criteria, references to existing resources) and carries no implementation detail. A DT has at most one live engagement. It is done when the workflow is published and the new worker version is healthy.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text: A sandbox is an isolated workspace that Karkhana (karkhana-cluster-1) runs for a caller in the caller's tenant namespace: one pod with a persistent workspace volume and its own ServiceAccount, created from a SandboxType. Pausing deletes the pod and keeps the volume; resuming starts a new pod. Desired state is a row in Postgres written by sandbox-manager-1; sandbox-operator-1 makes Kubernetes match it. Design: Karkhana sandboxes.

docs.title: SandboxType
docs.text: A SandboxType is the cluster-scoped custom resource (karkhana.budy/v1alpha1) that is the catalog of what a sandbox can be: image, workspace volume, resources, lifetime limits, placement, network profile, secrets, the identity it gets, the roles allowed to request it (allowedRoles) and per-tenant and per-requester limits. Example: claude-coder-1.

docs.title: Workload session
docs.text: A workload session is a short-lived platform identity that a platform service creates in authz-manager-1 for one workload it runs on a tenant's behalf, such as a sandbox. It is a user homed on the tenant, with the workload's ServiceAccount as its only identity and the roles a reviewed configuration allows, until an expiry. It is released when the work stops and ends by itself otherwise. Standard: Component Authorization Module Standard.

docs.title: glassboxId
docs.text: glassboxId is the claim in a tenant STS session that names the billing entity: the entity that pays for what the session does, either the tenant or a digital teammate of it. STS decides it and a caller cannot set it; a workload session has its entity fixed when it is created. Services record it with their usage and never derive it. See the Usage Metering Standard and the authorization standard.

docs.title: Network profile
docs.text: A network profile is a named set of allowed network destinations for pods that a platform operator creates in tenant namespaces. It is one cluster-wide Cilium policy, selected by the pod label budybot.io/netpol: <profile> in namespaces managed by a UserOrg, and the label is reserved by admission policy. Example: sandbox-coder-1. A SandboxType names its profile in networkProfile. See Network Policy & mTLS.

docs.title: Platform Console Standard
docs.text:
Status: confirmed by the nainai console (October 2026). A user signed in through the portal and saw the fleet. Corrections from that build are folded in below; the runbook and the list of snags are in the wiki skill scaffold-platform-console.

A platform console is an internal web UI for platform staff (support and admins), and later for tenant-scoped views, that sits behind the platform portal. It is a non-Nexus component of a cluster: one catalog entry, one chart, one image, released independently, like any other component in the cluster standard (scaffold-nexus-cluster-repo). Consoles are never meant for tenants to reach directly.

docs.title: What a console is
docs.text: Part Choice Shape One container: a static React single-page app plus a small Node backend-for-frontend (BFF). No database. Not used React Server Components, Server Actions, server-side rendering, an image optimizer. Diagrams Left-to-right workflow and fleet views are client-side: @xyflow/react for the graph and @dagrejs/dagre or elkjs for layout, fed by JSON from the BFF. No server framework is needed for them. Sign-in The platform portal (Platform UI): sign-in through Dex (Google), then the STS one-time application handoff, redeemed by the BFF into an encrypted host-only cookie. The browser never holds a JWT. Data The BFF reads through adapters (k8s, temporal, gateway) and returns normalized view models, never raw provider objects. Shared code One npm package, @budybot/console-kit (sub-paths /server, /ui, /adapters), published from budy-common-modules to GitHub Packages, plus one base image.

docs.title: The scope rule: the token decides
docs.text:
A console does not have a fixed "mode". Every request carries a verified STS token. Its scopeType claim is platform for system scope (platform staff acting for the platform) or tenant for tenant scope (acting inside one tenant), with scopeId and a sessionBoundary of viewer, editor or admin (claims contract: auth-service-1, docs/v2-token-claims-contract.md). Each adapter declares the scope it requires.

  1. The session token is verified on every request (signature, issuer, audience, expiry). The cookie only transports it. The audience is the console's origin, except for a console launched through a nexusTarget route: there it is the Nexus resource of the console's own cluster gateway (urn:budy:nexus:<endpoint>:<service>), so the same token is accepted by the console and forwarded to that gateway. Only a console that writes through its own gateway uses this (today: DT Consulting); it sets CONSOLE_STS_AUDIENCE and CONSOLE_HANDOFF_RESOURCE to that URN.
  2. An adapter that uses the pod's own credentials (k8s, temporal) may only require system scope. The shared server refuses to start otherwise. A tenant-scope token on such a route gets 403.
  3. An adapter that forwards the user's token to a gateway (gateway) may serve either scope; tenant enforcement stays in the gateway. Exception, the cluster's own store: a tenant console may read its own cluster's database with the pod's credentials only when all of these hold: the credentials are a Vault-issued member of the database's read role (SELECT only); the adapter requires tenant scope; every query is filtered by the verified token's tenant (and by its subject for per-user records), never by a request field; and the data is the cluster's own, not another system's. The pod credential then grants no reach beyond what the token's tenant filter allows. Writes still go through the gateway as the user. Today only the DT Consulting console uses this; console-kit does not yet model it (its adapters are declared credential: "user"), and a store credential kind that enforces the tenant filter belongs in console-kit before a second console needs it.
  4. A deployment lists the scopes it accepts. A cluster that serves one scope leaves the other off; a cluster that serves both enables both. Unlisted scopes are rejected before any adapter runs.
  5. Tenant and user identity come from the token only, never from the request.

Current expectation: nainai and Pit Crew system scope; DT Consulting tenant scope (built, November 2026: the first tenant console that writes, launched through a nexusTarget route so one token serves the console and its gateway; see the DT Consulting console); gitjib both.

Pit Crew (system scope, built November 2026, in review). The operator console shows how a system-scope console splits its data path. Non-confidential reads (the queue, filters, stats and ticket history) come straight from the cluster's own database through the standard read role, which the database grants limit to the meta schema: no Temporal and no gateway call. Anything client-specific (opening a ticket's content) and every change goes through the cluster's gateway as the signed-in user, so the gateway verifies the user's STS token and the platform authorizes it. Two consequences are new to the standard:

  • Who is staff. A platform-scope token states the scope and the session boundary, not the Agent Success role. The console asks the OpenFGA read-only proxy before every query and gateway call and fails closed. A platform that puts a role claim in the token would replace this check.
  • Gateway results. Temporal's Nexus HTTP endpoint answers 201 for an asynchronous call and posts the result to a callback URL. The console passes an in-cluster callback URL, keeps the waiting request in memory and serves the callback on a second, non-public port. A callback lands on one pod, so such a console runs one replica, and the platform must allow Temporal to reach the callback (Temporal's callback allow-list and a network policy). The context-cluster control plane uses the same pattern.

docs.title: Security baseline
docs.text:
Consoles are behind Google OIDC, which removes anonymous exposure but not supply-chain risk or the value of the credentials a console pod holds.

  • No server-component framework. The server-component layer had critical and high advisories in consecutive months (September and 14 October 2026). A static SPA with a plain JSON BFF has no such protocol to attack. If a cluster insists on Next.js, it uses a patched release, route handlers only, no Server Actions, no use cache, unoptimized images.
  • Supply chain. Exact pins and a committed lockfile; npm ci --ignore-scripts; no dependency that needs an install script; no non-security third-party version younger than 7 days (min-release-age=7, npm 11.10 or later) with our own @budybot/* packages exempt (min-release-age-exclude[]=@budybot/*, npm 11.20 or later), because we publish and update them as needed instead of working around them in the consumer; few dependencies; no Kubernetes client library; automated updates (security immediate, others weekly, through the age gate); an audit step in CI. Publishing uses the short-lived workflow token; no long-lived npm token exists.
  • Runtime. Non-root numeric user, read-only root filesystem, capabilities dropped, strict CSP, __Host- HttpOnly Secure SameSite=Lax cookie, authorization inside every handler (never only middleware), projections instead of raw objects, no tokens or cookies in logs.
  • Kubernetes access. A read-only ClusterRole where workloads live in their own namespaces: get and list on named resources only, no secrets, no write verbs.

docs.title: Versions policy
docs.text: Stable releases only; not younger than 7 days; prefer a major line already proven in our repos or a few months old; add a library only when needed. The lockfile is the record of what is pinned; the table in the nainai plan is the starting set. Node 26 (LTS "Lithium" since 26.13.0, October 2026).

docs.title: Build and release
docs.text:
validation.kind: node in .github/components.json; the shared platform-actions@v1 pipeline validates, builds and releases it. Consuming a private package needs read access granted on the package for each consuming repository and a packages: read token in CI and as a BuildKit secret in the image build.

Every new cluster repository must be added to the package's settings (@budybot/console-kit → Manage Actions access → Add repository → Read) before its first console build, or npm ci fails with 403 or 404. This is a manual owner step: GitHub's npm registry accepts only a classic personal access token or the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN (for repositories added to the package), not GitHub App tokens, and there is no organization-wide grant. A read-only machine-user token kept as an organization secret would avoid it at the cost of a long-lived credential; that option is deferred. The scaffold skill carries the same reminder.

docs.title: Wiring map
docs.text:
A console touches these repositories, in this merge order. Every row is a separate pull request.

Order Repository What 0 budy-common-modules @budybot/console-kit (once); the cluster repository is granted read on the package 1 cluster repository component, chart (off by default), catalog entry, root workspace, both lockfiles, changeset 2 vault-gitops role and default KV policy; then write the cookie key in each environment 3 k8s-security ingress, egress, STS peer, netpol identity, ReferenceGrant, ingress gateway egress, VaultAuthGlobal allowed namespaces 4 argocd-critical-stack AppProject cluster-resource whitelist for the ClusterRole and binding 5 argocd-eks-stack OIDC-protected Ingress and HTTPRoute for the host, with group.order if a public route shares it 6 de-v2 STS redeemer policy, httpAudiences, platform client resources; the cluster app values (enabled, URLs, Vault) 7 portal config and portal the portal route for the console (add-app-to-platform-ui)

The two rows in bold in step 3 are the ones that were missed in the first build and surfaced as an unreachable console and a secret that would not sync. Check them first on the next console.

docs.title: Decisions from the first build
docs.text:
• Two lockfiles. The console is a root workspace (changeset validation requires it), so CI installs from the root lockfile and root .npmrc; the image build installs from the component's own lockfile. Regenerate both together.
  • The portal is a dependency, not a given. The first portal only launched Nexus-target routes and Auth Manager; a plain web app needed a systemSession route block. platform-ui-1 carries that block over, so a console is added as a route (see add-app-to-platform-ui).
  • Hand-written chart. charts/console-1 does not use a library chart. Extract a shared platform-console chart when a second console exists, so the shared part is taken from two real charts instead of guessed from one; the part that differs per cluster is the ClusterRole rules.
  • Comments and labels. Comments carry what a maintainer needs (why, or what to change alongside). Descriptions do not call a console "read-only": the first phase only lists, and writes will come later through the operator's CRDs.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Each cluster with a console has a console page next to its service document, for example the nainai console. The procedure is in the wiki skill scaffold-platform-console.

docs.title: Platform UI
docs.text:
Document Platform UI reference Component platform-ui-1 in frontend-cluster-1 (source: apps/platform-ui) Status Phase 1 (moved from platform-base-ui, same behavior). Phase 2 (simplify and refactor) is not started. Audience Platform engineers adding an internal UI, and on-call operators Last Updated October 2026

The platform UI (the portal) is the one entry point to the platform's internal web UIs. A person signs in once, picks an app and a scope, and the portal obtains the right STS session and hands them over to that app. It is for platform staff only; no tenant or customer reaches it. To add an app, follow the skill add-app-to-platform-ui.

Today there is one user

At the time of the move, the author is the only user. That is why the move from platform-base-ui was a hard cutover with no period where both portals ran, and why all environments were enabled together. Do not read this as a pattern for a portal with users.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Signs the person in through the shared Dex (Google). Dex returns the person's Google groups.
  2. Decides what they can see from those groups: which apps are listed, and the highest session boundary they may ask for.
  3. Exchanges identity for a session. It trades the Dex ID token at the STS for an actor token, then requests a target-bound session (system or tenant scope, with a boundary) through a pushed authorization request, and hands the result to the app.

It stores nothing: there is no database and no user list. State is a sealed cookie and the STS and OpenFGA are the sources of truth.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Browser ──► ALB (no OIDC on this host) ──► ui-gateway-1 ──► platform-ui-1 (frontend namespace)
   │                                                             │  in-cluster, mTLS
   │ 1. /login                                                   ├──► Dex :5556          token + signing keys
   └────────────────► Dex (public, Google)                       ├──► sts-service :8080  exchange, PAR, handoff, queries
                                                                 └──► authz-control-plane-1 :8080   Auth Manager proxy
Launch: portal ──► STS (actor token, PAR) ──► STS authorize ──► portal /oauth/callback ──► STS handoff ──► app /auth/callback?handoff=…
Piece Where App, image, chart, CI frontend-cluster-1, apps/platform-ui, charts/platform-ui-1, catalog entry @budy/platform-ui Values (access groups, apps, hostnames) de-v2 gitops, charts/apps/frontend-cluster-1/values/{base,env/*} (platform-ui-1:) Host and gateway argocd-eks-stack: ALB ingress for the portal host on ui-gateway-1; Dex client platform-ui-1 in dex-1 STS side auth-service-1 (Dex subject-token verifier); de-v2 auth-cluster-1 values (oidcBroker, externalAudiences, handoff allow-lists, client resources) Network policy and secrets sync k8s-security (frontend namespace policies, Dex namespace ingress, VSO objects) Vault vault-management-1, de-v2-services stack, platform_ui_1 role; Dex client secret path under the Dex namespace

docs.title: Sign-in and access
docs.text:
• Sign-in: authorization code with PKCE against https://dex.<env>.orangebox.ai, scopes openid email profile groups federated:id. The last one is required: Dex only adds federated_claims (the connector and the Google user ID) to the ID token when it is requested, and without it the portal refuses the sign-in as not from the Google connector. The portal verifies the ID token (RS256 signature from Dex's keys, issuer, one audience, expiry, nonce, verified email, Google connector) and keeps it in a sealed, host-only session cookie (__Host-platform-session, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax). The browser's JavaScript never receives the token. The session lasts as long as the ID token (one hour), at most eight; a new sign-in is silent while the Google session lives.
  • Identity: the person is the Google user ID (federated_claims.user_id), not Dex's own sub. The STS reports it as google:<id>, the same identity the person had behind the old ALB gate, so OpenFGA relationships did not change.
  • Access is by Google group. The same three groups used by Grafana, Argo CD and pgAdmin:
Group Highest session boundary Typical apps platform-dev-admin@orangebox.ai admin everything, including Auth Manager platform-dev-editor@orangebox.ai editor consoles and Context platform-dev-viewer@orangebox.ai viewer read-only apps

A person in none of the listed groups sees "Access unavailable". access.groups in the values lists the groups and their boundary caps. A group not listed there grants nothing, even if Dex returns it.

  • The cap is an extra layer. The STS and OpenFGA still decide what a session may do. The portal refuses a launch whose boundary exceeds the cap before it calls the STS.

docs.title: The app catalog (route contract)
docs.text:
Each launchable app is a route in the values. What an app is (name, target, which groups see it) is in routeDefaults, keyed by route id and set once in base. Where it lives in this environment (URLs) is in routes in env/*. The chart merges them (environment wins).

Field Meaning id Route id. It is also the STS handoff app_id, so it must match the handoff redeemer policy. name, description Shown in the picker. redirectUrl The app's callback (https://…/auth/callback) that receives ?handoff=<code>. HTTPS only. routeGroups Google groups that see this app. No groups means the app is hidden. nexusTarget temporalNexusEndpoint and nexusService: a Nexus service. The session audience is urn:budy:nexus:<endpoint>:<service>. Tenant or platform scope. systemSession A plain web app launched in system scope. resource must equal the origin of redirectUrl; sessionBoundaries (default editor, admin) are the boundaries it accepts. resource: authz-manager-1 The Auth Manager, served by the portal itself at /authz.

A route with neither nexusTarget nor systemSession (nor the Auth Manager resource) cannot be launched. A malformed systemSession is ignored on purpose, which leaves the route unlaunchable rather than launchable with wrong values.

docs.title: Where each decision lives
docs.text:
Question Answer lives in Who may use the portal, and how high Google group membership, and access.groups in the values Which apps appear routeDefaults and routes, filtered by routeGroups What a launched session may do STS policy and OpenFGA, per the claims contract (auth-service-1, docs/v2-token-claims-contract.md) Which apps may receive a handoff STS handoffRedeemerPolicies and allowedRedeemerCallerSubs

The catalog is GitOps-controlled today (reviewed, versioned, one place). Visibility already follows groups, which are controlled outside Git. Moving more of it to a model-controlled registry is a phase 2 question (below).

docs.title: Operating it
docs.text:
• Health: GET /healthz on the pod. Logs are JSON; set logging.level to debug for OAuth stages and request ids. Debug logs never contain cookies, tokens, secrets or raw JWTs, and identify subjects by a short one-way fingerprint.
  • Secrets (Vault, synced by VSO, never in Git): the STS OAuth client file (platform-bff client) and the Dex client secret platform-ui-1. Rotating either reloads the pods (Reloader). Rotating the Dex secret signs everyone out, because the session cookie is sealed with a key derived from it.
  • A person cannot sign in: check the person is in one of the three groups; if the log has dex.login.failed with "no federated_claims", the federated:id scope was not requested; dex.login.rejected carries the error Dex sent back; check Dex logs for the group lookup (the directory service account); check /login/callback returns 502 (token verification failed: look for dex.login.failed in the portal log).
  • Launch fails with 502 or "not trusted": the STS rejected the exchange. Check that platform-ui-1 is in the OAuth client's externalAudiences and that the STS has oauth.oidcBroker set to the environment's Dex.
  • Launch redirects but the app rejects the handoff: the app's service account is missing from allowedRedeemerCallerSubs or handoffRedeemerPolicies.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Dex is public on purpose (it is the login page for every client). The portal host has no ALB OIDC gate, because the portal does its own sign-in.
  • The pod's network is closed: ingress only from ui-gateway-1; egress only to DNS, istiod, Dex, sts-service and authz-control-plane-1.
  • Redirect targets after login are restricted to local paths. Launch destinations are the configured redirectUrls only.
  • The cookie holds a one-hour token for a staff identity. Treat the portal host like any admin surface: the groups are the access control, so manage group membership as such.

docs.title: Hostnames
docs.text: The portal is the one prod host that is not <name>.prod-2.orangebox.ai: it is platform.orangebox.ai, the stable home people bookmark. Every app it launches uses the standard host, including Context at context.prod-2.orangebox.ai. Dev and stage use platform.dev-1 and platform.stage-1.

docs.title: Design system
docs.text: The pages use the Budy Internal design system, the third alongside the consumer app and e-commerce systems, for staff tools. Its tokens (design/budy-internal-design-system-1/project/tokens.json) generate tokens.css; portal.css holds the components and may use tokens only. CI checks that the generated file is current, that text pairs meet 4.5:1 in light and dark, and that no raw colour appears in the component CSS. A new internal tool should use the same system rather than add a fourth look.

docs.title: Phase 2 (not started)
docs.text:
Candidates, in rough order of value. None is decided.

  • Sign out of the Google session as well as the portal; show who is signed in and with which groups.
  • Split server.mjs (about 1,300 lines, including the page) into modules and move the picker script to a static asset.
  • Refine the look. Phase 1 already moved the pages to the Budy Internal design system (below); phase 2 is about layout and flow, not a new foundation.
  • A scope-first picker: choose system or tenant scope and a boundary first, then show only the apps that scope can use.
  • Model-controlled catalog: apps publish a small manifest, and visibility comes from OpenFGA rather than routeGroups; GitOps keeps only what must be reviewed (audience, redirect, scope type).
  • Remove the ALB allow-lists from the STS now that nothing uses the ALB assertion.

docs.text:
